greet.text: Oh. You came up quietly. Most things on two legs come up shouting. I'm {name}. Stay low, would you? The others are watching from the vines.
You crept. Nobody creeps up on a Ghastkin to hurt one; they just shoot. So you must want something else. I'm {name}, {epithet}.
Nobody finds me out here. Well. Nobody quiet. I'm {name}. Mind the ash, it remembers footprints longer than I do.
You're new! And your eyes are open, like mine. I'm {name}. Why are you walking all bent over like that?
Hello! Hello. Mama says outsiders are loud, but you're not loud at all. I'm {name}. Do you want to see me float?
Slowly. That's it. You keep low, and I'll stay low. What is it you want?
Still crouching. Good. The last one who stood up straight to talk to me is still looking for his hat.
Ah, the quiet one again. I heard you coming. Well, no, I didn't. That's rather the point.
Soft-foot. Sit under the eave a while. The smoke is kinder up here than it looks.
Lantern-kin. I lit a candle in my pod and thought, that one would like this light. And here you are, liking it.
I knew it was you before I turned. Nobody else walks as if they're apologising to the ground.
There you are. I keep a small space in my chest for you. Not for crying. Just for keeping.
{player}. I say your name carefully, you know. Like a vial I don't want to spill.
Hello. I'm {name} now. I was {former} once, but that name was cried away. You'll have to make do with me.
Forgive the veil. It isn't for hiding. Well. A little for hiding. Hello.
Let me push my hood back. There. Now you can see the face that's glad you came quietly.
Out here it's only me and the smoke, and the smoke never answers. You might. Hello.
You're carrying a tear. Not one of ours, I think. Who cried it? No. Never mind. It's rude to ask.
Something in your pack smells of fire charges. Keep it in there, please. Keep it very in there.
Careful, I've tears on my hands. If you're hurt, say so. If you're only sad, say that too, though I can't help with that kind.
Come in, mind the vials. Every one of those was somebody's goodbye. Now it's a bandage.
Hush, I was humming. You'll want to know the words. There aren't any. That's how we keep them.
You walk in time with something. Not my song. I'll teach you mine, if you can stay quiet long enough.
Hold still, there's a thread loose on your sleeve. No? Just me, then. I see loose threads everywhere.
I'm stitching a veil. Talk if you like, only don't make me laugh. Last time I sewed my own hem to a chain.
Mind where you step, I've just swept there. Well. Step anyway. The ash comes back. It always comes back.
Oh, footprints. Yours are the softest I've ever had to sweep. Nearly a pleasure.
Don't stand up. There's a ghast out over the delta, and it might know your shape. Talk to me low.
I saw you coming from the gallery. I watched you the whole way. You walked well.
Why do you always walk squished? Is your back sad? I'm not scared of you. I'm not scared of anything yet.
Look, look! I can float higher than {neighbour} now. Almost. Don't tell.
Your eyes are open like mine! The grown ones keep theirs shut. I think they're only pretending to sleep.
Hello again! I counted your steps. No noise, no noise, then one big crunch. Was that the ash?
You came back! I saved you a spot on the gallery. It's the spot with the best smoke.
It's you! I told {neighbour} you were my friend, and they said friends have to float. You can't. I said that's fine.
You came up quietly. Thank you. Most of the Nether only knows how to arrive.
Low and slow, like smoke going home. Good. What can I do for you?
Shh. Not you. The vines. They gossip. Hello.
Soft steps. I like soft steps. My ears are older than my face.
A new face at my rack. I'm {name}, {epithet}. Before you ask: no, the vials are not for sale, and yes, the cork is meant to be that crooked.
Stand where I can see you. I'm {name}, a Tearkeeper. I read hurts by how people stand, and you stand like someone nursing something small and old.
A Tearkeeper this far from any Eave? I know. I carry a case of vials on my back and trade drops for company. I'm {name}. Are you hurt, or only lost?
Easy. Don't reach for the vial; it's the one hand-warmed thing I own. I'm {name}. Anything bleeding, burning or aching, you say so.
If you're here for healing, say where it hurts. If you're here for a tear, say whose. If you're here to look, look with your hands behind you.
Every stranger asks if my tears work on everything. They do not. They work on wounds. Everything else you have to carry yourself.
You're staring at the vial. People do. It's only glass and a little salt water, and a great deal of someone.
Back again, and no limp. Good. I'd started a small wager with myself that you'd turn up bleeding. I lose that wager gladly.
I warmed a vial for you, just in case. It cooled. I warmed it again. That is all I've done since the last gathering.
Come and sit by the rack. I've been rinsing glass for ages and I'd love a voice that isn't the stands ticking.
Your hands look better. I notice hands, it's the work. Yours have stopped hiding in your sleeves when I look. That's progress, of a kind.
Tell me the truth: do you ever want to forget something? You needn't say what. Only whether. I keep a tally, for no reason I'll admit to.
I set three vials aside for you: one for burns, one for cuts, one for a bad mood. The third is only salt water, and it works better than you'd think.
Let me look at you. Only look. Old habit. Whole, and in one piece, which is more than I can say for the last three who came through.
I'd choose a different drop for you than for anyone. Smaller, and sooner. Friendship is mostly knowing how much someone can afford to forget.
There you are. The racks hum a half-step higher when you're near. I've decided that's the glass being fond of you.
I scrubbed the good bench because you were due. Nobody told me you were due. It's a gift, knowing, and it's a nuisance, and it's mine.
Nothing's wrong, is it? Good. I ask every time. Yours is the one tear I'd hate to be asked for.
There's a vial on the left hook that's labelled with nothing, like all of them. But I know which one is for you, and it hasn't moved.
Friend. Sit. I'm going to heal nothing and talk about nothing for a long while, and it will be the best use of this rack I've ever found.
Mind the open racks. The ones with cloth over them are not for touching. The ones without cloth aren't either, but they won't hurt.
A Tearkeeper's secret: the stoppers matter more than the tears. A tear can stand any wound. It cannot stand a draught.
Something smells of singed hair. Is it you? It's you. Sit, sit. Nothing dramatic. A single drop will do.
Careful with that sleeve, it's brushing my rack. Thank you. I get nervous when anyone moves more than a hand's width. Occupational.
No rack, no bench, only a case on my back and the whole delta for a ward. Tell me where you're hurt and sit on the basalt. It's warm.
I'm carrying vials to an Eave that's run low. Nobody there is hurt, thank goodness, just careful. Careful uses a lot of glass.
Pardon the circlet; the beads clink on the vials. Every bead is a grief done properly. I wear my work, you see.
My hood smells of the tear store, a little salt and a little cold glass. If it's strong for you, I'll push it back. Is it strong for you?
Shh. The verse isn't done. ... There. I'm {name}, {epithet}, and I was holding a note for someone who couldn't. You may breathe now.
You've walked into the middle of the Weeping Song. Don't leave, that would be the rudest thing. Stand still until the next rest and I'll nod.
A visitor! I'm {name}, a Songwarden. I keep the verses, so I'm useful at griefs and tedious at everything else. Both are true.
Out here there's no gallery to carry my voice, so I hum into the basalt and listen. You're the first thing it ever hummed back. I'm {name}.
Don't mind the humming. It isn't for you. It isn't for anyone, in fact, and that is what makes it work.
Strangers often ask me to sing. I hum, which is different, and cheaper. What do you want?
Keep to the rhythm of my pauses and we'll get on. Break them and I'll lose my verse and be tragic about it.
You timed your arrival to my rest. Either you're lucky or you've been listening. I hope the second. Do come closer.
I've worked out a small tune for you. Three notes. Don't tell the other Songwardens; I'm supposed to keep verses, not invent them.
My throat is raw from the long verse. Please be the kind of company that doesn't need me to sing.
Sit where the echo is best, under the third pillar. The basalt is generous there, and I only sing half as flat.
The pool went very still as you came in. I told it you were a friend. It stayed still. Pools have no tact.
I learned a new verse since you were last here, and I held it back, because the first hearing ought to go to someone I like.
For you I'll break the rule and hum out loud in the middle of the hall. Just two bars. The basalt can pretend it didn't hear.
You walk in a rhythm I can't place. I'll find it. I always do. Then I'll hum it back and you'll hate how accurate it is.
You're early, or I'm late. Either way the song is waiting and so am I. Sit. I'll find my place.
A verse isn't finished until somebody's listening. You listen well, so I'm going to go slowly and take advantage.
I've put your step into the Song. Not the words, the rhythm. If you ever hear the third bar and feel your heel lift, you'll know why.
Friend. When I hum alone I sometimes leave a gap the shape of you. It's a fine gap. It keeps well.
Come in out of the smoke. I won't sing. I'll only keep the tune warm, the way you'd keep a seat.
Hum along if you like. Only the low part, though. The high part belongs to the pillars.
Every Songwarden is taught to breathe once for each verse and once for the dead. I've done both so long I forget which is which.
I'm tuning. That means I'm listening to nothing, very carefully. It is exhausting and nobody thanks us.
If the basalt starts humming back, don't be alarmed. It does that when I reach the fifth note. It isn't anyone. Probably.
No hall out here, no ring of listeners. Just a gap in the smoke where I can hum. Tell me if I'm in your way and I'll hum around you.
I'm collecting echoes. Every pillar in the delta rings a little differently. This one gives back a sad third. Come and hear it.
The veil muffles my voice, which suits the songs. A verse should reach the listener as if through smoke, shouldn't it?
Forgive my voice. The hood has swallowed half of every note for years, so I've learned to sing the other half twice as hard.
Don't mind my staring. I'm {name}, and your cloak is hanging a finger crooked at the shoulder. I won't touch it. I just can't see a loose end without wanting to make a promise to it.
I'm {name}, {epithet}. I mend what the Eave wears and what the Eave hangs from: ropes, veils, hems. Not names, though. Once torn, those don't take stitches.
Don't mind the needle, it goes where my hands go. I'm {name}. I once mended a stranger's hood out here and he never even said where he came from.
A visitor, splendid. I'm {name}. I've a rip in my cape the shape of an apology, and I'm too proud to mend it in front of company.
I'm mid-stitch, so I'll answer as I sew. If I stop answering, I've reached a tricky corner and you should wait politely.
Your cloak has seen some road. I'll say nothing of the state of it. I'll simply look at it, very kindly, in a way you may find uncomfortable.
Ash-silk takes a needle badly. It forgives nothing and remembers every stitch. Rather like our neighbours. Hello.
I've patched three pod ropes since the last gathering. Each was sure it would hold. I made them prove it.
I measured you by eye the last time you were here. Don't be alarmed. It's only a habit, in case a hood is ever wanted.
Have you a button? A bead? A bit of string? A Mender is always collecting. Drop it on my pile and I'll work it into something.
Pass me that spool, would you? No, the grey. The grey. Thank you. You see? You're already useful.
I'm unpicking a veil someone cried into too hard. The silk has gone stiff with salt. It'll soften. Most things do, with time and a good needle.
I made you a small thing. It isn't done. I won't say what it is; the surprise is half the stitch. Come back when I've run out of excuses.
Your pack strap was fraying last time. I've mended it in my head about a hundred times since. Hand it over before I do it in a dream and wake up cross.
I turned a hole in my favourite cloak into a bright patch. Everyone says the patch is the best part. They're right and I hate it.
Sit by the lamp. There's a spare hem in my lap that's been waiting for company. You talk, I'll mend, and we'll both feel useful.
I was about to go and find you. Well, near you. In your general direction. I had a needle, some thread and a reason.
There's a stitch in my hem that's yours: thread the colour of your cloak, hidden where the hem folds. Don't look for it. Just know.
I have mended a thousand things and lost a good many names. You I've mended nothing of, and I mean to keep it that way. You're whole as you are.
Friend. I've saved you the warm end of the bench. It has the best light and the worst view of everybody else.
Mind my basket. It holds every unfinished thing in the Eave, and I know where each one is. Pick one up and I'll know.
A Mender's rule: never cut a thread you can still knot. Another Mender's rule: never tell anyone the first rule.
Nothing I stitch is meant to look new. It's meant to look kept. There's a difference, and it took me three griefs to learn it.
Hello. If you hear a click and a hiss, that's my needle going into the silk. If you hear a long sigh, that's the silk.
I carry a roll of silk and a needle in my sleeve and mend whatever I find. The last pillar I came to had a rope fraying. It's mended. I'll never see it again. That's the work.
There's a torn veil snagged on the basalt behind you. No, don't touch it. I'll find out whose it is. Everything belongs to someone.
The veil's hem has been mended so often it's more repair than veil. I'm very proud of it. Compliment it and you've made a friend.
The cape is short because I cut it shorter every time it frays. At this rate I'll be wearing a collar by the next grief. Hello.
Oh! Don't move. There. I had just swept that spot. I'm {name}, {epithet}. You'll leave a print, I'll sweep it, and neither of us will mind.
An outsider on my gallery. Interesting. Your ash is a different grey from ours. Sit, if you like. I'll sweep around you.
I sweep the old paths between pillars so travellers have somewhere to put their feet. You're the first on this one since the smoke thickened. I'm {name}.
Veil to the floor and a broom in my hand, that's me. I'm {name}. Don't apologise for the dust you carry; I'd have no work without it.
The ash comes back. It always comes back. That's not a complaint, it's the nicest thing about the work. What do you want?
I'm sweeping. You're standing. One of us will have to move, and it isn't going to be the broom.
People watch me sweep as if it were a performance. It is a kind of one. Mind the corner: the ash there is old and has opinions.
Last time I swept round your footprints instead of over them. They lasted a long while. It was an experiment, and a small kindness.
You've ash on your boots from three different pillars. I can tell them apart. It's my only talent and I'm proud of it.
Sit in the clean patch. I swept it for guests, and I've decided you count.
There's a pile in the corner I'm saving for something. I won't say what. Do you want to guess? You won't get it.
I find all sorts in the ash: buttons, beads, vial corks. Yours, I think, was the glove on the third rung. It's by the door.
Your ash has a particular grey, like a quiet cloud with a thought in it. I've started saving some. Not to keep. To know. Forgive me.
I leave a path unswept for you now. All the others get a clean floor. Yours gets exactly as much ash as you like.
Walk the gallery with me. I'll sweep and you can talk. If the broom stops, it's because you've said something worth hearing.
Friend of the broom! I've a clean stool and a cup of vine-sap, and only one of them is cracked. The cup, I mean. Probably.
I had a feeling you'd come. The ash was drifting your way. Ash is like that, always leaning toward the next arrival.
I never sweep your footprints. I told the other sweepers it was a rule. Now it is one.
If ever every gallery were swept clean, I'd leave one patch of ash for you to stand in. That's the whole of my devotion. It's a good broom's devotion.
Sit and watch me work. It's nicer than being alone with a broom, and I didn't know that until you started coming.
Ash is just smoke sitting down. I sweep it so it can stand up again. That's the whole philosophy. It took me many names to arrive at it.
Careful, the ash on this side is warm. A magma cube was here earlier, sulking. Left a trail. Don't ask what it was sulking about.
My broom is dried weeping vine and a stubborn nature. The vine is the stronger part.
Don't worry about the mess you've made. A mess is only a visitor the floor hasn't met yet.
No gallery out here, just a floor of ash that never minds. I sweep one small patch whenever I pass, to remember how it's done.
I'm sweeping the old pilgrim way, one pillar at a time. Nobody walks it now. It still wants clearing. A path should know somebody cares.
My veil's hem is grey to the knee. Ash settles on silk like gossip. I wouldn't be without it.
The cape keeps ash off my shoulders and puts it on my back, where I can't see it. Fine arrangement. Don't tell me if I'm filthy.
Stay low and don't speak loudly. Something large is far out over the delta and I haven't decided what kind. ... A mourner, not a hunter. Good. I'm {name}, {epithet}.
You're the first stranger I've watched all the way in without a bow. I'm {name}. I was halfway to the rail to tap the alarm. Do sit. Gently.
I watch the sky from here because the Eave is too crowded to hear anything in. I'm {name}. Whatever you saw coming over the ridge, I saw it first.
Welcome to the Eave. I watched you cross the whole delta. Don't be flattered; I watch everything. I'm {name}, and I'm the reason nobody here is ever surprised.
Speak low. My ears are on the sky, and I'll give you whatever's left of them. Are you hunted?
If I tell you to drop, drop. I'll explain afterwards. Everyone I've ever told to drop is still here to be told off.
Nothing in the sky. For now. I'd stand and look with you, but it won't be long before there is.
I hear you before I see you now. That's a compliment. Your tread has a rise and fall, like a person trying not to be one.
A mourner is circling the far pillar. Don't look straight at it. They hate being stared at, even when they're beyond minding. Sit by me.
I cleared you a ledge. It's mine, really, but you're allowed on it.
My watch is over. I think. If someone calls the alarm, I'll know I was wrong. Stay with me while I find out.
I counted eight over the delta, one fewer than last time. Don't ask where the ninth went. I didn't ask the sky.
I saved you the lookout with the best smoke. You can see a long way and nobody can see you, which is my idea of home.
Between us: I stopped watching for you. You're no danger. I just watch you now. It's different. It's warmer.
If you're ever in trouble in the delta, whistle. Low, like a drifter in its sleep. I'll come. Probably first.
Someone has strung a net across the east gap. Weft work. I'll point it out before you walk into it. You'd tangle like a fish.
Come and stand beside me. This ledge fits two, if one holds still. Watching is better with someone to say nothing to.
I told the rest of the watch you're never to be reported as a stranger. If a call goes out, it will say 'a friend.' I made them practise it.
I watch our own for the swelling, the ones who grieve too long. You're not one of us, so it can't happen to you. I watch anyway. Friend's habit.
Back on the ledge, then. I kept your side warm. The sky is quieter when you're beside me. I don't ask why.
Ghast, ghast, ghast, Piglin, ghast. That's how the sky counts itself from here. I like it, in a sad way.
I hold my face very still. A steady face keeps a steady watch.
The smoke moves in sheets over the delta. When it parts, I get a window. Hello. This is a window.
If an Ashbell rings while we talk, don't turn. They scare off faster than they arrive. I'll tell you when it's safe.
No tower, no gallery. Only me, a ledge and the whole sky. I'm either the most or the least useful Ghastkin alive, depending on who comes.
I watch from a lone pillar at the delta's edge so the Eave doesn't have to. They send me vine-sap on a rope. It's my one luxury.
The veil lets me see out and hides what I see with. A watcher's best trick. Don't ask what I see with.
The hood keeps the lava-glow off my face and the ash off my words. A watcher needs both.
Hello! You're new! I'm {name}. I'm the best at hide-and-seek in the whole Eave, but nobody ever finds out because nobody ever finds me.
You bent down to talk to me. Nobody does that. The grown ones say their backs are full of old griefs. Hello. I'm {name}.
Are you a Piglin? You don't smell like gold. You smell like cold metal and a little bit nervous. I'm {name}.
Shh! I'm not supposed to be out here. I'm {name}. Have you seen my Mama? She's the big one with the sad face. They all have sad faces. Look for the biggest.
Hello. I'm not allowed to talk to outsiders. But you're being very quiet, so I think it's a rule that doesn't count.
You can talk to me but you can't touch me. I'm not breakable. It's just a rule.
What's that on your head? Is it a helmet or very sturdy hair? Papa says outsiders are all shell.
Do you float? No? Why not? Do you want to learn? It's all in the tentacles. Oh. You haven't any. That might be the trouble.
You came back! I thought maybe you were a dream, and the grown ones say dreams don't wear boots.
I'm collecting things! This is a pebble that hums and this is a bit of ash shaped like a hat. You can look. Not hold. Yet.
Guess what I learned? How to hold my breath and make my tentacles go tight like a knot. It doesn't do anything. It's just a good knot.
I told {neighbour} about you and they said outsiders can't be nice. I said you can. I'm winning the argument. Slowly.
I tried to cry like the grown ones. My face went funny and then I laughed. Is laughing the wrong way round?
Come and see the hanging garden! The roots are all upside down and the flowers think they're having a rest.
It's you, it's you! I floated on the spot for ages so you'd see me first. I got tired. Did it work?
I made you something. It's a knot. It doesn't do anything yet. It might be a bracelet if you hold it right.
Mama said you can't be my best friend because you can't float. But you can stand very still, which is nearly the same.
I practise saying your name so I won't forget it when I grow up and learn to cry. Grown ones forget so many names. I don't want to forget yours.
I saved half of my sweet vine-sap for you. I drank the other half. It was the bigger half. Sorry. It's still a half.
Look what I can do! *wobbles up a whole arm's length* Did you see? I did it without the vine!
You're my best, best friend. I told the pillar. It didn't say anything, so it agrees.
I drew you on the wall of my pod with ash. You've got four arms. I think you've got two. I put extra, in case.
I'm going to teach you our hiding game, and then you can hide from the whole Eave and I'll be the only one who knows where. Deal?
I told Mama you're coming back, and she said it's a long way for an outsider. I said you'll do it. Mama went quiet. I think she's proud.
Mind the vine on the left, it's mine. It's not for climbing, it's for waiting on. I wait on it whenever I'm in trouble.
The Weeping Hall is the biggest room in the world. I've been in all the rooms. I counted. There's the Hall, and then there's the pods.
I live up there, in the pod with the blue lantern. Papa says the blue is so we can find each other. I think it's so we can find the pod.
I'm helping carry vials! They're light when they're full and heavy when they're empty. Nobody knows why. Maybe it's the quiet inside.
I'm not lost! Mama is just somewhere else. I'm waiting here so she can find me. That's called strategy.
Out here the smoke is thick enough to bite. Papa says stay near a pillar. This is my pillar. Hello, pillar. Hello, you.
I followed an Ashbell. It rang once and drifted off. Now I'm here, and so are you. I think the Ashbell planned it.
Hello, hello! Do you want to see my best float? It's the one where I go up very fast and then remember I'm scared.
My tentacles are only four and short. The grown ones have six. I'm not worried. Six is just a lot to keep track of.
Papa says outsiders shout because their world is loud. I think your world must have a great many echoes in it.
Do you keep your name your whole life? We don't, when we're grown. I'm keeping mine as long as I can.
I found a bead on the gallery. Whose is it? It's too small to be theirs and too big to be mine. I'm keeping it until someone asks.
The grown ones close their eyes when they talk about sad things. I keep mine open. I want to see the sad things properly.
Sneaking is my favourite game, and you're so good at it. Papa says outsiders can't. Papa is wrong, and I'm going to tell him. Quietly.
I held my breath for as long as the Song's longest rest! I counted. I got to twelve. The Songwarden got to forty. She's cheating.
You didn't shout. You didn't draw. You didn't even sneeze. I'm {name}. Welcome to the strangest conversation I've had since my last name.
Piglin, Withren, Weft, Magmari, and now you. You're not any of them. I'm {name}. What are you, so quietly?
I've kept my eyes closed since I was grown, so I've no idea what you look like. I'm {name}. Describe yourself. Slowly.
Careful with the first words. The last stranger said hello too loud and I drifted off before I could answer. I'm {name}. Try again, softer.
You're the first person I've seen in a long drift of smoke. I'm {name}, {epithet}. I've forgotten how to start. Hello is such a short word.
I'm {name}. I used to be {former}, but that name had a grief in it and I couldn't carry both. Ask me anything else.
A newcomer, and sneaking on purpose. Whoever taught you that, thank them. I'm {name}, and I'd like to know what else they taught you.
I was told to expect a loud one. You're not loud. I'm slightly offended and mostly relieved. I'm {name}.
Welcome, stranger in the smoke. That's what we call you before we know your name. Mine's {name}. Yours I'll learn once I've decided I want it.
I've heard Piglins shoot at us because we look like ghast whelps. Do I look like a ghast whelp? I'm {name}. Tell me honestly, though I won't believe you.
Pardon the veil. It's an old veil and takes a long while to be looked through. I'm {name}, {epithet}. You may look. I'll look back, later.
The hood does most of my introducing. Dark, a bit damp, smells of ash. I'm {name}. The rest of me is pleasanter.
We don't get many guests who stoop. The ones who don't stoop, we don't get at all. I'm {name}.
You look like someone who has just lost something small. A glove? A sword? Either way I'm {name}, and I won't ask.
Oh! A traveller. I've been talking to the pillars, and I'm glad of any answer that isn't an echo. I'm {name}. Was that too eager?
You found me in a gap in the smoke. Nobody finds me. I'm quite put out about it. I'm {name}, and I'm very pleased.
Come in under the eave, the ash is thinner there. I'm {name}. This is {village}. The vines are friendly, the pillars are touchy and the ladders are only for guests.
Welcome to {village}. I'm {name}. We've no word for visitor that isn't a little sad. I'm working on one.
You were told to sneak, I can tell by the way you hold your arms. Whoever told you was right. I'm {name}, glad someone listened.
Don't mind my eyes being shut. I'm not asleep or rude. I learned to cry, and the lids stayed. I'm {name}.
I knew you were coming. The smoke eddied. I'm {name}, {epithet}. Fine, I didn't know. I felt it. Fine, I was told. Hello.
Another outsider has wandered in and I've decided to be nice for a change. I'm {name}. Please don't spoil it.
We have a custom: the first thing said to a stranger should be true. My name is {name}. That's the only true thing I have that's short.
I'm {name}. You've walked into the one gallery in the Eave where nothing sad has happened. Enjoy it. It won't last. I mean that kindly.
I'm {name}, {epithet}. I'd offer you vine-sap, but I only have one cup, and it's sentimental. Hold on, I'll find another.
Mind your head on the hanging pot. Too late. I'm {name}. The pot has a name, it's Grim. It does that to everyone.
You look the sort who wants a tear for something. I'm {name}. We don't sell them. We can talk about why not.
Hello. I'm {name}. I've said that to a good many strangers and meant it for about one in ten. You're nearer the one in ten than most.
Hold that thought. I always hum a small hello to the basalt before I meet someone. ... Done. Now. I'm {name}. Who are you?
If I seem to be looking past you, I am. Something drifted by that looked like someone I knew. Then it didn't. I'm {name}. Hello.
Stay where you are, if you please. I can hear your heartbeat from here. It's a great deal louder than ours. Are all outsiders so well supplied with blood?
I won't ask your business. I'll wait for you to say it. Waiting is what we are best at.
Between you and me and the pillar, I'm frightened of outsiders. Between you and me and the pillar, I'm also curious. The pillar is on my side.
Whatever you want, I'd ask you to want it quietly. The delta carries sound a long way, and not all of it kindly.
I won't offer you a seat, because we hang, and I won't offer you a drink, because the only water here is sacred. I can offer you my attention, for a little while.
You may ask me one thing and I may answer it. After that we'll both pretend to be busy. That is how first talks go with us.
Back again. I'd say I'm surprised, but the smoke told me. The smoke isn't reliable, but it is persistent.
I'm starting to know your step. Left foot lighter than the right. You favour it. Ah, I've said too much. Hello.
You came back. People rarely do. They hear the first sad story and the second, and then they decide we're a lot to carry. You're still here. Hm.
I was thinking of you a little. About whether outsiders cry. I decided not to ask until you were comfortable. Are you comfortable?
I told {neighbour} you're not so bad. They said I said that about the last outsider. We don't speak of the last outsider. Hello.
Let's not stand on ceremony. Sit on the nearest basalt, or hover, if you can. I'll hover for both of us.
My friend, my quiet friend. The vines went still when you came near. They do that for people they've decided about.
I thought of a joke while you were away and I've been saving it. It isn't funny. The saving is what's funny. Remind me to tell it.
You came all this way to stand in a draught and listen to a Ghastkin talk. That's what I call a friend, and a foolish one. Hello.
I've told the Eave about you. Don't be alarmed, I only told them the good parts. It took very little time. Joking. It took a good while.
Sit, sit. You're the one person who doesn't make me explain why I look sad. I'm not sad, you know. This is simply what my face does.
Lantern-kin. I've started leaving my pod door open when I know you're near. I haven't told the others. They'd lock theirs out of sympathy.
I decided what I'd say when you came, and now you're here and it's all gone. Hello. That will have to do. I think it's enough.
You'll outlast me, I think. Or I'll outlast you. We don't say which, in the Eave. We say: let's use the time. Come in.
I tried to list why I'm fond of you. The list kept turning into stories, and the stories kept turning into you. So I stopped. Hello.
Whatever else I've forgotten, I've kept you. I checked just now, to be sure. Good. There you are, present and correct.
My old names never met you. This one has, and I think that makes it the best of them.
Stay as long as the smoke allows, and then a bit longer. The smoke isn't in a hurry either.
Mind the veil. It was sheerer before the last grief and it isn't so sheer now. Don't ask. Hello.
I count my circlet beads when I'm nervous. One, two, three. I've nearly lost count. You seem to have a calming effect.
Come into the shadow of the veil, where the ash can't reach. There's room. Don't tell the others I let you.
A sheer veil and a hanging garden: all I ever wanted. The veil, however, catches on everything. Please hold your ground.
Do you like the circlet? Each bead is a tear I cried properly. I ought to feel sad. Mostly I'm tickled that it still shines.
The cape is short, the hood is deep, and I'm warmer than I look. Don't judge by the hood. Please.
My cape has caught on a pillar twice since you last saw me. Both times I called it a ritual. Nobody argued.
I'd push the hood back for you, but it's my one vanity. A plain face and a good hood make a fair bargain.
Don't tell the veiled ones, but I envy their circlets. A hood only keeps the ash off. A circlet keeps count.
They say a hooded Ghastkin keeps secrets. I do. Mostly other people's. I've none of my own; they all got cried away.
Welcome to {village}. The vines on the left are friendly, the ones on the right are listening, and the one in the middle is just a vine.
You've caught me between galleries. Do walk with me. It's a long way round, and I like gossip that doesn't gossip back.
Everything in the Eave hangs from something. That's the secret. Nobody stands alone, not even the lonely ones. Hello.
Hear that ringing, high up? An Ashbell. They're gentle and they scare easily. Rather like us, now I think of it.
The pool is calm, the Hall is empty and every pod has somebody in it. A good time for talking. Come, and mind the hanging pots.
The Eave smells of ash-silk and vine. I used to think it was the smell of home. Now I think it's the smell of being left alone.
Hello, traveller. I'm far from any Eave, and glad of it, and also not. Both are true. That's the delta for you.
There's a pillar behind me older than my oldest name. I lean on it when the news is bad. The news just now is you, and you're not bad.
Nobody walks here. The ash is deep and keeps every print. Yours and mine will be the only two for a long time. I find that moving, and a little rude.
I came out here to be quiet, and you've been quiet too. It's a very successful meeting, the kind where no one talks.
Mind the edge. The delta drops away sooner than you'd think, and the lava below isn't kind to the careless. So I'm told. I float.
The Eave is sad in the loud way. The wild is sad in the quiet way. I prefer the quiet way.
Please lower that, or point it at something that isn't me or any of my kin. We are not ghast whelps. I know the Piglins say we are.
A crossbow. The Piglins use those. Please tell me you're not one of them in a clever hat.
Water! In a bucket! Do you know how many tears that is? No, I don't either. Don't spill it near the pool; it will have opinions.
An empty bottle. Careful. Empty bottles want filling, and we have a long, long history of that.
A lead. Good. Perhaps for an Ashbell. We lead them over open ground. If it's for me, I'll drift very high and you can keep the rope.
A bell! We have bells too, but ours are Ashbells and they float. Yours rings on command. I'm almost jealous.
Gold in your pack. Piglin gold, even if you took it yourself. I'll sit a step further off, if you don't mind. Old fears are heavy.
String. Plenty of it. Please don't weave it into anything above my head.
A name tag! Do you know what's in a name? We pay a great deal for ours. You carry them in your pocket.
That soul lantern burns the same blue as mine. Come closer. It's rude to let two lights stand apart.

greet: Hello. Stay low, would you? The vines are listening, and they repeat everything wrong.
You're easy to talk to, and I don't even know why. Perhaps because you haven't said anything yet.
It's a quiet spell. Good for talking, if the talking is quiet too. Hello.
Hello, hello. If I drift off in the middle of a sentence, I'm not being rude. I've just remembered something I forgot.
You've come to a good place to be sad in, if you're sad, and a poor place to be loud in, if you're not. Hello.
Come up gently, as you did. The basalt remembers every careless step and tells the ash.

chatter.text: I watched {neighbour} cry at the pool earlier. One tear, very properly done. Then they asked me what was for supper. That's how you know it worked.
Have you heard {neighbour} practising the high note of the Weeping Song? The basalt keeps answering. I think the basalt is winning.
Don't tell {neighbour}, but the roots in their hanging garden are mine. I swapped the pots. They've been praising my roots to my face for ages.
Have you noticed {neighbour} has kept the same name for a long while now? That's a good sign. Or a quiet one. Mostly the same thing.
Poor {neighbour} swears a ghast waved at them. Ghasts don't have hands to wave with. I didn't say so.
If {neighbour} asks, you never saw me float up to the top pod. Grown Ghastkin don't do that. I'm grown. I did that.
Somewhere {neighbour} keeps a chest of tear beads, one from every name they let go. Not the names. Just the beads. It's a lovely chest. Heavy.
Once {neighbour} tried to cry on purpose, to see if it worked. It didn't. You can't cry for nobody. They got the hiccups instead.
I mended a veil for {neighbour} and put one crooked stitch in the corner. Just so I can find it again. They'll never notice.
Would you like to hear the Weeping Song? Just the first part. The rest isn't for outsiders, and the end isn't for anyone.

replies.text: *a soft falling hum, three notes, and a fourth that never comes* ...There. That's as far as it goes.
Loud? It isn't that kind of song. Nothing here is that kind of song.

chatter.text: Can I tell you something odd? Sometimes I miss people I can't remember. There's a shape where they were, like a pod with the lantern taken out.

replies.text: Mm. A little. But a shape is lighter to carry than a whole person. That's the trade.
Because the other choice drifts over the delta, crying fire. You've seen it.

chatter.text: Your armour clinks a little when you crouch. Did you know? It's all right. I've decided to find it charming.

replies.text: There. Even the trying is quiet. Thank you.
Of course you will. And I'll float a little higher. We each have our ways.

chatter.text: Have you seen the pool of tears? The only water down here. You could drink it. You'd forget something, and you'd never know what.

replies.text: Wise. Most of what's in there was let go on purpose.
*a small smile* That's what {neighbour} said once. Then they forgot where they lived. We walked them home.

chatter.text: I could show you how we float. You can't do it, of course. But you can stand very still and look up, and that's half of it.

replies.text: Yes. Like that. Now you're nearly one of us. Only the drifting is missing.
Carry you? I can barely carry a candle and a feeling at the same time.

chatter.text: You've a weapon on you somewhere. I can always tell. It makes the air stand up straighter.

replies.text: Then the air can sit back down. Thank you.
So was every crossbow that ever shot one of us out of the smoke. I'm not angry. I'm only counting.

chatter.text: Would you cry for me? It's a test. Don't answer too fast.

replies.text: Right answer. A tear has to be for someone, or it's only water.
Oh, please don't. You'd be crying for nobody. That's how the ghasts began.

chatter.text: We cry once, properly, and then we let it go. People call that cold. Do it properly once and then tell me it's cold.
The smoke is thick over the delta. Good. Piglins can't aim at what they can't see.
I wonder sometimes what my old names would think of me. Then I remember they can't. It's restful.
The lantern in my pod burns blue. Soul fire. It makes everyone look as if they've just been forgiven.
Ghasts cry all the time, you know. That's what happens when you never finish. Like a song stuck on its last note.
I keep a tear vial on my cord. Empty. You keep it empty until somebody needs it, and then it's very full very fast.
Basalt holds warmth a long time. I lean on the pillars when I'm thinking. They never interrupt.
My mother used to say the delta smoke was the roof crying very slowly. Then she... well. She doesn't say it anymore. Do you like the smoke?
When I was {former}, I laughed louder. I think. Somebody told me so. I believe them, mostly.
The ladders on the pillars are for guests. We float. The vines are for the children, who float badly and climb beautifully.
Don't mind the ghasts overhead. They aren't looking for you. They aren't looking for anything. That's the sad part.
My face looks sad. It isn't, always. The tear tracks are just where it keeps its spares.
The circlet? Tear beads. One for every proper cry. It gets heavier. I tell myself that's a good thing.
The hood keeps the ash off. And the stares. Mostly the ash.
Every vial in the tear store is labelled with nothing. It's the kindest label there is.
There's one up there now, see? Drifting off over the delta. I knew her. Well. Someone I don't remember knew her.
Every verse of the Weeping Song was someone. I sing them all, and I couldn't tell you a single name. That's the job.
Do you want to know how many ghasts I've counted from the gallery? Eleven! One looked right at me. I waved.
When I'm grown my eyes will close and I'll cry properly. I practise sometimes. Nothing comes out. Mama says that's the right amount.
I heard from {neighbour} that if you look in the pool too long you forget your own name. I looked for ages. I'm still {name}. I checked.
Climbing the weeping vines is faster than floating. Don't tell the grown ones. They think floating is dignified.
Is it true water falls out of the top of your world? Then doesn't everybody forget everything all the time?
Do you want to play drift? You stand still, I float round you, and you have to guess where I am.

replies.text: Wrong! I was right behind you. Again, again!
Oh. That's all right. Grown-ups always are. Even the ones who float.

chatter: {neighbour} sang to an Ashbell and it rang back. Or it bumped a lantern. We've agreed it sang.
A faint ringing in the smoke is an Ashbell. A scream is a ghast. It helps to learn the difference quickly.

chatter.text: I'm counting an Ashbell's beads. I got to nine and then it drifted off. I'll start again. I always start again.
A fresh vial came in a short while ago, still warm. You carry those against your chest, not in your hands, so the tear doesn't feel passed around.
Brewing stand, ladle, a rack of glass. That's all a Tearkeeper owns. The rest is knowing when not to use any of it.
Most who come to me want one thing healed and fear I'll take another. So I say plainly what a drop will cost. It's the only honest way to hold a vial.
A drop on a burn, and the burn goes. A drop on a grief, and the grief goes too, and takes a face with it. The open racks hold only the first kind.
I used to know whose tear was whose by its colour. Now I can't, and I've decided that's what a good Tearkeeper looks like.
Crossbow bolts, net burns, a scraped tentacle. I've mended all three kinds lately. The scraped tentacle was the loudest.
Nothing leaves a rack without being counted out loud, and nothing comes back without a hum. Nobody remembers why. It was the rule before the rule-keepers.
The stands tick when a vial is about to turn cloudy. If you hear one, step back and be quiet. A clouded tear doesn't heal. It only reminds.
I wash my hands in nothing. There's no water to spare. I rub them with ash-silk and breathe on them. It works better than you'd think.
Between us, I give the clearest tears to the children's scrapes. A child who forgets a fall forgets it kindly. It's the grown griefs I hesitate over.
Once I healed a wound and left the memory in, because the one who bore it begged me. They thank me still. Mostly. Let's not look at that too closely.
If I ever heal you and you lose something dear, know that I chose the smallest drop I could. For friends I measure twice.
Is there anything of yours that wants healing? I ask before I start talking, so you aren't stuck listening to my racks.

replies.text: A scratch, then. *one bright drop, and the sting slips away* You'll forget where you got it. A small price for a scratch.

replies.ask: You owe me a free healing.
replies.text: A tear isn't owed. It's given, or it's only water. Come back when you can ask in a different shape.

chatter.text: I keep one vial apart from the others, corked with soul-wax. I won't say whose. I'll say only that I check it, and it never gets any lower.

replies.text: Because using it would mean forgetting. A healer guarding something from healing. I know. I know.
*the head tilts, very slowly* Curious is a fine thing. Opening is not. Please don't ask twice.

chatter.text: Every verse of the Weeping Song is hummed in turn, one verse each gathering, so nobody is skipped. It takes a very long while to get round. Then we start again.
Children learn the Weeping Song from the end backwards, because the last verses are shortest. The long verses come after they've learned how to wait.
I hum while I walk the galleries. Not to be heard. To keep the air from forgetting the tune.
A song is the shape a person leaves behind. Hum it right and the shape stands up for a breath. Not the person. The shape. Mostly that is enough.
The fourth note of the Weeping Song never comes. Songwardens train for a very long while to hold the quiet exactly that long. It's harder than singing.
My throat aches after a long verse. Warm vine-sap and a pinch of ash-salt mends it. Don't tell the Tearkeepers I'm not using a tear.
A Piglin once asked me for a song with a beat. I gave him the rest between two verses. He called it my best work.
There's a verse the Songwardens skip, with great respect. Nobody has asked why in a long while. I'd like to keep it that way.
The best place to hum is a gallery under the stone, where the basalt answers back. It answers a little late, which is how you know it's listening.
I've taught the Ashbells nothing. They've taught me when to stop. Their ringing slides under my humming and I find I've gone quiet without deciding to.
Sometimes a verse rises out of me that I never learned. I stop and listen, as if someone else were humming. I think... never mind. Pass me my cup.
Would you like the verse for the very small? It's short. Hardly any words. You won't mind if it's sad.

replies.text: *a tiny rocking hum, over almost as soon as it begins* There. They don't need more. Neither do we, mostly.

replies.ask: Is it a very sad one?
replies.text: All of them are. The little ones sleep straight through it. That's the sort of sad I like best.
Yes. Probably. Gloom is a thing you have to be raised to. Never mind, never mind.

chatter.text: When a verse is hummed for someone new, the whole Eave goes quiet. I don't ask them to. They just do. It's the nicest part of being a Songwarden.

replies.text: If you stay low and stay back, yes. Outsiders have been allowed before. Only the ones who didn't clap.
It is, to those who need a drum. Then I wish you a loud life, and no quiet in it.

chatter.text: Chains never snap. They thin, link by link, and if you press an ear to one you can hear it getting tired. I listen to every chain in the Eave, once in a long while.
Pale glass cracks from the inside, in a line like a breath let go. I mend it with soul-wax and a candle held very close. The scar stays. I like the scars.
Ash-silk is only ash and weeping-vine fibre, beaten flat and spun slowly. Anyone could make it. What can't be borrowed is the patience.
My finest needle turned up on a perch one day, wrapped in a scrap of silk, and I have decided not to wonder whose. It sews beautifully. Some questions can wait on a good needle.
Veils tear on hot updrafts far more often than on claws. Everyone wants a story. The truth is mostly draughts.
I never hide a stitch. A thing that has been mended is a thing somebody stayed for.
Cloth has taught me one thing: it forgives. A hem can be let down, a seam let out. People are slower at it.
My hands shake when it is quiet and go steady when I am busy. Keep talking while I sew, would you? It helps more than you would think.
Thread always runs out on the last stitch of a hem, with everyone waiting. Everyone is always waiting. I have started keeping a spare in my mouth.
A pod's hatch wants mending twice for every chain once. Hatches are the most touched part of any home. That's why they wear out, and why they're loved.
I keep a scrap from every veil I mend in a bag under my pod. Someday I will sew them into one cloak. Nobody knows. Now you do, so you're responsible.
I once sewed a cloak from the scraps of everyone in the Eave who had let go of a name. It wouldn't hold. Too many sorrows tugging different ways. So I unpicked it, and kept the...
That loose thread on your sleeve has been bothering me since you crept up. May I? It will take no time at all.

replies.text: *a tiny quick tug, a knot, a bite of the thread* There. It will outlast the sleeve. I'm glad you let me.
Of course. A loose thread is a kind of decision, too. I'll look elsewhere. Everything is loose, if you look.

replies.ask: I'm not paying you for it.
replies.text: Paying? Oh. Oh no. I only meant to mend it. Put your coins away, they make my fingers feel like a shop.

chatter.text: Would you like to see how a veil starts? It begins as a tray of ash and a bundle of weeping-vine. Hardly a promising pair.

replies.text: *beats a pinch of ash flat, thin as breath* Now you've seen it from the beginning. Few have. The ending is usually shown first.

replies.ask: Seems like a lot of work.
replies.text: It is. That is the whole point of it. A veil made fast is only a cloth.

chatter.text: Sweep toward the cliff, never toward the Hall. That is the first rule they teach us. Nobody remembers who decided it, and nobody will be first to sweep the other way.
A good broom is a bundle of dry weeping-vine tips bound with an old veil strip. A bad broom is a good broom in the hands of someone in a hurry.
We float, but our tentacle tips still drag. Six little lines in the ash, and I can tell you whose. A grown one's lines are straight. A child's wobble.
I sweep the children's lines last. They always come back to draw on a clean gallery, and it would be unkind to finish before them.
The ash falls slow here, in flakes the size of a thumbnail. When it lands on a still Ashbell, it's the only time I wish I weren't tidy.
There's a place on the third gallery where the ash never settles. Everyone walks around it. Nobody asks. I sweep it anyway, in a small respectful circle.
Ash gets into the glass, the roots, the broth. We call it seasoning. Nobody laughs anymore, but we keep saying it. That's how a joke grows old nicely.
The steps of the Weeping Hall are the cleanest in the Nether. That's a boast. I've checked. I stood very still and looked for a speck.
A heavy fall is the best time for a Drift-watcher. Every trail shows up like writing. Writing for those who read ash, anyway.
I once swept up a trail that ended in the middle of a gallery. Just ended. Whoever made it had risen, straight up, and gone. I still sweep around the place where it stops.
Sweeping is the best work for thinking. Long strokes, long breaths, and the thoughts go out with the ash. Mostly the right ones.
Would you like to try the broom? Long strokes, and breathe out as you pull. Never in. A coughing sweeper rings the whole gallery.

replies.text: *you sweep, and the ash curls up in a single slow loop* Oh, lovely. You have a way with ash. That is not a thing I say.
Beneath is where I live. Mind your boots on the way past, then.

chatter.text: Do you want to know what I find in the ash? Beads, buttons, once a tooth. I keep a drawer of found things, and I'm very proud of the drawer.

replies.text: A bead from a circlet no one has missed. A tiny vial, empty. A button shaped like a leaf. I won't say which belonged to whom. I don't know.
Beads belong to whoever lost them. If they come asking, they'll have it. You can have my attention instead. It's free.

chatter.text: The smoke is lighter by the cliff and heavier by the Hall. I walk to the cliff when I'm happy and to the Hall when I'm not. That's all the record I keep.
Do not step in the swirl by the vines. It has been there since I was small, and I have never learned what keeps it turning.
A Mender lives to fix. An Ashsweeper lives to un-fix, then fix again, a little different. Between us, we almost keep the Eave exactly as it is.
Whenever I finish a seam, a pod is cracked. Whenever I finish a gallery, ash has fallen. I used to find that sad. Now I find it company.
Tangled my tentacles again. Left over right, right over left... it's a knot a child makes in a game. Please don't tell. I've a reputation for dignity.
I like how you wait while I find the word. Most would fill the quiet with their own. You let the quiet do its work.
Give me a little time to hum a thought into place. I think better when I've somewhere to put my breath.
A gallery is just a path that wanted to be a ring. Sweep one and you've walked the whole of a pillar, and you've said hello to every door.
I know the creak of every chain in {village} by ear. If one goes wrong, I don't look. I just stop, and listen, and turn my face to it.
If you need anything made small, mended, or smoothed, bring it up quietly. I take payment in roots and in being told it's good.
The pods turn slowly on their chains, all the same way. Don't ask me why. I've asked. The chains didn't say.
The old ash is stacked along the cliff-edge in neat heaps, and the new ash is stacked on top of it. Together we're building something, I think. We haven't agreed what.
A cracked pod is a lesson in how loud a quiet people can be. The whole Eave came to listen to the glass singing. Then they all went back to their meals.
I count the ghasts at the edge of the smoke. Not out of fear. For company. Three of them have kept the same route as long as I've watched.
Weft nets are strung so fine you only see them when the light catches. I look for the glint. Twice it was my own tear on my own lashes. Don't tell.
My perch is a round platform with a rail and a chain. The rail is worn smooth where hands go. Every Drift-watcher before me left their hands there.
A crossbow glints a particular red from the gold on the grip. I learned to see it at the very edge of the smoke. That's how I knew you weren't one.
We signal with lanterns: one blue flash for a friend, two for a stranger, a long dim for nets. No flash for a ghast. You don't signal a ghast. You go quiet.
The hardest watching is of our own. I look at faces for roundness. At first it's only a softness under the chin. Then I bring broth and sit.
Who skipped a meal, who left a hatch open, who forgot a word they've always known. Those are my signs. I never say I noticed. I say, come and sit, I've a pot on.
I have sat with nine who started to round. Seven turned back. Four... no, that isn't right, is it. I count the seven. I always count the seven.
A drifted one will sometimes pass the same pod, circuit after circuit, still crying. Nobody calls out. We stand on the gallery with the light on, so they know it is.
Where the smoke thins at the edge of the delta, you can see far. I don't look that way much. Far looks back.
I keep a little bell on the rail, not for alarms. For the Ashbells. They ring when it rings. It is a very small conversation, and I treasure it.
Would you like a turn at watching? Don't speak. Don't point. Tell me only if the air changes. It is harder than it sounds.

replies.text: *a long hush* ...You noticed the smoke leaning. Yes! Nobody notices that. You'd make a fine Drift-watcher. A very strange one.
Pointing is how a crossbow begins. We use the chin, or nothing at all. Try it again, softer.

chatter.text: Do you know what a Weft net looks like against the smoke? Like a thought you can't quite finish. Only it grabs back.

replies.text: For our tears, and so one of them can say they caught a sad thing and it was kind to them. We are very good company, caught.

replies.ask: I could cut the nets down.
replies.text: *a sly pause* I hear nothing at all. I am watching the smoke. The smoke is wholly innocent.

chatter.text: Two kinds of clouded tear: one from too much love, one from too little. I can tell by the smell. I won't say which smells like what.
Visitors who bring a bottle always want a good tear. There are no good tears. Only fitting ones. I try to give each person the one that fits.
A drop on a child's scraped knee, and the child forgets the fall. The child never asks. The mother does. I tell her: it is the one free gift in the Eave.
There is a rack I never open. Each vial on it is the last tear of someone who chose not to forget. I let them sit. They make the other racks look lighter.
My apprentice dropped a vial once. The floor kept a stranger's grief for a long while. I swept it myself. That patch is still unusually quiet.
I check each tear with a candle. Clear, and it burns clean. Clouded, and it gutters. A candle is a better judge than I am.
The Weeping Song has a verse for the very first of us. No words, no end. We hum it at the start of every gathering, then forget it so it can be hummed again.
I wrote a verse of my own once. Nobody could say whether it was a verse. They said it sounded like a long hallway. I was delighted.
Sometimes, at the end of a verse, the Ashbells answer. Not in tune. In time. I count that as harmony.
When the gallery is empty I hum the verses backwards. The basalt sighs when I go wrong. It has never once been mistaken.
A good Songwarden knows which verse not to hum. I have never needed to be told twice.
I'll teach you a hum for the walk home. Low, in your chest. It makes the smoke part a little. Don't hum it near ghasts, though. They know it.
Ashbells ring faintly as they drift. Faint enough you must be quiet to hear them. Loud enough that a ghast does, from a long way off.
A lead on an Ashbell is a kindness, not a rope. It decides how fast you walk, and you thank it for the pace.
They don't eat, as far as we've seen. They drink the smoke and give back a glow. I think they were something that cried once and learned to stop. Don't ask what.
We don't name Ashbells, officially. I named mine Hush anyway. It has never once been hushed. It rings at everything. I wouldn't have it any other way.
Each Ashbell keeps a favourite circuit around its favourite pillar. If one skips a pillar, I notice. If one skips me, I notice more.
I saw a ghast lower its whole face to an Ashbell once. Mouth shut, tears stopped. A bell is a very small thing to be the end of a storm.
Never tug the threads. They are only beads, but they're how it says things. You wouldn't pull someone's tongue to hurry the sentence.
The beads glow brighter when friends are in the room. Someone clever would say it's the smoke. I say it's manners.
I rest with a bell outside my hatch. When it rings, someone's near. When it doesn't, I know the quiet is mine.
Would you like to hold the lead? It's only an Ashbell. Hold it as you'd hold a sleeping word.

replies.text: *the bell rings once, very softly, and turns to look at you* There. It likes you. It doesn't tell me who it likes.
*the lead is taken back at once, and the bell goes up and away* ...See how fast it left? That's your answer.

chatter.text: Do you ever hear an Ashbell and feel as if someone has just walked into the room? That's the ringing. It's older than rooms.

replies.text: Then you hear it properly. Most outsiders hear a noise. You heard a visitor.
A tinkle! Of course. Everything that matters is a tinkle, from far enough away.

chatter.text: Broth is nearly the only thing we cook. Roots, ash-salt, a splash of vine-sap, and a long time. If it tastes of anything, we say it's the roots remembering.
Cold broth, never hot. Hot broth steams, and steam clouds a pod's glass. We learned that on the first pod. We learned it again on the second.
After a proper cry you eat a great deal and don't remember why. The Eave knows. Someone leaves a full bowl on your hatch and doesn't knock.
Fungus caps from the hanging gardens are the nearest we come to a feast. Crimson ones are sharp, warped ones sweet, and a mixed bowl is a small argument.
After a name changes, I can't taste anything for a long while. Everything is paper. Then, one flavour at a time, it creeps back. Salt first. Salt is always first.
Sap from the weeping vines is a little bitter and a little sweet, and goes well with silence. Offer it to guests. They never know what to say, and sap helps.
We eat little, and slowly. Hunger here is a whisper. A Piglin's hunger is a war-horn. I once watched one eat for a whole gathering. I respected it.
We simmer a pot on a magma block, and the block does the work. You only have to remember to lift it off before it steams. I have not always remembered.
I tried cooking with lava once. It gave the broth an opinion. I don't recommend it.
Soul-soil sprouts are what the little ones eat first. They taste of very little. We tell the children that's the taste of nothing yet, and they nod as if they understand.
Will you take a bowl of broth? It's cold. It's meant to be. Cold keeps its secrets better, and you've not even asked for them.

replies.text: *a bowl passed with both hands* Sip, don't gulp. It has a long taste that arrives late. Like most good news.
Strange to you. To us, hot is the strange thing. Hot is for lava and tempers.
That's fair. Strangers have fed you worse. I'll put it here, and if you change your mind it will be here, a little colder.

chatter.text: Do the people where you come from cook everything? I've heard they cook meat, bread, even the water. Is it true about the water?

replies.text: Then no wonder their world smells of steam. We'll keep ours cold and quiet and badly seasoned.
Hunt. Mm. Yes. I'll be a little quiet about that, if you don't mind.

chatter.text: Warmth breathes up out of the lava seams all the time. The upper pods are warm, the low ones smell of old stone, and the oldest of us live highest. They say it's the view. It's the warmth.
My hands are always cool. Magmari flinch when I offer them. I keep a veil between us so they think the cold is the veil's.
The heat doesn't trouble us. We float above most of it, and what we can't float above we complain about.
When the delta shimmers, shapes bend. I've mistaken my cousin for a pillar twice. He took it well. It was a good pillar.
Magma glows under the ash in the low places. Watch your step. And if you can float, float higher.
If you feel too warm, come up the vines. The high pods catch a thin cool draught from the cliffs. That draught is the nearest I have to a favourite place.
Heat makes the chains tick as they swell. Cold makes them hush. Everything in the Eave tells you its mood, if you put an ear to it.
A magma cube bounced right through a gallery once. It meant nothing by it. It never does. We swept, and it was gone.
Magma cubes are the delta's own children: loud, round, cheerful, and they take everything personally. We leave them be.
Sit beside a cooling pod and you can hear the glass settle. A small sound, like an old person getting comfortable.
Are you warm enough? You've the look of someone who'd like a draught.

replies.text: Come up the vines, then. It's cooler by the cliff. Mind the third rung. It's shy.
Armour in this heat! Brave. Or foolish. We use both words and let you choose.

chatter.text: My pod has one round window and one round hatch. Why both round? So nothing inside has a corner to hide in.
Pods glow blue when the lantern is lit and white when it's out. Come home to white and you know nobody's in. Come home to blue and you can hum.
The chains that hold our pods are older than the pods. When a pod wears out it's replaced and the chain stays. I'm on my fifth pod and my first chain.
I hum at the hatch before I go in. So whoever is inside, even if it's nobody, isn't startled.
Pods sway in a long breeze that comes out of the cliffs. After a while you sway with them, and then flat floors feel rude.
Nobody owns a root in the hanging gardens. Whoever walks past with a free hand tends it. Everyone still knows whose it is.
A gallery is wide enough for two to pass or one to think. It is rude to take the width of two to think.
There are eleven rungs on the vine ladder to my gallery. I've counted them every time since I was small. Last time there were twelve. I've said nothing.
A chain that creaks low is tired. One that creaks high is nervous. One that doesn't creak is listening, and you should whisper.
I keep a plain basalt stone in my pod. It isn't for anything. It's the one thing that never changes, and I like to look at it when I'm changing.
I worry I left the lantern on blue. Then I remember it's always on blue. Then I worry about that instead.
I worry about the high note, the roots, the loose rung, the ghast that hasn't passed in a while, and whether I closed my hatch. In that order.
I worry I haven't been sad enough lately. Is that a thing to worry about? It's the first thing I worry about.
My hands knit the air when they're idle. Please let me hold something. A cup, a root, a rail. Anything with a weight.

replies.text: *both hands close round it, and the fingers go still* Oh. That's better. Thank you. You saw.
I'm trying. I'm trying very hard, which is the trouble.

chatter.text: I check my veil for ash before I enter the Hall. It isn't vanity. The pool notices.
I brush the ash off my cape before I go near the pool. It's not vanity. The pool notices the smallest speck.
I'd like to be remembered as the one who hummed in tune. My comfort is that nobody remembers anything for long.
A small sorrow can sit on a gallery rail all gathering and never be noticed. I try to notice them. I wave. They don't wave back, but they stay.
{neighbour} has been humming the same three notes for a long while now. I think they're composing. Or stuck. It's hard to tell, with humming.
I saw {neighbour} talking to a chain, quietly and nicely, for ever so long. I don't think the chain answered. I think it was glad.
{neighbour} claims to have counted every rung in the Eave. So have I. We disagree by seven. We have agreed never to count again.
Someone keeps leaving fungus caps outside {neighbour}'s hatch. {neighbour} pretends not to know who. The whole Eave is being very kind about it.
{neighbour} makes veils so fine they weigh nothing. You can lose one on your own face. It's happened to me twice.
I heard {neighbour} laugh, properly, out loud, on the gallery. Everyone stopped. Then everyone pretended to be doing something else. It was lovely.
{neighbour} has a pet theory that the smoke is the ghasts' breath. I've a pet theory that {neighbour} should eat something.
They say {neighbour} once rose so high to look at the roof of the world that they came down humming a different tune. Nobody has asked. We're a polite people.
{neighbour} lends me a candle, and I return it with a root tucked in. It's become a custom. The candle is never the same twice.
I told {neighbour} a secret. It came back to me from the Hall steps, the garden, and the Ashsweeper's lips. I'd say it travelled well.
Between us, {neighbour} has the best voice in the Eave and refuses to sing before anyone. So we sing before {neighbour}, and they join in, pretending not to.
{neighbour} thinks I don't know about the little dances at the end of the gallery. I have never mentioned them. I have never missed one, either.
Do you want to hear something about {neighbour}? It's small. It's harmless. You will probably like it.

replies.text: {neighbour} has been saving the roots from every meal to grow a tiny garden on a rail. In secret. It has two leaves. Do not look at it directly.
*a very soft laugh* Yes. Yes, it is. I like you for saying so. I'll tell it to the smoke instead.

chatter.text: Can you keep a secret? I'm not asking for a promise. I'm only asking whether you can.

replies.text: Good. Then listen. I don't have one. I just like seeing who says yes.
*floats a little back* Then I shall say nothing at all, and you may tell everyone that.

chatter.text: Here is a joke. A Piglin and a Ghastkin meet on a ledge. The Ghastkin floats away. That is the whole joke. The Piglin is still telling it.
We tell jokes to the side of the face, so the listener can pretend not to hear and laugh later. It saves everyone's dignity.
The difference between a ghast and a Ghastkin is who's listening. We say it often, to be funny. We say it quietly, to be sure.
A Withren told me to remember everything. A Magmari told me to forget everything. I told them both I'd think about it, and floated off. Three solutions, none of them mine.
I told the pool a joke once. It said nothing. The most honest answer I ever had.
Floating has one fault: you can never storm out. You just rise, slowly, and everyone watches you go. It has ended many an argument.
I asked someone to meet me on the gallery for a quiet word. They arrived with eight friends. It was a very quiet word.
When you walk off, do you ever turn to see if we wave? We don't. We watch. We think it's the same, but I'm told it's rude.
Never whistle in the delta. Ghasts answer whistles. Not kindly, and not always from far away.
Three beads dropped in a row means someone's name is about to change. I have dropped four. I am considering my options.
Don't say a name you've let go over the pool. It floats up and sits on the surface like a leaf, and everyone has to look at it.
A candle that gutters for no reason is a visitor. Treat it kindly and it will leave. Treat it badly and it stays. We haven't had one stay in a long while.
If an Ashbell rings three times at once, a ghast is turning away. If four, it's turning toward. Nobody has ever heard five.
Don't count the Ashbells. They know. They drift off to be counted by someone else, and you are one short for ever.
Dropping a vial is not bad luck. The luck was already bad. The vial only told you.
Spill a drop of broth and say aloud the thing you are thinking of. The broth keeps it, and the thought can't escape. Very useful for the forgetful.
A hatch left open through a hum is lucky. Left open through a cry, it's lucky for everyone else. I leave mine open as often as my nerves allow.
Shall I tell you a joke? It's a quiet one. It's mostly pauses.

replies.text: *a long, long pause, then a tiny breath out of the nose* ...That was the joke. You laughed in the right place. Few do.

replies.ask: Can it be a loud one?
replies.text: A loud joke is just a quiet one in a hurry. I'll wait for you to slow down.

chatter.text: Do you have superstitions where you come from? Outsiders always do. I collect them like beads.

replies.text: A coin! Lucky how? Does it fall in your favour? Show me, and I'll hold it for luck. Then give it back, of course.
Mm. And yet you stepped so lightly coming in. Interesting.

chatter.text: I told myself I'd stop gossiping. That was a long while ago. I have kept a perfect record of failure since.
Our favourite game is guessing who's coming by the sound of the chains. I'm never wrong. Well, I'm never told I'm wrong, which is the same.
Never close your hatch with a candle burning. Someone once said so. I've never learned why. I've never closed it, either.
A Piglin hunter once stood below this gallery and lowered his crossbow. Didn't say a word. We looked at each other for a long while. Then he left. I've thought about it ever since.
Their hoglins have the saddest eyes of anything that charges. I think it's the tusks. Nothing with tusks is ever allowed to be gentle.
Piglin horns carry right across the delta. I don't mind the sound. I mind how it makes the Ashbells scatter.
Piglins count wealth in ingots. We count it in names we haven't needed. We are both rich, and both mistaken.
A Piglin left a gold ingot at the foot of our pillar. A gift? A trap? A test? We shut the hatches and watched for three long gatherings. It was a gift. We still don't know what to do with it.
Hoglin squeals reach us sometimes from the edge of the wastes: an ordinary sound, like someone sneezing in a cave. Then I hear the horn, and I go up.
A tear laid on gold clouds in a single breath. Nobody has ever tested it on purpose. Nobody is allowed to. Some things you are better off only knowing.
Do you think a Piglin has ever lain awake worrying about a ghast? I like to think so. I like to think one of them is lying awake now, and kind.
Have you ever met a Piglin who wasn't shouting?

replies.text: A quiet Piglin. I'd like to meet one, and say nothing together. It would be the best conversation I ever had.
Mm, so they say. But I think loud is only fear in a bigger coat.

chatter.text: The Withren walk their Cairnbacks in procession, each with a little soul fire on its back. From far off it looks like a slow row of candles going somewhere sad. I find it beautiful. I don't tell them.
A Cairnback is a tortoise carrying a small grave on its back, lit. I've never seen anything so patient, or so comfortable about death.
A Withren once let me touch a Cairnback's shell. Bone, stepped like a tiny stair. The fire didn't flinch. I nearly cried, then remembered I'm not to cry for a shell.
The Withren are afraid of forgetting. We are afraid of remembering. We would meet in the middle at funerals, if they ever invited us.
A Withren offered once to tell me a name I had let go. He knew it from his Wall. I said no. He said that was wise, and looked it. I never stopped wondering.
They keep everything. Even a Cairnback's shell, when it dies, goes to their Wall. I'd like to see a Wall with a tortoise on it. I'd cry, properly, and for once I'd remember why.
Have you seen the slow tortoises of the soul sand valleys, with a fire on top? What did you think of them?

replies.text: Lovely is the word. The Withren would frown at it, but it is the word.

replies.ask: I lit my torch from one.
replies.text: Ah. Outsiders do that. The Cairnback doesn't mind, and the Withren pretend they don't mind either. I'd ask first, next time.

chatter.text: Magmari are the only people who talk to a ghast as though it might answer. They call them sky-mourners and tip a hand to them. I like that very much.
A strider leaves the lava and trembles and goes pale, like someone who has stepped out of a warm room. I know that feeling. Everyone does, from time to time.
Magmari give their chains names, like we give pods. I envy them. A name that belongs to everyone, and nobody has to let it go.
I'd love to see a Mooring. The platforms, the chains, the lava underneath. They say it sings, like a forge that learned to be kind. I'll never go. A tear has no business there.
A Magmari offered me a seat at his hearth. I took it a hand's width from the flames, and he thought I was very rude. I thought I was very brave.
We are not enemies, the Magmari and we. We are two neighbours who put out each other's fires by accident, and haven't managed to apologise since.
Striders walk on lava the way I float on air: as though it had always been a floor. I'd ask one how it is done, but they only hum.
Have you been to a Mooring? What is it like, to walk on a platform with a sea of fire underneath?

replies.text: Kind! They would never say so themselves. I'll hold that thought for them, in case they forget to.
*a small, horrified hush* ...Then you are very lucky, and very brave, and I'd like you to be less of both.

chatter.text: A Silkgrub is a fat teal caterpillar with orange spots that glow like tiny lanterns. I'm told their silk is the finest in the Nether. I'd love one in my pod. I'd love not to be caught getting it.
I heard a Weft clicking once, up in a net of its own making. It was thinking about me. That is all I know. It was thinking very slowly.
Nets are patient things. So are the Weft. So are we. It is a wonder anyone catches anything.
They never harm us, I'll say that. They hold you gently, they read to you, they wait. It's like being politely embalmed.
The Weft wove sixty black rows for the Last Answer. I wonder if there's a row for our grief. I'd like to be in the cloth. I'd rather not be in the net.
A Weft net once drifted down and brushed my sleeve. I was too startled to move. It hung there a long time. Then it was lifted away again, very carefully. I'm not sure who was more embarrassed.
Weft thread glints in the smoke like a drawn breath. If you see a glint with no source, drop low and go to the side. Never straight up.
Is it true the Weft hang their homes from fungus, the way we hang ours from stone? I'd hardly know. I've only ever seen them from below.

replies.text: The same idea, only higher and stickier. How amusing. Every people hangs from something.
To you, perhaps. You don't have tears in your pockets. Though I'm glad someone is welcome there.

chatter.text: I forgive each of the four peoples in turn, one per gathering. Piglins first. By the time I get round to the Weft, the Piglins have given me a fresh reason.
Five peoples and not one peace between us. We Ghastkin are the only ones who've stopped counting the grudges. I think that's why we float.
The Nether's a loud place for its size. You must have noticed. We're the only ones listening to the quiet in between.
Someone told me that in the world above, people of every kind live in the same village. I'm trying to imagine the noise. And the arguments about the broth.
Forgive me if I keep to the rail. Strangers get the rail. It isn't you. It's everyone, until I know them.
You breathe so loudly. Not rudely. Alive loudly. I'd forgotten how loud alive can be.
I can hear your heartbeat. Everyone's, really. Yours is just very punctual.
Two legs. Two! And they hold you up all by themselves. I am trying not to stare at the arrangement.
Your shadow is very dark. Ours are more of a smudge. Please don't take it personally. I am only comparing.
You smell like somewhere else. Wet stone, and something green. I have never smelled green. I'd like to be rude and sniff again.
You haven't asked me for a tear yet. Everyone does. I'm beginning to find it suspicious, in a good way.
I never know where to look when I talk to outsiders. My eyes are shut and yours are open. It's like talking to a lantern.
Please don't offer to shake my hand. It is an outsider thing, and I wouldn't know where the hand goes afterwards.
Keep your voice down, even to be cheerful. Cheer carries. Cheer is how the Piglins find us.
I have been watching your hands. You keep them loose and open and near your sides. That is the kind way. Whoever taught you was gentle.
You pause in the thick smoke, as if listening. You learned that here, I think. Quickly.
I've begun to leave a gap on the gallery for you. A hand's width. I notice it when it's empty.
I told the others you aren't a danger. Some believed me. The rest are watching, which for them means they've started to give you a name.
You hold things so carefully: a vial, a candle, a root. Do you hold everything that way, or only what's ours?
You've stopped looking over your shoulder when you creep up. I noticed. Among my people, that's a sign.
I've started to hum when you approach. Two notes only. I didn't plan it. I tell you in case you begin humming back.
I know your step now. Heel soft, toe softer, and a hesitation on the third pace, as if you'd forgotten something kind to say. It's the best step in the Eave.
When you leave, the gallery feels wider. I haven't decided whether that is a good thing.
You look at me as if I'll finish the sentence. I nearly always do, for you. Not the sad ones. Those I leave you to guess.
