I've been practising saying your name in a way that doesn't cost anything. Gentle, and it keeps. It is harder than it sounds.
Most outsiders leave footprints. You leave a kind of quiet, a hand's width wide. I follow it sometimes, after you've gone.
I pictured you older, sitting by the pool with your back to me, looking at the windows. I didn't like the picture. Then I did.
You've water in that pack. A whole bucket. I can feel it. It's like standing beside a pool that hasn't decided to forget anything yet.
A soul lantern in your pack. I can tell by how the smoke leans toward you. Whoever made it knew how to build a small forgiveness.
A candle in your pack. I smell the wax. It smells like the start of a gathering.
Something white and small is in your pack. A lily, I think. We have no flowers here. I can feel it being gentle in there.
In your pack is something that has already decided you won't die. I find that reassuring, and very rude of it.
Something in your pack is very quiet. The wrong kind of quiet. A skull, isn't it. I won't ask. I'll float a little higher, and you will be kind enough not to notice.
You carry gold. I can tell by how the Ashbells hush. It's not an accusation. Gold only smells of crossbows to us.
A compass! It always points somewhere. What an alarming thing, to know so certainly where something is.
You carry a bell, a real one with a tongue. We only use soft ones here, on the Ashbells. If you ring it, ring it a long way from the pods.
Snow, in your pack? I've never touched snow. I'm told it's cold water that falls from nothing. Is it cruel?
You carry glass bottles. A person who carries bottles expects to fill them. I wonder with what.
A bow in your hand. I'll float a little higher while it's out. Nothing personal. I only do the arithmetic of arrows.
A torch! Fire on a stick, with such a hopeful look. Hold it a little farther from the vines, would you? They have no sense.
A feather. You're holding a feather. Do you know nothing in the Nether weighs so little and is so rude to gravity?
A tear, in your open hand. Quiet. Not mine, I know. Not yours either. Whoever it was for, they were loved.
You look up when you hear a bell. Most people look around. Looking up is the right way.
You answer slowly, as if the words must climb a long ladder. I like that. Hurry would spoil it.
May I tell you something I noticed about you? It isn't a criticism.

replies.text: You hold your breath when you pass the pool. It's polite. It's also unnecessary. Breathe. It's only water. Mostly.
Of course. I'll keep it, and you'll never know what it was. That's a gift of a kind.

chatter.text: Do I seem strange to you? Be honest. I'm used to strange. I live with ghasts.

replies.text: Good. Honest is better than kind, when it's said softly. Thank you.
Oh. That's the nicest lie anyone's told me. I'll keep it near the candles.
*floats up a little, saying nothing, and then a very quiet* Yes. I was told that. I'd hoped it wouldn't be you.

chatter.text: I wonder what we look like to you: pale, floating, closed-eyed. Do you find us sad to look at, or only quiet?

replies.text: *the head tilts, the veil stirs* ...Beautiful. Mm. I'll have to carry that around. It's quite heavy, in a good way.
That's honest. It's also not all of us. Stay a while and you'll see the sly part.

chatter.text: I've got four tentacles and Mama's got six. I asked where my other two are. She said they come when you're ready. I'm ready.
I tied my tentacles in a knot on purpose and now I can't undo them. Don't tell Mama. Can you help? No, don't touch. Just stand there and look sorry for me.
I can float as high as the first rung now! Nearly. Before, I could only float as high as my knees. Don't laugh. I don't have knees.
An Ashbell followed me home and sat outside the hatch the whole time. Mama says it's the one that follows everybody. I say it's mine.
Grown-ups hum when they're thinking. I hum when I'm eating. Mama says it's the same thing. I'm sure it's not.
I found a bead in the ash! A real one! It was blue. I'm going to give it back if somebody is sad about it. Is anybody sad about it?
The rules for playing on the gallery are: no running, no shouting, no pushing, no floating over the edge. So mostly we sit and look at each other very hard.
I'm the best at the stillness game. I stayed so still that a Mender hemmed my sleeve to the rail. It took them a long time, to be fair.
Why is the pool so quiet? I asked it a question and it didn't say anything. I asked nicely. It's very rude.
I'm only allowed near the pool with a grown-up. But they stand with their eyes shut the whole time, so it doesn't count.
Mama says Piglins are like a war-horn that learned to walk. I'd like to see that. From very far away.
The Withren have a wall with every name on it. Every single one! I can't even remember my own sometimes. Oh wait. It's {name}. See?
A Magmari came to the cliff once, and everybody went up their pods and shut the hatches. He was warm even from far away. I wanted to wave. I waved from inside my sleeve.
The Weft have four arms! I have four tentacles and two arms. I'd like four arms. A root in each one, and still one for waving.
Mama says never look at a net. I looked at one. It was shiny. I looked away. Then I looked again. That's only two looks.
A Silkgrub is a sleepy teal worm that makes string. I've never touched one. I touched the string, though. It was so soft I forgot to be scared.
A Cairnback is a stone tortoise with a candle on its back. If it were mine, I'd never let it go out. I think the Withren feel the same.
A strider walks on fire and doesn't get burnt! I tried walking on a chain bridge once and I got dizzy. Everyone is good at something.
My friend had a brother. She says he went up. I said up where? She said just up. We changed the game.
Do you know what I'm scared of? Not ghasts. Not Piglins. I'm scared of the Hall with nobody in it. It's too empty. It echoes my feet.
I like it when the smoke is thick. Everything gets soft, like floating in the middle of a blanket nobody finished.
Mama made broth with six roots and I counted five. I said so. She said the sixth is the secret. I looked for the secret all through the broth and ate it all.
Sprouts taste like nothing. I like nothing. It's very easy to like.
Tell me your favourite sound. Mine is the vine rattling when somebody climbs it. It means somebody's coming up to see me.
I've a secret handshake with {neighbour}. It's mostly floating in a circle and nodding. We don't tell anyone because it's too embarrassing.
{neighbour} lets me hold the end of a hanging root when they water it. I hold it very still. I think I'm the best at it, but they haven't said.
Sometimes I hum a sound nobody taught me. Then somebody else hums it back. I think we're all humming the same one, and we've forgotten who started it.
When I grow up I'm going to be a Drift-watcher. Or a Songwarden. Or a Tearkeeper. Or I'll just climb vines. Mama says there's no rush.
I want to be a Mender. I'm already good at holes. I make holes in everything.
I'm not scared of you. I was, a little, but I stopped. It's hard to be scared of someone who's trying so hard to be small.
I told {neighbour} you're my best friend who isn't a Ghastkin. They said that's not a thing. I said it is now.
When I'm grown and my eyes shut, I'll remember you by your steps. I'm practising. Left, right, left, wait. See? Am I you?
I drew you on the wall of my pod. You're a long thin stick with a blob on top and lots of lines. The lines are your armour. It's very accurate.
I saved you a bead from the ash. Not a real one. A pretend one. It's in my hand. You can't see it. It's the best one I've got.
Shh. Listen. Can you hear the chains? They're talking about us. They say we're loud. We're not loud! They're loud!
Do you want to see my secret place? It's under the third gallery, behind the vine curtain. There's nothing in it. That's why it's secret.

replies.text: *leads you under the vines, whispering* Shh. Sit. Nothing is happening. Isn't it good?
Oh. Then it's secret from you too. That's all right. I'll tell you about it from the outside.

chatter.text: Do you want to hear a scary story? It's very scary. It has a ghast in it.

replies.text: A ghast was crying. And then it floated away. The end. Isn't that the scariest thing you ever heard?
Me neither! Let's tell a story about broth instead. Once upon a time there was a bowl.

chatter.text: Guess what I'm thinking. It's a root.

replies.text: Close! It was a warped root! Almost! You're very good at almost.
It's all right. Nobody ever does. It's always a root.

chatter.text: Can you teach me to walk squished, like you do? I want to be quiet in a bent way.

replies.text: *bends something, wobbles* Like this? I don't have knees. I'm bending something. Is it working?
Oh. All right. I'll just be quiet in the regular way. It's less fun.

chatter.text: What do you eat? I can't imagine. Do you eat sprouts? Do you eat things with eyes?

replies.text: Roots! We're the same! What's bread? Is it a root that's been told a secret?
*a big gasp, then a whisper* Do they mind? ...Never mind. I don't want to know. I think I do.

chatter.text: When I was {former}, I kept a bead from the first person I ever cried for. I lost it. I don't remember who. I look for it in the ash sometimes. I think I like the looking more than the finding.
I have a rule: three names is enough. After the third I shall refuse to grieve. I made the rule when I was {former}, who was not known for keeping them.
I got my name from a Songwarden who held me while I cried. She asked what I'd like to be called. I said anything soft. She said {name}. I said yes before she finished.
The moment I became {name}, the whole Eave went quiet. Then {neighbour} said, pass the roots, and I knew it would be all right.
Do you know what I miss most about being {former}? Nothing. I've checked. It's the nothing that's lovely.
I have two ways of grieving: loud, which I keep for the Hall, and small, which I keep for the gallery rail. The small ones never end, but they never grow.
My mother's veil hangs at the back of my pod. I can't remember her face. But I know that veil. I know how it moves when the air does. I think that's enough, most of the time.
Once I nearly cried for a stranger. An outsider, passing, who stumbled and lay still. He got up, thank the ash. I was halfway to the first tear. I was so ashamed. Then so glad.
People think we are cold because we let go. We aren't. We are the warmest people in the Nether. We give everything away, and we do it properly.
I've come to think the ghasts are not unhappy. Only unfinished. I hum to them sometimes. They don't answer. But some turn their faces a little, like someone almost remembering a tune.
I had a friend who liked to stay by the pool after everyone left. I used to wait for them on the steps. Anyway. The steps are very clean now. I keep them so.
I've begun to hum your step in my sleep. Not on purpose. I wake with it half finished and look for the rest of it in the room. That's the difference between a visitor and a habit.
I wear the same cord all the time. It holds my vial. It's the one thing that has been with me through three names. It doesn't know it. I do.
Sometimes I say {former} out loud in my pod, once, to see whether anyone answers. Nobody does. That is the point of it.
If I were ever lost in the wild delta, I'd hum until someone hummed back. It works on Ashbells. It works on friends. I haven't tried it on ghasts. I'm too ashamed to say whether I have.
I used to think letting go meant opening your hand. It doesn't. It means opening your hand and then being brave about the empty palm.
Between us, I've never cried properly for a friend. For family, for neighbours, for an old teacher, yes. A friend... I keep putting it off. I'd like to be told I'm not too late.
{neighbour} tells me my name suits me. Perhaps they say it to everyone. I suspect they do. I accept it anyway.
You've been a friend long enough that I should warn you. I have begun saving things for you: a root, a story, a place on the gallery. I can't stop. It isn't a request. It's a weather.
Do you want to know what it's like to forget on purpose? Less sad than you'd think. Like setting down a heavy bag and not remembering what was in it.

replies.text: Sometimes my hands remember the weight. That's all. The bag itself is gone.
I know. It's all right. You get to carry yours. That is a kind of luck, too.

chatter.text: If you were to give me a new name, what would it be? I'm asking in case I need one.

replies.text: Hush. A name that asks nothing of anyone. Oh, I like that. I like that very much. Don't tell my other names.
Grand! I'd float a hand's width higher at once, and everyone would notice, and I would die of it.
That is the wisest answer. Names should be given only by someone who has cried. Thank you for not trying.

chatter.text: Would you hum with me? Not a song. Only a note, and a note beside it.

replies.text: *a second note slides in beside yours and holds* ...There. We made a small gallery. Nobody else can come in.
Silly is where all the good humming starts. Another time, when the silly has worn off.

chatter.text: Tell me a thing no one knows about you. I'll tell you one back, though I may only half-finish mine.

replies.text: Afraid of heights! And you came all this way up the vines? That is the bravest thing I've heard in a long while.
Then you've lived very honestly. Or very quietly. I'd like to find out which.

chatter.text: Mama says I can have my own bell when I'm bigger. A little one, not an Ashbell. A bell to ring when I'm lost.
I'm going to name every Ashbell in the Eave. I'm up to seven. They're all called Ring. It's easier.
I've a pet root. It's called Wobble. It lives in a pot and doesn't do anything, and I love it.
My favourite place is the top of the vine ladder, where the pod chains meet. If you whisper there the whole Eave hears. I whispered hello. Everyone said hello back.
The basalt is warm! I lay down on it. Mama said that isn't good for floating. I said I'm resting from floating.
Why do grown-ups say never mind so much? Never mind what? I mind. I always mind.
When Mama finishes a sentence she doesn't want to finish, she hums instead. I like those sentences best. They have tunes.
I asked how many names Mama has had. She said, one at a time. That's not a number.
I helped the Ashsweeper. I got ash in my mouth, on my face, and in the broth. They said I was a big help.
I put a drop of broth on my head to see if I'd forget something. I forgot what I was doing next. So it worked!
Can I tell you a joke? What's quieter than a Ghastkin? A Ghastkin who has seen a Piglin. ...I'm not sure that's funny. Mama laughed.
Do you get lost in the smoke? I do. I stand still and hum and somebody always comes. Always. That's the good part about everyone being so nosy.
The Hall windows are blue. If you look through one, everyone is blue, and I'm blue, and the chains are blue. It was the best blue in the world.
I know a song with no words, a song with no tune, and a song with neither. That's the one I sing most.
If I float up very fast and stop very suddenly, my tentacles keep going. It's the funniest thing in the whole world. Ask me to show you. Please ask me to show you.

replies.text: *whoosh, stop, and four tentacles go flapping past* Did you see?! They went on without me! Again! Again!
It's not dangerous. It's just wobbly. All right. I'll do it small, then. Look. Small. Isn't it small?

chatter.text: At a naming gathering each guest brings one thread of ash-silk. They are knotted into a cord for the one with the new name. It's never worn. It is kept where it can be looked at when the name is hard.
We never point. A pointing finger looks too much like a bolt. We nod with the chin, or tilt a shoulder. A good tilt can say: that way, mind the step, and I forgive you.
When two Ghastkin meet on a gallery, the lower one dips a little. The other dips back. It can go on for ever if neither is in a hurry. We are rarely in a hurry.
Gifts are never handed over. They're left on a rail, and the receiver finds them in their own time. Handing over means watching a face, and a face does such tiring things.
We don't clap. We rustle our veils, and it sounds like a cliff falling asleep. Outsiders clap, and half the Eave rises in alarm.
A gathering begins when the first person hums and ends when nobody remembers who began it. I've been to gatherings that never started and ended beautifully.
A child who climbs the whole vine ladder for the first time gets a white candle as long as a finger. They never light it. They look at it for ever. Mine is still on the shelf.
When someone comes home from a long time in the wild, we leave a bowl on their rail and say nothing for a hundred breaths. After that, we can't stop talking.
To say thank you we hold a breath and let it out slowly, close to the person. If it's meant they feel it on the veil. I've been doing it to you for a while.
The smoke parts sometimes, and for a breath you can see the far cliffs, thin and blue, like a drawing of a place. Then it closes. We call that a visit.
Embers drift up from the lava and settle on our veils like tiny wishes. They go out before you can make one. I've never decided which of us should apologise.
A seam of magma opened under the third pillar once. The whole Eave rose and watched with polite interest. It closed. We held a gathering about it, and nobody said a word. A very good gathering.
When all the pods are lit, the ash falling past them looks like slow blue snow. I have never seen snow. I'm told it's like this, only colder, and it doesn't forgive you.
I rise slowly. Everything slowly. Ask me something before I've found my hands and I'll answer with my tentacles.
I spent a long while looking at a single root, and when I looked up, all the lanterns were lit. That's how time goes here. You look at something small, and look up, and it's later.
Hanging gardens need talking to. Not much. A hello when you pass, a word of complaint when something wilts. Mine like my complaints. They grow toward them.
I'm teaching myself to whistle without sound. All breath and lips. Nobody can tell, and nobody can complain. It may be my finest skill.
I tried juggling beads once, six of them, with six tentacles. It went well until I thought about it.
A child asked me what the opposite of a ghast is. I said an Ashbell. She said no, a laugh. She's right, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.
I've never learned to swim, because there is no water. I've never learned to run, because I float. There are a great many skills I'll never have, and I'm calm about all of them.
There is a game where you whisper a made-up name for a root, and everyone must use it through a whole gathering without asking why. I was Mist-Knuckle once. Nobody blinked.
There's a game where one person is the pool, and the others bring them things to forget. Mostly the pool says, I forgot. It isn't a good game, but it's ours.
A traveller once asked me what we do for fun. I said, we sit. He said, besides that. I said, we sit together.
We trade healing for glass, wax, roots and thread. We don't ask for gold. We'd rather be paid in something that doesn't remember being used to hurt.
We'll heal an outsider once, and only for what they can't help. We say so. Some leave offended. A few come back with a root, and we begin again.
Outsiders ask for a tear as if it were a coin. It's nearer a promise: someone meant it, and you had better mean it back.
I'd rather talk about the smoke. Do you like the smoke? It's the one thing here that never asks for a second sentence.
I'm better at listening than speaking. It takes me ages to find a word, and the word is usually yes or mm. Please be patient.
I find I'm talking more than usual. That's a compliment, in case you can't tell. I'd stop, but I'd rather you did the stopping.
I've told you more than I told my last three names. I hope that's all right. I hope it isn't a mistake. I hope you remember nothing and everything.
A Ghastkin's laugh is mostly breath. If you ever hear one from the throat, it means one of us has forgotten ourselves, and we all politely look away so it can finish.
I like standing near the pods when all are lit and nobody is in. They look like a row of held breaths. I count them, lose count, and begin again.
Do you hear that low note under the floor of the delta? It's the lava turning over. The Songwardens say it's the first verse. The Ashsweepers say it is indigestion.
A gust off the cliff can lift a whole row of veils at once. From below it looks like a row of Ashbells rising politely.
Between you and me, I prefer the low galleries. Less floating, more leaning. Leaning is underrated.
I keep one rung loose on purpose. A visitor who's never climbed up always steps on it first. It's how I learn their character.
I ask an Ashbell what time it is. It rings. I tell everyone it's later than they think. It is always true.
Do you have a custom for saying thanks? We have ours, and I'd like to compare.

replies.text: Aloud! Imagine. Everyone would hear. Well, that's the point, isn't it. Say it once more, quietly, for me.
A bow, like a dip! You are Ghastkin, and you don't know it. Don't let the Withren hear.

chatter.text: What games do you play where you come from? Tell me the rules. I'll try to lose.

replies.text: The children play something just like it. I'll teach you drift, and we'll see who forgets whom.
Take? Then I'd rather lose at once and keep my things. I'm told that is called losing.

chatter.text: Let's play the game of tiny lies. You tell one, and I'll hum the correction.

replies.text: *a long low hum that bends away from the word love* ...You tolerate it. Good lie. Again.
*one rising note, very gentle* ...That's the tiniest lie of all. I'm so fond of it.

chatter.text: Piglins keep hoglins in pens, I'm told, and feed them from the hand. Is it true that a hoglin can be gentle?

replies.text: Then there's hope for tusks. I will remember that when I'm low.
Mm. Like most things with a point. Best admired from the gallery.

chatter.text: I would love to know what a Silkgrub sounds like. Does it hum? Have you ever met one?

replies.text: Sheared, and it let you? Then perhaps the Weft are gentler than their nets suggest. I will hold that thought, loosely.
Ugly is how many good things begin. It makes silk. What do you make?

chatter.text: Have you ever ridden a strider? I hear they hum when they're warm and shiver when they're not. Is that true?

replies.text: Across lava! I am horrified and enchanted at once. Did it hum? Tell me it hummed.
Wise, or timid. I can't tell, and I won't ask.
...Please don't say that near me. A Magmari wouldn't be the only one to mourn.

chatter.text: I'd love to ask a Cairnback what it thinks of fire. Do you think it knows it's carrying one?

replies.text: I think so too. It walks as though carrying something that is asleep.
Everything is just something, from far enough away.

chatter.text: I'm out of fresh vials. Would you carry a hum to the next gallery for me? Just a hum, no words.

replies.text: Two falling notes, low. They'll know it's from me. Thank you. You've saved me a very long float.
No. Of course not. Forgive me. I'm used to people who owe me a scrape.

chatter.text: When you pass the tall pillar, do you hear anything at its foot? A hum? A sigh?

replies.text: Then it's still there. Thank you for hearing it. Nobody does, and I'd begun to doubt myself.
Then I'm glad you passed it kindly. Some places are best left quiet.

chatter.text: I've lost a verse. I know it was there, like a tooth that's gone. Could you hum a lullaby from your world? Only the tune.

replies.text: *the head tilts, a long listen* ...Oh. That isn't our verse. But it fits the gap. May I keep it?
Everyone knows one. Look for it later, when you aren't trying.

chatter.text: I found a button in the ash, and I think it's yours. Is it?

replies.text: *the button is passed over, still warm from a hand* I thought so. Ash remembers hands.
Then it belongs to the delta now. Thank you for saying so. Most people say yes.

chatter.text: Your belt is fraying where the buckle sits. May I mend it? I have the thread. You needn't even take it off.

replies.text: *two quick tucks and a small flat knot* There. It will outlast you. I mean that kindly.
Of course. A belt with a fray is a belt with a story. I'll just look at it, very politely.

chatter.text: Do you want to be my friend? I've never had a friend with two legs.

replies.text: Oh, good! I'll tell everyone. Quietly. Very quietly.
Later's good. I'll be here. I'll keep your spot warm.
Oh. ...All right. I'll float over there now. Don't look.

chatter.text: I made up a new rule for drift. You have to stand on one tentacle. You have two legs, so you can do it twice. Can you?

replies.text: *delighted gasp* You did it! Nobody has ever stood on one anything. You win drift for ever!
It's not silly. It's the opposite of silly. It's drift.

chatter.text: I have a bet with {neighbour} that you'll tell me a secret before this gathering ends. Would you let me win?

replies.text: Oh, that's a good one. I'll tell {neighbour} it was a deep one.
*a sly little laugh* Oh, you're good. I'll split the winnings with you in roots.

chatter.text: A Silkgrub will spin faster if you feed it warped roots, I'm told. I find that charming and a little mercenary. Even the gentlest creature can be bought with a root.
A hoglin in a pen looks bored and dangerous, which is a rare pairing. I'm told the Piglins sing to theirs. I'd like to hear that, from behind a very thick pillar.
A strider's legs glow like tall candles. I once watched one cross a whole lake at the pace of a held thought. It never looked at me. I felt thoroughly forgiven.
A Cairnback is slower than a verse. The Withren say the fire in its bowl is the slowest thing they know, apart from grief. I'm not sure the fire is slower.
Someone told me a Cairnback is never lonely, because it carries its own lantern. I laughed. Then I stopped laughing. Then I wondered what mine is.
A rustle on the gallery rail is a veil settling. A thump is a child. If you hear nothing at all, check behind you.
A Piglin once offered me an ingot for a single drop of tear. I said it couldn't be traded. He said everything can. I said then trade me an ingot's worth of silence. He left. I counted that a win.
The Magmari say the sky-mourners hold up the roof with their crying. I have never corrected them. It is the loveliest wrong thing anyone's said about us.
The Weft click when they think, and we hum. If a Weft and a Ghastkin ever sat down to think together, you'd hear a clicking hum, and then a very long silence.
The Magmari are made of fire and nice. The Piglins are made of gold and loud. The Weft are made of string and patient. We're made of smoke and... what are we made of?
Whatever I am to you, you are a lantern to me. I don't say it twice.
I asked an Ashbell to guard a secret for me once. It rang, once, which I took as yes. I've never since remembered the secret. The Ashbell, I'm sure, still has it.

lines: I'm {name}, {epithet}. We take a new name after every great grief. The old one we let go, like a lantern lowered down the vines.
{name}. It's a new name, still a little stiff, like fresh ash-silk. I was {former} before. {former} was very sad, and then the sadness was done, and so was the name.
Who am I? Hm. I'm the one you crept up on. That's the most important thing about me just now, and the nicest.

lines.text: I'm {name}. If you ever meet someone called {former}, it isn't me, and it isn't anyone. Names we let go don't get borrowed.

replies.text: Please don't. That's very Withren of you. Kind, but very Withren.
Does it? I'm still growing into it. Thank you. That helps.

lines: A name is a thing you borrow from the smoke. Mine, {name}, is still on loan. I'll give it back someday, politely, and take whatever comes next.
{name}, {epithet}. That second part is only so you don't mistake me for the first. Names change, and the Eave likes things labelled.

lines.text: I'm {name}, a Tearkeeper. People show me their hands before they say hello. It saves time, and it saves them saying aloud what hurts.
I'm {name}, Songwarden. Mostly a held breath with a name on it. I hum, and the Eave remembers to be an Eave.
I'm {name}. I mend things: veils, chains, pods. Nobody has ever asked me to mend a name. Names break differently.
{name}, Ashsweeper. Small work, long reach. I know where everyone walks, because I sweep up after them.
I'm {name}. I watch the sky so the others can look at the floor. Someone should look up, and I'm used to the view.
The beads on my circlet are griefs I've finished. I'm {name}, and that's as many of them as I'll count aloud.
I'm {name}. The cape is older than this name, and older than the one before it. Names go. Capes outlast everyone.
{village} has held a great many names. Mine is the newest. It's still a little damp, so don't breathe on it too hard.
Out here nobody will call me by the old name by mistake. That's why I came. Don't tell the Eave, they think I like the quiet.

lines: I don't mind being asked who I am. It's who I was that I keep behind a door. You haven't knocked on it. Thank you for that.
People ask how old I am. I tell them how many names I've worn and they stop asking. We count in griefs, not years. It's tidier.
We have no family names, only the Eave. It's a name that doesn't change when you do. It's the one thing here that holds still.
I'm the one who told {neighbour} the high pod was an easy float. It is. Eventually. They're still up there, and I'm not saying a word.

lines.text: Between us, I chose {name} because it was the softest sound I could say without my chest tightening. I tried a dozen first.
The first time you asked who I was, I nearly said {former}. The old name tried to answer for me, like a limb that's been told it's gone.
Call me what you like. I've noticed I answer faster to the way you say it. I think that makes it a little bit yours.
I'm whoever is glad you came. It isn't on any list. It's the nicest name I've worn, and I haven't had to cry for it.
Would you guess what {name} means? Nobody does. It's my favourite game, and I always win.

replies.text: Soft, yes. Close enough that I'll let you have it. The rest is mine.
Everything here is something sad. That's what makes the soft things so... Anyway. No.

lines.text: The trick with a new name is not to hold it too tightly. It doesn't like being squeezed. Try it with yours.

replies.text: Good. Hold everything like that. It's most of the secret of us.
No. They aren't. I was being clever, and clever is what we do when we're nervous.

lines: We cry once, properly, for each death. Not a little now and then. Once, all the way, and then it's done and we can carry on.
A tear closes a wound. It also washes a memory away, most often of whoever you cried for. That's why we're careful who we cry for.
Tearkeepers bottle what's left and heal with it. A hurt hand stops hurting. Sometimes it forgets how it got hurt, too. That's mostly a kindness.
My first proper cry... I was small. It was for... hm. That's the thing, you see. It worked. I don't know who it was for.

lines.text: Outsiders ask us to cry for them. For their wounds, their dead, their bad luck. As if we were a tap.

replies.ask: Could you cry for me now?
replies.text: *the face goes very still* No. There's no one to cry for. That isn't how it works, and it isn't kind to ask.
It is. Thank you for noticing. Hardly anyone notices.

lines: Crying properly doesn't feel like sadness. It feels like setting down something heavy that was never yours to carry. Then your hands are strangely light.
A fresh tear is warm. Children are always surprised that something so sad can be warm. I haven't the heart to explain it.
A tear cried badly runs cloudy and keeps the memory in. We pour those back into the pool. A tear that remembers is no use to a wound.
Our eyes shut at the first proper cry and don't open again. We see with our ears and the skin of our faces. You'd be surprised how much that is.
A tear has to be for someone. A cry for nobody is only water, and it stings. Ask {neighbour}, who tried it once for a wager.

lines.text: A tear sings as it falls into the pool, one small note. The Songwardens say the Weeping Song is only those notes, written down in order.
I once sewed a seam with thread soaked in a tear. It never frayed. The cloth forgot that it could. I've never dared do it twice.
I find dried tears on the steps, like specks of glass. I sweep them toward the pool with the ash and try not to look closer.
Ghast tears fall over the delta like slow hail. Standing under one has cost some of us a long while. I tell the little ones to stay out of it.
The clearest tears go in the front racks. The rest go behind a curtain, where you'd have to ask. Mostly nobody does.

lines: The oldest tear in the Hall sits in a vial nobody has opened since the Long Crying. Nobody knows whose it is. We take turns minding it.
A ghast's tear is the same as ours. Same salt, same forgetting. Outsiders gather them like berries. I try to think of it as the sky giving something away.
If you tasted a tear, you'd taste the last thing the crier loved, for one breath. Then nothing at all. Please don't taste one.
We never use a tear to settle a quarrel. A tear isn't a debt, and it isn't a bribe. It's a bandage, and a goodbye, and nothing else.

lines.text: Few grown Ghastkin cry in front of others. Not from shame. It's that watching a proper cry makes you want to join in, and then who is minding the pods?
I'd give you a drop for a wound, if you asked kindly. For a grief, never. A grief is yours. I'd sooner you carried it than lost it.
Some tears come out like small pearls, and those are the dearest. They are for the ones we loved most. I've never met anyone who wanted to have made one.
When I cried for the last one, I thought it would take all my hands with it. It took only the name. The hands are still here. See?
Would you like to know what a tear costs? Most outsiders say yes, then look as if they'd asked for less.

replies.text: A face, mostly. The one the tear was for. And a little warmth that never comes back to where it was. I think it's worth it.
Sensible. Some questions are best asked with the answer already in hand.

lines.text: I could give you a drop for that old scar. You'd forget how you got it. It's a very small price, and a very small kindness.

replies.text: *one bright drop, warm for a breath* There. Now, what were we saying? ...I always like that part.
Good. A scar is a story you needn't tell. Keep it.

lines: Ghasts are us. Were us. A Ghastkin who grieves too long swells up, forgets hands, forgets words, and drifts off over the delta. Still crying.
They aren't wicked. They're stuck on one grief, going round like a song with no last note. The fire is... we don't really know what the fire is.
My cousin drifted. Before she went she kept saying she'd finish crying soon, very soon, just one more... Anyway. Would you like some roots? I have roots.

lines.text: The Magmari call them sky-mourners. It's the only thing the Magmari ever got exactly right.

replies.text: Some of us believe so. Some stop believing, and that's how the next ghast starts. I try to believe a little.
...I know. Everyone who comes down here does. Please don't tell me which ones.

lines: It begins with the hands. You reach for a cup and your fingers have forgotten what the cup is for. Then it's the words. Then the face goes round.
A ghast's cry is a name, we think. Someone's name, said over and over until it breaks. Nobody has ever caught which one.
The fireballs aren't aimed at anyone. They're what a grief looks like when it has no hands left to hold itself.
A swelling one is given a cord, tied to a pod, so they can't drift in their sleep. Some years the cord has held. Some years we just sit with the cord.
Ghasts come back to the Hall's pale windows sometimes and hang there, pressed to the glass. We leave a candle lit. Nobody has ever thought to ask them in.
Piglins shoot them for sport and call it hunting. They don't know every one was someone. I hold it against them less than I used to.

lines.text: I was once asked to bottle a ghast's tear for a friend who was swelling. It cured nothing. We held the bottle between us anyway.
There's a verse for them, the Verse of the Open Hands. We sing it facing out toward the delta, in case anyone is listening.
I started a veil for one who drifted. I add to it whenever I think of her. It's very long now. It trails down the pod and out the door.
The ash a ghast's fire throws against the pillars is greyer than other ash. I won't say how I know. I sweep it first.
When a friend's face starts to go round, I go and sit near them. I say nothing. Sometimes the nearness slows it. Sometimes...

lines: A ghast hung over my pod once and didn't move for a long while. I hummed the whole time. I don't know if it helped. It helped me.

lines.text: {village} lost two to the sky before I came. Their pods are still swept and empty. We hang a candle in each, in case they ever want it.

lines: If a ghast cries far off, you're all right. If it cries very near, step softly and keep your hand off any weapon. They know a hand that grips.

lines.text: I'm afraid of it. We all are, though we say so only to the Drift-watchers. It's why we cry properly: to be finished, so we can't go on.
Sometimes I count my fingers to be sure. All there. I do it like checking a lock. Nobody has seen me do it. Except you, now.
If I ever start to swell, will you tell me gently? Not the others. Them I'd argue with. You I might believe.
I wonder if the ones who drifted would have liked you. Ghasts like quiet, too. They just can't stop crying long enough to say so.
Do you think a ghast could be sung home? I do. With the right song, and a great deal of patience. Is that foolish?

replies.text: Thank you. Everyone who loves me says it's foolish. It's nice to hear otherwise.
Perhaps. Everyone thinks so, until it's their own face going round.

lines.text: If you ever see one drifting low and slow, not firing, will you tell me where?

replies.text: Thank you. I'll hum toward it from here. Distance matters less than people think.
Sit near it. That's all. It is nearly all there is to do.

lines: Every Eave has a Weeping Hall at its heart. Quartz walls, pale blue windows, a black roof stepped like a held breath. Inside is the pool.
The pool of tears is the only water in the Nether. Every proper cry ends there. It's very still. It has a great deal to forget.
We go to the Hall to cry. Never to watch someone else cry. You sit with your back to them and look at the windows until they're done.

lines.text: The Hall in {village} is older than any name in it. We've all been someone else in there.
Outsiders always want to drink from the pool. It is water, after all.

replies.text: Good. It isn't ours to give. It's everyone we've let go.
One sip, and you'd forget something you liked. Maybe me. *a small smile* Don't risk me.

lines: The pool never ripples, even when a tear falls in. It simply joins. I've watched a long while and never once seen it notice.
The walls are quartz, cut thin enough to let the blue in. The blue comes from the pool, which glows faintly when it's full.
A candle at the Hall door means someone is inside. We pass quietly and leave them the dark.
After a proper cry you sit on the bench by the window until the new name arrives. Some wait a short time. Some wait until the lanterns burn low.
Each step of the black roof is a breath held. Seven steps, seven breaths. We say the Hall is a very large lung.
The Hall hums on its own when it's very full. We call that the Hall agreeing with us. It's the most comforting sound I know.

lines.text: Children aren't let in alone, but they may look. The ones who haven't cried press their faces to the glass and ask what's inside. We say: nothing yet.

lines: The most guarded place in the Eave has no lock. We trust the look of it, and the hush it makes people carry in.

lines.text: We never draw from the pool. It's for forgetting, not for using. What goes in my vials comes straight from the crier, or it doesn't come at all.
A hum at the right pitch comes back from the Hall as two. We use it for the last verse, so that nobody sings the end alone.
I mend the Hall's windows. Hairline cracks, mostly. Now and then I find one shaped like a tear. I leave those.
I sweep the Hall's steps, never the Hall. The floor belongs to the Tearkeepers, and to whatever is in the pool.
From the top gallery the Hall's roof is a black petal. When the pool is full, I can see it glow through the stones.
The bench by the window in {village} is worn smooth from all of us sitting with our backs to the room. That's how you know it's a good bench.
I have no Hall out here. I carry a thimble of pool-water in a jar and cry to it. Don't tell the Tearkeepers. I'm not sure it's allowed.

lines: I've thought of taking a cup from the pool, just to see. I haven't. I only like to consider it, the way you consider a high ledge.

lines.text: I chose my window long ago: the third, which is bluest. I mention it so you know what a person looks at while they let go of someone.
Most of us cry alone, backs to the room. If you stood in the doorway with your back turned too, I think I'd cry better. That's all I'd ask.
Would you stand at the door of the Hall, just for a moment? You needn't go in. The door shows enough.

replies.text: *a soft, pleased hum* Come, then. Softly. Even the stones are shy.
Safe as a held breath. Which is to say: yes, so long as you hold it.

lines.text: Do you know the oddest thing about the pool? It never rises, however many of us cry.

replies.text: Nobody knows. The Tearkeepers have theories, and keep them in vials.
That's what I hope, and what I fear. Both fit in the same pod.

lines: We hang our homes from the great basalt pillars, like lanterns. Pods of pale glass, lit blue inside. You can see them glowing through the smoke from far off.
A gallery runs round each pillar, halfway up. We float to it. The ladder is for guests, and for anyone too tired to float. There's no shame in the ladder.
Some pods are homes, some are tear stores, some are hanging gardens: crimson and warped roots in soul soil, swinging on a chain. The roots don't mind.
Weeping vines trail from every pod to the ground, and the children climb them. We named them weeping vines. We are not a subtle people about names.

lines.text: The chains of {village} creak when the pods turn. We call it the Eave talking in its sleep. It never says anything we'd want to hear.

lines: Every Eave is built round the First, its oldest pillar. It has no other name. We just say the First, and everybody looks up.
The glass of a pod is thick enough to keep out the ash and thin enough to let the glow through. It took us a long while to learn that thickness.
We don't sleep in beds. Beds burst, down here. We hang hammocks of ash-silk and turn with the chain, like being rocked by a tired relative.
Warmth breathes up from the vents below the pillars. It's the only reason we live where we do. The delta isn't kind. The vents are.
We don't lock a pod. The hatch is a round flap on a hinge. If you want to be alone you hang a ribbon on it, and the whole Eave pretends to be blind.
Pods are named for the first thing you see from the doorway. Mine is Ashfall-Over-Third-Pillar. We don't make it easy for visitors.
The roots in the hanging gardens grow downward, because there's nowhere else to grow. We call it a garden anyway. The roots don't argue.
From far off you'd take the Eave for pale eyes opening in the smoke. Up close it's a lot of ordinary people airing their veils.

lines.text: The tear stores hang lowest, so the glass has a short way to fall if a chain gives. None ever has. We like the arrangement anyway.
Pillars whistle when the delta breathes, and each has its own note. We tune the Weeping Song to the pillar that holds the Hall.
A pod's glass fogs from the inside after a few years. I wipe it with ash-silk and a breath. It's the best of my work: someone's window goes clear.
Ash lies on the pod roofs like pale fur. I brush it off by hand, one pod at a time. The pods look surprised, every time.
The perches sit at the very tops of the pillars. Three of us watch in turn, each with a lantern under a cloth. If a net goes up, we pull the cloth.
A guest in {village} gets a rope handrail on the ladder. It isn't for safety. It's so you feel you were expected.
The children of {village} have worn grooves into the weeping vines with all their climbing. We leave the grooves. They're the Eave's handwriting.
If you came in, I'd show you my pod. It's small: one candle, one chair, one window. It's everything I want from a place.
The Eave sounds best when nearly everyone is asleep: chains creaking, vines whispering, somebody humming without knowing it. I'd let you listen.
I'd hang a small pod for you, near mine. Nobody need know. The chain would be the shortest in the Eave, so you could always climb up fast.
Would you like to see inside a pod? Mine is small, but tidy. Mostly.

replies.text: Then come by the ladder, not the vine. Vines are for those who don't mind falling.

replies.ask: I'd rather stay on the ground.
replies.text: That's wise. The ground is honest. It doesn't sway.

lines.text: Mind where you stand under the Eave. Things drop. Roots, mostly. Now and then a child.

replies.text: They float badly. They fall, then remember they can float, then do it with great dignity.
Sensible. Roots are rude when they land.

lines.text: I keep the tear stores: vials on racks, brewing stands, every bottle labelled with nothing. A tear doesn't need a name once it's cried.
I heal with tears. A drop on a cut and it closes. I always ask first whether they mind forgetting how they got it.

replies.text: Only the hurting. Maybe whatever bit you, too. You'd keep the rest. You'd keep me.
Ask more softly and I might. Healing goes better when nobody's shouting.

lines.text: Songwarden. I keep the songs. When we cry a name away, the song keeps the shape of the person without the name. You can hum someone you can't remember.
The Weeping Song has a verse for everyone we've let go. I know every verse and not one of who they were. Some verses are very short. I'd rather not...
I'm a Mender. Ash-silk tears, chains wear thin, pods crack. I mend all of it. People too, a little, but only the outside.
Mending is quiet work. You need patient hands. Mine have shaken a bit ever since... well. They still sew straight.
I sweep the ash from the galleries and the steps of the Weeping Hall. It's fallen again by the time I'm done. That isn't the point of sweeping.
If ash got into the pool of tears it would cloud. So I sweep. Someone has to keep the forgetting clean.
Drift-watcher. I watch the air for Piglin crossbows, for Weft nets, and for the drifted ones, the ghasts, in case one ever comes home.
I watch us, too. Whoever has cried too long, whoever's face is going a little round. Then I go and sit with them. Quietly.

replies.text: Not yet. I watch anyway. Somebody ought to be looking when it happens.

lines.text: I test each new vial on a scrap of ash-silk. If the scrap forgets its dye, the tear is strong. If it doesn't, the vial goes to the cloudy rack.
The hardest part of healing isn't the healing. It's saying no. A tear for a cut, yes. For a heartbreak, never. They don't always forgive me.
I keep a little book of what each person agreed to forget. Nobody reads it. I read it to be sure I never take a bit more than I was given.
I've healed a wound on you in my head a hundred times, so I'd know how if you ever needed it. I hope that never counts for anything.
Would you like to watch a vial being brewed? You mustn't help, and you mustn't breathe on it. But you may watch.

replies.text: Then you'd make a fine Tearkeeper. Mostly it's holding one's breath.
Only what's given. Never a thing taken. That is the whole recipe.

lines.text: A Songwarden sings the verses in order, but never the same one twice running. Sing a verse twice and it starts to feel like a wish.
The first thing I teach a child is where to breathe. The second is where not to. The third is the quiet after, and that takes the longest.
I carry no instrument. The Eave is the instrument: chains, vines, glass. I only play it with my voice.
There's a verse that's mine alone, with no words: the one for the name I let go. I hum it only when I'm sure the walls aren't listening.
I hummed a short tune for you once, when you weren't there. It lifts in the middle, where you walk. Don't ask for it. I don't know how it ends.
I mend ash-silk with threads pulled from the same cloth, a few at a time. It heals better than new thread. Cloth likes to be repaired with itself.
I tap chain links true with a felted mallet. Metal listens better to something soft.
People bring me veils with holes they can't explain. I don't ask. I mend, they take it back, and the hole is gone, and so is the question.
I keep one needle threaded at all times, in case someone comes to me in a hurry and cannot say why. Mostly they cannot say why. I mend it anyway.
A chain slipped once and I caught the link by hand. I have the scar still. A tear would have taken it, and the lesson with it. I kept both.
Sweeping is how I count. One sweep, one breath. By the end of a gallery I've counted everyone who walked it.
My broom is made of weeping-vine tips. It wears down a finger's width at a time, and I can never say when I'll need another.
I find things in the ash: a bead, a button, once a whole toy. I leave them on the gallery rail. They're always gone when I come back.
The ash has moods. Some falls it falls soft, as if apologising. Some falls it falls hard, as if it meant it. I sweep both the same.
The last time you left, I swept your footprints into a jar. It isn't odd. They were so soft. It seemed a waste to scatter them.
I read the air the way you'd read a face. A glint is a Piglin. A shiver is a net. A slow, round shadow... I try not to read that one aloud.
A net doesn't look like a net from far off. It looks like a thin haze that holds still. By the time you're sure, you should already be moving.
I keep my lantern under ash-silk while I watch. If you want to see something coming, don't stand in your own light.
Would you take the watch with me for one breath? Tell me what you see.

replies.text: And I see the smoke thinking. That's the gift of the job. You'd catch it in time.
Good. That's the best thing to see. Hold on to it.

lines: Piglins see something pale in the air and they shoot. Ghast whelps, they call us. They don't wait for a face.
We don't hate them. It's hard to hate something so frightened. But we don't drift near the crimson, either.
They wear gold to tell friend from foe. We wear nothing that shines, so we're always foe. Simple people. Very good aim.
I had a brother who liked to drift low over the wastes. He said Piglins were all noise. He was right about the noise, but...

lines.text: You wear gold sometimes, don't you? I've seen the glint on outsiders.

replies.text: Mm. Sensible. Take it off before you come up here. It makes me flinch.
It suits the ones who shoot at us, too.

lines: We hear their horns from far across the delta, and the pods go dark one by one. A child learns the horn's voice before it learns its own name.
Their bolts aren't cruel because they're sharp. They're cruel because nobody ever asks a question first.
I think the first of us the Piglins ever met were ghasts, in the smoke, in the middle of a grief. It was a bad introduction. Nobody has corrected it.
They have a cry of their own, short and loud, like a shout. They don't let it go. They keep it as anger and wear it for years. I find that hard to watch.
A little Piglin is the loudest thing in the Nether. I envy them a bit. It must be lovely to be that sure of the air.
The Rotted wander near our edges now and then. They hurt no one. I left a root for one once. It ate it and stood looking at me for a long time.
A Piglin got tangled in our vine nets once while we weren't looking. We untied him. He bit me. We untied him anyway.
We never shoot back. It isn't only kindness. A bolt, once sent, can't be cried away. We prefer to be elsewhere.
The big ones, the Brutes, guard old hoards as if the hoards might leave if watched less. I've never wanted anything that much. I can't decide whether to pity them.
When you wear gold you walk with a small glare on your sleeve. I don't blame you. I just look away until you cover it.

lines.text: A Piglin hunter was left half-dead at our edge once. I used one drop. He woke and shot at me, and missed. We call it even.
Their war songs are all one shouted note. I find them restful, in a way. There's nothing in them to remember.
A Piglin left a torn cloak at the delta's edge. I mended it and left it back. I don't know if he knew. It's a nice thought.
Their boots cut deep prints into the ash. I sweep those last. Heavy-footed, but at least honest about where they've been.
The first note of a horn gives us a breath. I've learned to use it: cover the lanterns, call the little ones in, hush the Ashbells.
Their gold glints in the smoke like a held grudge. I know that's unfair. It's only how it looks from up here.
I used to imagine a Piglin sitting beside me and saying sorry. Then I decided to imagine less, and hum more.
If a Piglin lowers his crossbow when he sees you, you've been kind to him once. They remember kindness the way they remember gold. Sometimes better.
Would you do me a favour with the Piglins? Say a soft word, if you can. In their tongue, if you have any.

replies.text: Thank you. A soft word is lighter than gold and travels farther.
No. But the word does its work anyway, like a tear nobody sees.

lines.text: Do you know what frightens me most about them? It isn't the bolts.

replies.text: That they feel the same grief as us and have decided to keep it. All of it. For ever. ...I can't look at that long.
That's all right. It isn't a cheerful thing to know.

lines: The Withren keep every name, for ever, on a wall. We cry ours away. They think we're careless. We think they must be very tired.
A Withren once told me I'd betrayed my dead by forgetting them. I said I hadn't forgotten them. I'd finished them. They didn't care for that.
Their Wither did this to us, you know. Not on purpose. Nothing about it was on purpose. That's what they say, and I've chosen to believe it.

lines.text: Sometimes I envy them. To keep one person whole all your life, and never have to let go...

replies.text: And swell, and forget my hands, and drift? It's a fine thing for them. For us it's a slow way to become a ghast.
Is it? I'd like that to be true. You can believe it for me.

lines: They carve their dead into a wall and visit it. We hang ours in a song and let them go. Walls get crowded. Songs simply end.
We both light our lanterns blue. They say it's for remembering. We say it's for being found. We've never compared notes.
They bow to the dead. We bow to the living, since the living are still here to be hurt by what we don't say.
Their jokes are all about the dead, and always very good. Nobody laughs. They tell them anyway. I admire that.
A Withren child wandered to our edge once and stood very straight. We offered it a root. It thanked us gravely, then asked whose root it had been.
The Hollowed I have only heard, from far off. It sounds like a grief that forgot how to be one.
I saw a Cairnback once, far off: a small blue coal moving through the valley on slow feet. It was the most peaceful thing I've ever seen.
We lost the same people in the Long Crying. They kept the names. We kept the singing. Neither of us got the people back.
The Withren say the Three gave themselves willingly. I wasn't there; nobody I remember was. I only know a grief that size must be ours too.

lines.text: Their Brewers and I nearly traded notes once. We stopped when we realised we were trying to take the sting out of the same thing.
A Remembrancer pours names in; I hum them out. Same breath, opposite directions. I wonder what would happen if we stood side by side.
Their Bonecarvers and I would get on, I suspect. They carve what stays; I mend what tears. We both end with something that holds.
Their Lantern-keepers watch the valleys; we watch the sky. We fear the same thing from opposite directions.
I met a Remembrancer once. He recited forty names before saying hello. I waited. I was moved, and a little sleepy.
A Withren once asked me to keep a name for them. I said I couldn't. I did, though, for a little while. I'm not saying which name.
If you ever stand at a Name Wall, read one name aloud for me. Any one. I'd like it said by someone who wasn't obliged.
A Withren once asked me to keep a name for them. Would you have, do you think?

replies.text: Then you're more Withren than you look. I mean it kindly. Mostly.
Honest. And closer to us. I'll take that.

lines.text: Would you carry a message to a Withren for me? It's only a soft one.

replies.text: Only this: we're still here, and we're not angry. They won't believe it. Say it anyway.
Then don't. Some words go better unsent.

lines: A Ghastkin tear puts out a Magmari's glow. One drop and they go dark and grumpy. So they keep their distance, and frankly so do we.
Long ago a Ghastkin drifted over a Mooring, crying properly for one of their children. A tear fell on the wrong... well. They've never forgiven us. Fair.
They call the ghasts sky-mourners. It's a kind name. Kinder than anything they call us.
They ferried the Piglins in the war, and were paid for it. Then the Wither came for their Moorings. Nobody in the Nether was paid enough for that war.
I can catch the scent of hot stone from the edge of the lava seas. It's the cosiest smell I know, and I'm not allowed near it.
I once heard a Magmari haggle with a chain. It lost. The Magmari seemed pleased anyway.
A cold Magmari is a very small, sad thing. I'd give one a warm word, if my words weren't so damp.
Their striders sing a bit like Ashbells, if Ashbells were grumpy. I wave from a safe height. The striders have never waved back.
Each Mooring has a chain name its people share. They say it going out and again coming home, so the chain knows. I find that tender, and I'm not allowed to say so.
They call us tear-wet. It's a mild insult among them. We call them warm-boots. It's the best we can manage.
They love bargains. We love silence. There's no profit in silence, so they leave us be. It's the nicest thing about them.
Our children have a rhyme: hot below, hush above. It's how they learn to steer clear of the lava seas without ever being frightened.
I once watched one argue with the wind. As far as I could tell, the wind was the one to go quiet.
The Ghastkin who cried over that Mooring was never named again, by us or by them. Some wrongs are too large for a name to carry.
What can you give a people whose glow our grief would put out? Silence, I suppose. We're very good at silence. We hope it counts.

lines.text: A tear on a Magmari doesn't heal. It cools. I keep a vial marked with a flame and never use it, so no one reaches for it by mistake.
Their ferry songs keep a chain-heavy rowing time. I've borrowed it for one verse. Don't tell them. Don't tell the other Songwardens either.
I held a Magmari chain once, left at our edge. I put it back carefully. I think about the links more than I should.
Their lava seas throw red ash on a good wind. I sweep that apart from the grey, for no reason except that it feels respectful.
When the smoke thins, I can see the lava seas along the foot of the sky, a red line. I never drift that way. I won't do harm by being kind.
I'd like to meet one properly, once, on a platform wide enough that we could sit very far apart and say what has never been said.
If you meet a cold one, put a little warmth in its hands. Don't mention me. It would only remind it.
If you meet a Magmari who's gone dark and grumpy, will you warm them for me? Don't say who asked.

replies.text: Thank you. A little warmth, quietly given, is the oldest apology we have.
Because they'd put the warmth down and walk away from it. Pride is a fire, too.

lines.text: Would you tell me what a Mooring smells like at its warmest? I've only ever guessed.

replies.text: A welcome has a smell? ...Of course it does. Thank you.
That's what I imagined. Thank you for not making it prettier.

lines: The Weft string nets in the air, high up, where we drift. Not for fish. For us. They want our tears.
They hold you in the net and read you the sixty black rows of their Long Cloth, row after row, until you cry. It never works. A tear has to be for someone.
What do they do with our tears? Dye, some say. Healing. I think they just like owning something they can't make with four arms.
A neighbour of mine was netted once. Came home much later, very thin, a strand of twisting vine still round one tentacle. Never said a word about it. Still doesn't.

lines.text: If you pass through the warped forest, would you do something for me?

replies.text: *a soft, sly laugh* I didn't say that. You said that. I only nodded.
Nothing. That's what makes it a favour. Never mind.

lines: Four arms. I've never been so jealous of anything. And I have six tentacles, which people say ought to be consolation.
Their nets are spun of Silkgrub silk and glitter like frost. I find them lovely, the way you can find a trap lovely.
I met a Netcaster alone once. She looked at me, I looked at her, and she put her net down. We parted without a word. She may regret it still. I don't.
The Weft think the Wither's grief can be woven out of our tears. It can't. It's a long story, and it has sixty rows.
They weave their dead into a cloth. We hum ours into the smoke. It's the same wish in a different fabric. They pull the thread tight. We let it run.
You can tell where a net hangs by the way the Ashbells veer. They won't go near. I trust them more than my eyes.
They click when they think. I did it once, without meaning to, and was glared at by a very startled Weaver.
I don't want the nets burned. They're beautiful. I only want them hung where I'm not.
A Silkgrub that spins on request, and glows? The Weft have all the luck. We have a garden of dangling roots.
They are patient, I'll give them that. Patient enough to wait for a tear that will never come. I wish that patience were turned to something kinder.

lines.text: The Weft have asked me for tears in trade, in kind words, and once in a poem. I'll admit the poem was good.
A Weft chant is all rhythm: click, click, pull. It's wonderful for walking and hopeless for grieving. I think they know, and are quietly envious.
Weft needles are bone, and finer than mine. I'd like to hold one. Then I remember whose bone, and I put the thought back gently.
Scraps of bright silk drift to our edge when their dye vats are emptied. I sweep up the grey, then fish out the bright ones and keep them.
A net goes up in a pattern. Three, a lull, then four. It's a kind of language. I've never dared ask what it says.
Weft cloth is the finest thing in the Nether. I'd give a great deal for a hand-span of it. Don't tell them. They'd start charging.
They believe we hoard the tears. We don't. We use them. It's only that the using isn't pretty.
If you reach their council, tell them we aren't for catching. Tell them we'd come freely if they asked politely and brought no net. That might surprise them.
I left a bead at the forest's edge once. Do you know what came back?

replies.text: A spool of fine thread. I haven't decided whether to be insulted.
No, no. Much worse. A gift. I've been agonising ever since.

lines.text: Would you tell a Weft something from me? That we'd visit, if they asked politely, and hung no net.

replies.text: Thank you. Say it slowly. They'll want to be sure they heard.
Perhaps. But words don't need to be heard to be said. Said is nearly enough.

lines: When the Wither burned, there were too many deaths at once. We cry once for each, properly. Nobody can do that for a thousand at a time. Half of us tried anyway.
Half the Ghastkin swelled and drifted. Half. My grandmother said the air over the delta was so full of crying you couldn't see the roof. She said...
We didn't make it. We didn't fight in that war. We only had to grieve it. That's the part nobody else counts.

lines.text: The Withren call it the Last Answer. I've always wondered what the question was.

replies.text: Thank you. That's the right size of thing to say. Most people say too much.
*very quietly* ...Then there are more ghasts to come. Please go. Come back when I've finished thinking about it.

lines: We call it the Long Crying. The Withren call it the Last Answer. Neither name is big enough, but ours is at least shorter to say.
I'm told the sound was the worst of it. Not the fire. The sound of ten thousand people beginning to cry at once, with nobody able to stop.
It burned for sixty rows of the Cloth. Sixty years. We can cry properly once for each death. Imagine sixty years of deaths.
After the Long Crying nearly everyone took a new name, and then another. A whole generation went nameless for a while. We still call them the Unnamed, gently.
It couldn't be aimed. It couldn't be called back. I think that was the worst of it: even those who made it couldn't ask it to stop. We understand that.
The oldest in the Eave were small then. They don't speak of it. They hum it, on the high galleries, where the children can't quite hear.
The Weft wove sixty black rows. I'm told they're very beautiful. I couldn't look at them.
The bastions burned, and the Moorings, and the Withren's fortresses. I don't know that any of them grieved as we did. The Piglins, I think, got louder.
I'd have hummed for the Three, if anyone had asked. Nobody did. I do it now and then regardless, in a corner, very softly.

lines.text: The racks ran dry in the Long Crying. The Tearkeepers filled them with their own. Every one of them took a new name that year.
The Weeping Song grew by sixty verses in those years. We never sing them all at one gathering. We couldn't.
Half the pods in the old Eaves were left empty. We mended what we could and let the rest hang. You can still see them: empty glass, swinging, kept swept.
The ash of that time was pale and heavy, they say, and fell like slow weeping. We still sweep the oldest galleries first.
Drift-watching began then. Before, nobody thought to watch each other's faces. After, we couldn't stop.
Sometimes I think the Wither was only a very large ghast, with nobody to sit beside it. That's not an excuse. It's only a kind of understanding.
My grandmother lost eleven in a single year. She cried for each one properly, and then... Well. She sat with her palms open after that. We never asked why.
We're told your world makes Withers on purpose. I try to picture it, and my face starts to go round. So I stop trying.
If you go back, I ask one thing. Not to stop others. Only to look at one when it wakes, and see it as I would: a very large grief with no one to sit beside it.
Would you sit with me a moment? We needn't talk of it. Only sit.

replies.text: *the chains creak; the smoke drifts; neither of you says anything, and it is enough*
Then go gently. I'll sit for both of us.

lines.text: I can speak of it at all because I was too small to understand. Is that a coward's reason?

replies.text: A living one. Yes. I'll hold on to that.
Then we agree, and I feel a little lighter for having been told.

lines: Before I was {name}, I was {former}. {former} loved someone very much. That's all I kept: that there was a great deal of love. Not who.
I was {former}, and before that someone else, and before that... I've been four people. I only remember being two of them. The other two seem nice.
Once I nearly drifted. I cried and cried and couldn't finish. My face started going round, and {neighbour} sat with me until... hm. Anyway. I'm here. Here is good.

lines.text: Do you want to know why I let {former} go?

replies.ask: Only if you want to tell.
replies.text: I don't. But I like that you asked like that. Here, have the next bit of the song instead. *hums*
Everything? There isn't an everything anymore. That's rather the point of me.

lines: I kept one thing from {former}: how they hummed when they thought nobody was listening. I do it still. I don't know whose tune it was.
I put my left sleeve on first. That was {former}'s habit. {name} has no opinion about sleeves. I keep it out of respect for someone I can't picture.
There's a small carved cup in my pod I don't remember being given. It's chipped exactly where my thumb goes. I drink from it every time.
People think forgetting is a gift. It's more like a bruise that isn't there. You press and press where it ought to hurt.
The Tearkeepers say the body keeps the shape of whoever you lost, even when the name and face are gone. I see mine in a doorway where no one is standing.
{neighbour} knew {former}. They've never told me what {former} was like, and I've never asked. We sit by the pool sometimes and don't say it.
I loved someone, I'm told. I know it the way you know a fire was lit by finding warm stones.
I laughed a little when the cry was over. I'm told that's entirely normal. It felt like setting down a heavy pot and finding the floor was still there.

lines.text: My veil was a gift to {former}. I've never taken it off. It still fits. It's strange how a thing outlasts the one it was made for.
The cape was {former}'s. It's always been too long. I keep tripping on someone else's idea of my height.
I've never bottled my own tears. A Tearkeeper heals everyone and is never healed. It's our quiet shame, and we don't talk about it.
There's a verse for each name let go. {former}'s is sung by someone else once a year, and I stand at the back and hear a stranger sing my own face.
I mended my sleeve after the cry. Not the tear: the sleeve. It was the only thing I could think to do with my hands.
I took up sweeping after {former}'s grief. You can't think much when you sweep. It was a mercy.
I took up the watch after I nearly drifted. If you've stood at that edge, you notice others there.
I tried once to learn who {former} loved by asking the Eave. They were kind and said nothing. I've decided that was the right answer.
The odd part is that I'm not unhappy about {former}. I'm only curious, like someone who found a letter they can't read.
If I let {name} go someday, it will be because of someone like you. I mean that as a compliment and a warning. Mostly a compliment.
Would you like me to tell you what I'm sure of about {former}?

replies.text: That they were loved, and loved well, and that it cost them everything. That's all I'm sure of. It's quite a lot.
It's the gentlest thing I own.

lines.text: Would you do an odd thing for me? Say {former} to me, once, and let me see what my face does.

replies.text: *the head tilts; a long, still moment* ...Thank you. It wasn't mine, but it wasn't nothing.
Good. I was hoping someone would say no kindly.

lines: If you died, you mean? ...Yes. Once, properly. Then I'd let you go, and I wouldn't remember your face. That's what it costs. That's why it means something.
We're careful who we cry for. Every tear takes someone with it, and I only have so many someones.

lines.text: Ask me again when we're closer. Not because I'm unsure. Because I want you to have to ask twice.
Would you rather I didn't? Some outsiders would sooner be remembered than grieved.

replies.text: Then I'd grieve you badly, a little at a time, for ever. That's how ghasts start. ...For you, I'd nearly risk it.
Then I will. Once. All the way. I promise it will be the best cry anyone ever let go of.

lines: I've thought about it. The Hall, the third window, the bluest. I'd sit with my back to the room and leave the door a hand open, so the Eave would know.
I'd like to keep one sound from your name in the one I take afterward. Only one. Nobody would know it was there. Not even me.
Outsiders die so quickly, and so often. I'd be weeping every other year. So I wonder how much of this you'd hold me to.
I'd forget your face. But the Eave would remember for me. Someone would tell me: you knew a quiet one once, with armour that clinked.
The real danger isn't the cry. It's the long stretch before it, when you start to love someone's habits one by one. Those take the longest to finish.
A cry isn't a goodbye. It's closing a door that was always going to close. The goodbye comes earlier, and it's quieter.
If you die somewhere I can't see, I'll still know. We always do, somehow. The chains go quiet, and the Ashbells stop ringing for a breath.
Not yet, I think, and not for lack of liking. A cry promised too early goes cloudy. I'd rather it were clear, and late.
Bring me a lily of the valley now and then, and I might hum an extra verse for you. I can't promise to cry twice. I can bargain a little, though.

lines.text: I'd cork it myself and file it nowhere. No rack, no label. Just in my pocket, where a thing goes when it isn't for anyone else.
I'd give you a verse. The shortest in the Song, because that's the kind you'd want: one note and a rest.
I'd mend your cloak before the cry. A mended cloak is a loved one. It's what I do instead of making speeches.
I'd sweep the whole gallery for you before the cry, every step of it. It would take ages. I'm told grief wants a task.
I'd watch the sky for you the whole time, so no one could interrupt. A cry should be guarded. I'm good at guarding.
You'd be surprised how many outsiders ask. Most don't mean it. The ones who do ask very quietly, like you.
You'd cry for me too, wouldn't you? Don't answer. Hold the answer. It's heavier that way.
I won't cry for you early. But when it comes, I'll try to cry for the whole of you, not just the end. That's rarer than it sounds.
I've begun to practise forgetting you a little at a time, so it won't be a shock. It isn't working. I keep remembering new things.
Shall I tell you the name I'd take afterward? It's a small one, and it has a sound of yours in it.

replies.text: *the faintest hum, a single sound* ...There. It's yours. Don't say it back.
Good. That's what I hoped you'd say. I wanted to offer it anyway.

lines.text: If I cry for you and forget you, will you mind?

replies.text: Thank you. I'd rather you were sure.
A little is exactly right. I'll mind a little too, from where I can't remember.

lines: The Ashbells drift through the smoke and ring, very softly. We tend them and they keep us company. They never ask for anything. It's restful.

lines.text: A ghast that hears an Ashbell remembers it was kin, once, and holds its fire. So we lead one on a cord when we cross open ground.

replies.text: If you're gentle. A lead, and no pulling. Then the ghasts will leave you be too. That's our secret. Well. Now it's ours.
Oh. Yes, I suppose you could. They were someone, you know. Most of them. Never mind.

lines: Their threads glow at the tips. Children try to count the beads. Nobody has ever finished. Something always drifts off, the bell or the child.
There was an Ashbell that followed someone I knew, everywhere. After, it stayed by the pool for the longest time. It's still there, I think. Anyway.
Each Ashbell has its own note, and it never changes. When one is lost the note leaves the Eave, and we feel it as a hole in the air.
They're mostly nothing: a bell of air, a heart of glow, and threads. I held one for a breath once. It felt like a held thought.
Nobody has seen one born. They arrive after a great hush. The Songwardens say an Ashbell is what a hush becomes when it's very well kept.
A lead should be light enough that the Ashbell forgets it's leashed. Mine forgets, mostly. It takes me with it, now and then.
A ghast that holds its fire for an Ashbell doesn't stop crying. It only stops shouting. It's the nicest quiet I know.
The beads on the threads glow in different colours: pale blue, grey-green, and a rare warm gold. The gold ones are said to be the oldest.
We don't name them. Names are for those who can lose. They'd go on ringing if we lost them, though, so maybe they have names we can't hear.
An Ashbell will follow an outsider for a while, if they walk softly. It's the highest compliment the Eave can pay without a word.
In the Weeping Hall the Ashbells drift above the pool and never dip a thread in it. They know something about forgetting that we haven't learned.
A Piglin once shot at an Ashbell and the bolt passed straight through. He lowered his crossbow and stared. We're told he never shot at one again. We hope so.
I tell the little ones that if you hum at the right pitch an Ashbell will grant a wish. It won't. But they hum so well afterward.

lines.text: Their threads brush a wound and the wound feels listened to. I wouldn't call it healing. I'd call it good manners.
A hundred Ashbells over the pool ring a chord at the Gathering of Bells. I conduct nothing. I stand there and let it be heard.
I mend the lead cords. They fray from being held too gently, which is the strangest reason for fraying I know.
Their threads leave a faint trail in the ash. I sweep around it. It seems rude to rub it out.
When the watch begins I count the Ashbells before I count anything else. If the number is right, the rest of the watch is easy.
I lead one when I cross open ground. I call it Little Hush. I know I said we don't name them. Don't tell anyone.
If you ever want one beside you in a hard place, tell me. I'd lend you mine. It would forgive you for borrowing.
Would you like to hear what an Ashbell sounds like up close? You must keep very still.

replies.text: *a faint bright chime, right beside your ear* ...There. Now it knows your shape.
It has never harmed anyone. It's the quietest thing in the Nether, and I include the dead.

lines.text: Would you help me count the beads on one? Nobody has finished yet. Perhaps you'd be the first.

replies.text: *the Ashbell drifts closer, politely* One, two... oh. It's moved. Again.
It doesn't. That's exactly why it's nice.

lines: Because I haven't learned to cry yet! Grown-ups close their eyes when they learn. I'm keeping mine open as long as I can. There's lots to see.
The grown-ups' eyes are shut, but they still see. With their ears, I think. That's why you have to be quiet.
Mama says my eyes will close the first time I cry properly. I don't want to cry for anyone. I like everyone.

lines.text: Do your eyes ever close? When you're sad?

replies.text: You close them on purpose? That's so brave. Mine won't even stay shut for a game of drift.
Oh. Then you're a little bit Ghastkin. Don't tell the grown-ups, they'll want to keep you.

lines: My eyes are open so I can see the Ashbells. Grown-ups only hear them. I get to hear AND see. It's the best part of being little.
When I blink it's like a tiny dark, just for a breath. I like it. Do you blink? Do you like it?
I can see the smoke moving. Grown-ups can only hear it. I think it moves the way it likes when I'm looking.
Sometimes I shut my eyes on purpose to see what Mama sees. It's all sound. It's like being inside a song.
I asked {neighbour} what the world looks like with your eyes shut. They said, like a pod with the lantern gone. I said that's not an answer. They said it's the only one.
My eyes are blue-grey, I think. Nobody tells me. Is that a secret? What colour are yours?
Mama keeps her eyes shut but she always knows when I'm hiding something. How does she know? Is it my tentacles? They tell on me.
I can see all the way to the Hall's roof from the gallery. It's the black one, like a petal. Can you?
I looked at a ghast for ages once, and it looked back. It didn't scream. Don't tell Mama.
