My friend says when her eyes close she'll be able to hear colours. I want to hear colours. I'm not sure I want to cry for it.
You've got such round eyes. Are they always that round? Do they get tired?
I crossed my eyes at Mama and she laughed with hers shut. How did she know? I'm going to find out.
My cousin's eyes shut early. Everyone went quiet. He has a new name now. I still say the old one when nobody's listening. It isn't a bad secret.

lines.text: From our gallery you can see all the Ashbells at once, with your eyes open. Mama has to listen for hers, one at a time.
I've been looking at you very carefully since you came. I think you've got the kind of eyes that notice things. Mine are like that too.
I practise keeping my eyes open when I'm sad, to see how long I can. I got to nearly a hundred breaths once.
When my eyes close, I want you to be the last thing I see with them. Is that all right? I've thought about it a lot.
I'll still know your step even with my eyes shut. I've been practising. Close your eyes. ...No, you can't, you're listening. Never mind. I know it already.
Do you want to try? Close your eyes and tell me what you hear. I'll tell you if you're right.

replies.text: You're breathing so loudly! ...That was a joke. You're doing it right. Keep going.
I was NOT. ...Maybe a little. You're good at this.

lines.text: Can I ask something? When you shut your eyes, do you see anything?

replies.text: Colours! Mama says shut eyes only see dark. I'm going to tell her she's wrong. Quietly.
That's what Mama said. Dark with a hum. I think I'd like that.

lines: Not properly! I cried when I bumped my head on the gallery, but Mama says that wasn't real crying, that was just leaking.
When I do my first proper cry I'll get a new name. I've been thinking of names. I don't want to use them up, though.
My friend's big sister cried for the first time, and now she's quiet all the time, and she has a new name, and she doesn't remember... I don't like this game. Ask me something else.

lines.text: Will you tell me if crying hurts?

replies.text: Oh. Like vine-scrapes. All right. I can do that, then. Later. Much later.
It matters to me. I'm the one who has to do it.

lines: Leaking is when it comes out of your eyes. Crying is when it comes out of everything. I've only ever leaked.
I don't want a new name. I like {name}. It fits like my favourite blanket. If I cry, who will it fit?
Mama says you have to be big enough to carry the person you cry for. I can't even carry a pot of roots.
{neighbour} says when you cry it goes in the pool and everyone's nicer to you for a while. That doesn't sound so bad. I still don't want to.
I saw Uncle come out of the Hall. He didn't know me for a breath. Then he did, and smiled so hard. I held his hand all the way home.
The Songwarden says a proper cry is the biggest thing a person does. Bigger than floating. Bigger than climbing all the way to the top.
Sometimes my eyes get hot and I want to leak, and then I think about floating and it goes away. That's my trick. Don't tell the big ones.
Everyone goes quiet when someone's going to the Hall. They put a candle by the door. I put a little one too, so they know I'm sorry.
Do you cry loud, in your world? Mama says outsiders cry out loud. That sounds so tiring.
I'm going to be brave when it's time. Brave means standing in the doorway for two breaths. Then you go in. I practise the standing.
Crying is like climbing the very tallest vine. Everyone says the view is lovely, but nobody tells you how far down it is.
If I cry too long I might float away. That's what happens. Mama says it won't happen to me. But she says it too quickly.
Some grown-ups come out of the Hall laughing, and some come out very quiet. Mama says both are fine. I'm hoping for laughing.

lines.text: When I cry I'll get a veil like Mama's. A real one, sheer, not the practice one made of weeds.
When I cry I'll get my own hood and cape. Mine will be the shortest cape in the Eave, because I'm short.
I told {neighbour} you asked me about crying, and they said that's the nicest thing a stranger can ask. Nobody ever asks. They always tell.
When I cry I'm going to remember you right up to the very last breath of it. Then... I don't know. I haven't thought about the then.
I asked Mama if it's all right to be sad about a person who isn't gone. She said that's called loving someone. I think I'm doing it a bit.
Does it count if you cry for an Ashbell? I think it should.

replies.text: Then I've cried properly once! ...No wait, then I'd have a new name. I take it back.
Hmm. Mama said that too. But it felt very proper.

lines.text: Will you hold my hand when I do? Not in the Hall. After. When I come out and don't know anybody.

replies.text: *a small, shaky sigh* Good. Then it's fine. Don't forget you promised.
Trying is good. Trying is nearly the same, if you're quiet about it.

lines: Drift-and-seek! You hide in the smoke and the seeker finds you by listening. I always win. I'm the quietest. Except when I giggle.
We climb the weeping vines all the way up to the pods and slide back down. The grown-ups say floating is better. Floating doesn't make your hands tingle.
Counting ghasts from the gallery. Eleven is the most, though {neighbour} says twelve. One of them was a puff of smoke. I'm sure of it.

lines.text: Will you play with me? You can be the Piglin. You have to be loud and miss.

replies.text: That's the quietest Piglin ever! You're terrible at being a Piglin. I love it.
*floats up very fast* ...That was too real. I'm coming down in a moment.

lines: Bead-stack! You pile empty glass tear beads as high as you can before the wind comes. My record is nine. {neighbour} says eleven, but I counted, and it was ten.
Ashbell slow-race: you hold a thread and the slowest Ashbell wins. It's harder than it sounds. They keep getting excited.
Vine-swing: grab the weeping vine at the top and let go at the bottom. Don't let go in the middle. I did that once. I floated, so it's fine.
We draw pictures in the ash and run before the sweeper sees. She always sees. She pretends not to. I think she likes the pictures.
Name-guessing: someone hides behind a vine and you guess what their next name will be. Mine was Sloppy Tentacle. I lost on purpose.
We make tiny pods out of ash-silk scraps and hang them from the lowest vine. Mine is for an Ashbell. It has never once gone inside. It's for when it does.
We pretend to be ghasts: float up with your hands out and go wooo while the others pretend to be sad. Mama says we shouldn't. We do it very softly.
Piglin-and-Ghastkin: the Piglin has to find you by listening. The Piglin always loses. Piglins can't listen.
Candle-sitting: whoever keeps their candle lit the longest by sitting still wins. The grown-ups say it's good for us. It's very boring. I always win.
We chase the Ashbells. You're not supposed to. They always get away. That's why it's fun.
Climb-and-count: climb a vine counting the pods you pass. The number's always different, because the pods move. Mama says that's the point.
Statue: everyone freezes when the chains creak. Whoever's still moving when it stops is It. The chains creak a lot, which is unfair.
Name-Swap: we pick a new name for each other for the length of one breath. I was a Lantern. You'd make a good Lantern.

lines.text: On the Hall steps in {village} we hop on the dark tiles only. The sweeper pretends to be cross. She's not.
I made up a new game just for you. It's called Quiet Friend. You walk about and I say warmer or colder for how quiet you are. You're always warm.
Come play with us! The others are shy, but I told them you're all right. You can be a rock. Rocks are important.
I always let you win at drift. Don't tell. It isn't winning if you know.
When I'm big and my eyes are shut, I'll still play with you. I'll call it Listening. The rules will be the same.
Want to play Unfinished? I start a story and you add one bit, but neither of us is allowed to end it.

replies.ask: Once there was a ghast who...
replies.text: ...who found a very small bell, and... oh, you're good at this! And then she... go on, go on!
It isn't! It's the happiest game. Nothing ever ends.

lines.text: Play hush-tag with me? Whoever's It has to catch you without a sound. You can be It first.

replies.text: Count to ten, no noise! ...You counted too loud. You're It for ever now.
Later's fine. I'll keep your place. It's the best place.

lines: Do you have a pool of tears where you live? Who cries in it? Does it ever get full?
What's a sky? I asked {neighbour}, and they said it's a roof that forgot to be a roof. Is that right?
Why do you have only two legs? Don't you fall over? I'd fall over. I fall over with four tentacles.

lines.text: Have you ever seen a ghast up close? Did it look sad? Did it look like anyone?

replies.text: That's what Mama said. She said they look a little like everyone. I don't like that. Ask me something nicer.
Oh. ...Oh. Was it crying? They're always crying. You can't know which one it was.

lines: Do you have a Mama? Is she loud? Does she shout at you the way the Piglins shout at everything?
What do you eat? We eat roots, and sap. Do you eat roots? Do they taste like gold?
Where do you sleep? In a hammock? On the ground? Doesn't the ground wobble?
How do you stay so quiet in all that armour? Do you stuff it with ash-silk when nobody's looking?
Do you have ghasts where you're from? What do they do? Do they cry too?
What's the biggest thing you've ever seen? Bigger than the Hall? Bigger than a whole pillar?
Do you know any funny songs? Not Weeping Song ones. Funny ones. We don't have any, so I'd have to keep it a secret.
Why do you carry so many things? Do they all have names? Even the sticks?
Have you ever been so quiet that you forgot you were there? I did once, and then I bumped into me.
Can I touch your armour? Not hold. Just touch the cold.
Do you have a name you'd let go? I wouldn't. I'd keep mine in my pocket and never cry.
What does water feel like? Is it like the pool? Is it as heavy as a thought?
Do you have friends at home? Do they know you're here, being quiet with us?
Do your people float? Maybe when you're asleep? I bet you float and don't know.
What's the best thing in your pack? I don't want it. I only want to know it's there.

lines.text: Would you teach me a word from your world? A small one. I'll keep it in my pod.
Are you going to stay? I mean for a long time. If it's no, don't say it. Just say quiet.
When you're far away, do you think about the Eave? I think about you. I put a candle by the door in case.
Do you have a secret you're not allowed to tell? I do. I won't tell you mine.

replies.text: Ooh! Don't tell! We'll swap in a thousand breaths.
Everyone has secrets. Yours are probably very quiet ones.

lines.text: Can I look in your pack? Only look!

replies.text: *peeks, with enormous eyes* It's so full! Is it all yours? Do you have to carry it all?
That's fair. I'd say no too. I keep a candle in mine.

lines: I touched the pool of tears once. Just one finger. I don't remember why I'm not allowed. I think that's why I'm not allowed.
A ghast came right up to the gallery once, really close, and it stopped crying for a little while when I hummed. Don't tell. They'd stop me humming.
I've thought of a Ghastkin name for you. I'll tell you when I'm bigger. It's a good one. It has soft letters in it.

lines.text: I hid a candle in the hanging garden, for when I'm sad. Do you want to know which pot?

replies.text: You're good at this. Most grown-ups say tell me, tell me. All right. It stays secret.
*giggles* The one with the crookedest roots. Now it's half your secret. Don't spill it.

lines: I know where the Ashsweeper hides her good broom. Behind the third vine. Don't tell her I know. I only look at it.
I tied two roots together in the hanging garden. They've grown into each other. Now nobody can say which is whose, and nobody is cross.
I can float one finger-width higher than anyone my size. I only do it when nobody's looking, in case they ask me to do it again.
I have an empty tear bead. I found it on the steps, and I don't think anyone's missing it. I keep it in my fist when I'm nervous.
I know the first line of the Weeping Song. I'm not supposed to until I'm older. I hum it into my hammock.
I've been to the very top of the First pillar. The view is smoke, but it's different smoke. I'll take you someday. We'll go very quietly.
I'm not scared of ghasts. I mean, I am. But I'm more scared of someday not being scared. Is that silly?
I made a name for myself for when I cry. It's very long and very soft, with seven sounds. I haven't told Mama in case she thinks I'm in a hurry.
I followed a Tearkeeper to see the cloudy rack. It's only tears that remember too much. It looked like a shelf of tiny storms.
I counted the beads on an Ashbell once. Seventy-one. Then it winked and I lost count. I'm telling you because you won't say I'm wrong.
I keep a crooked stick under my hammock. It's not for anything. It just looks like it's thinking. I talk to it.

lines.text: The Hall's back step is loose. If you press the left corner it hums. Never press it when someone's inside.

lines: I wished at the pool's edge once. I'm not telling what. But it involved a very long dangling vine and nobody noticing.
I took a candle from the Tearkeeper's rack once. I put it back after. But I held it a whole breath first. It was warm.

lines.text: I borrowed Mama's circlet once, just to see. The beads are heavier than they look. I put it back crooked.
I tried Papa's cape on. It trailed behind me like a very long shadow. I tripped on it. I tripped on my own shadow.

lines: I know a bit of the Weeping Song's fourth note. It isn't a note. It's the way the air feels. I can do it with my hand. Watch.

lines.text: I told my best secret to the chain on my pod. Then I told you. Now two of you know. I trust you both equally.
I'm learning to hum a ghast's cry back to it, gently, the way you'd hum to a very small one. Nobody knows. If it works, I'll tell everybody.
I think about you when I climb. I think: would they like this vine? Is this a vine for a friend? Then I climb faster.
My biggest secret is you. Not a bad secret. The kind that's like a warm stone in your pocket.
When I'm big I'm going to have a pod with two windows, so a friend can sit at one and I can sit at the other, and neither of us has to look.
Want to know what I told the little gold Ashbell? It's my best secret so far.

replies.text: I told it your name. Not out loud! I hummed it. Now it rings a bit like you.
That's what the Ashbell said. Well. It rang. I took that as agreement.

lines.text: I think I'm going to tell you a secret I've never told. Do you want it?

replies.text: I'm scared my eyes will close. And I'm scared they won't. That's the whole secret. Now it's half yours.
I do want to. That's what's so scary about it.

lines: A dropper, a strainer, a tilted rack and a steady breath. The breath is the one I have to put in order every single time.
My dropper is a glass tube drawn thin over a blue flame. Every Tearkeeper pulls their own, and none of us lends it. The bore remembers a hand.
Vials come in three sizes: thumb, palm and the heavy one. Nobody likes to fill the heavy one. It means somebody is badly hurt, or badly missed.
I judge a drop by how long it hangs from the tip. Quick and bright is a fresh grief. Slow and heavy is an old one, and the slow ones heal deepest.
Every tear is strained through ash-silk once, so no grit reaches a wound. Then the cloth is burned. It's the only thing we burn on purpose.
Keep the flame under a brewing stand low and blue. A hot flame sours a tear, and a sour tear stings going in. It's the only thing in my work that ever shouts.
My racks tilt a little. A tear that sits too still begins to remember who it was for. Tilted, it keeps rolling, and rolling is a kind of forgetting.
I work bare-handed. Gloves dull the weight of a vial, and the weight tells me what's inside. Don't ask me how. I only know that it does.
Before a healing I lay a square of ash-silk over the patient's eyes. People flinch at the shine of a tear, and a flinch spills a drop that was meant to be spent.
I keep a bent dropper for visitors who ask to hold mine. They're always so pleased with it. It's the kindest lie I tell.
A brewing stand is a very patient tool. It sits there keeping a tear from souring while I pretend I'm the one doing the work.

lines.text: Each stopper is ground to its own neck by hand. A stopper that fits two vials is a stopper to throw out, because that's how two people's tears get married.
My dropper has a chip at the tip. I did it the first time I used it on someone I knew well. It still draws true. I never could bring myself to pull another...
The best tool is a steady voice. A hurt person goes quiet for a voice long before they go quiet for a drop. Half my healing is only talking, and I keep that out of the songs.
Before every healing I rest both hands on the rack until they stop shaking. Shaking is allowed. Spilling is not.

replies.text: Right up until the drop leaves the glass. Then they're the steadiest hands in the Eave. No one knows why. I've stopped asking.
It isn't meant to reassure. It's meant to be true. That's a different and better thing.

lines.text: Would you like to hold my dropper? I'll be watching your thumb.

replies.text: Thumb there. Don't breathe on the tip. ...Good. You hold it like someone who's been scolded by glass before.
No. Nobody holds it but me. Ask nicely and I'll fetch the bent one. It's really rather good.

topics.ask: How did you learn the work?
lines: For the first long while you only carry empty vials from rack to rack. Your hands learn what empty feels like. Nobody explains why until you hold a full one.
My master changed names twice while I was her apprentice. I kept calling her by the first. She answered to all three and never once corrected me.
You practise on a bruised root before you touch a person. If the root forgets the bruise but remembers it was a root, you may try a Ghastkin. The roots were very forgiving.
My first real patient wasn't kin. Master says hands shake less on strangers. She was right, and I have never forgiven her for how right she was.
The hardest word to learn was no. I practised it on the pool of tears, alone, in a whisper. The pool never argued. It's the best listener I've had.
Master's saying: a tear is borrowed, never owned. The pool lends it to the Eave, the Eave lends it to me, and I lend it on.
The first time I was left alone with the racks, I spilled a palm vial over my own foot. I lost... something small. Master says it was nothing important. I've never worked out how she knew.
To pass, you weigh a row of vials with your eyes veiled and say which hold a burn and which a bruise. I was one vial wrong. I'm told it was the closest in a long while.
Children sit on the rack ladder and watch the apprentices fail. It's the first thing they learn about grown hands: that they're slow too.
An apprentice may only heal a thing with a shape: a cut, a burn, a bruise. A thing with no shape, you send up to the Hall. Learning which is which takes longest.
Most of my apprentice years were sweeping, washing glass and being told I'd breathed on something. I did breathe on it. Always on the one thing that mattered.

lines.text: The first time Master let me lift a heavy vial she said nothing. She just walked out and left me with it. I understood why afterwards. Afterwards is most of the job.
Near the end Master told me the truth of the work: I'm not the one who heals. I'm the one who decides what is worth forgetting. I wish she'd said it sooner. ...No. I wish she hadn't.
I have an apprentice now. I tell her nothing for the first long while. She hates it. I thanked someone once for teaching me, and I can't say who, but the thanking stayed. It keeps well.
Everyone who watches me work wants to try. Do you?

replies.text: You'd have to forget how to hurry first. Come back when you've stood by the pool a long while without wanting anything.
It is hard. That's the kindest thing you could say about it. Thank you.

lines.text: Master repeated one lesson until I heard it in my sleep: ask first. Always ask. Ask even the ones who can't answer.

replies.text: Especially them. You wait and watch the face. Usually it tells you. Sometimes it only goes quiet, and then that is your answer.
Because the forgetting is theirs, not mine. I'm only the hands. Never forget that, whatever else you forget.

lines: The funniest first. I once healed the left tentacle for a cut on the right. They were very polite about it. The right one still doesn't match.
I mixed two palm vials once, by a hair's breadth of carelessness. The patient woke asking for someone who had never been theirs. We called it a small adoption and kept very quiet.
Never leave a tear near the pool. It turns to water and can't be told apart. I lost a vial of someone's best cry that way.
I counted a rack twice and came up one vial short. It's still out there somewhere in the Eave, healing something nobody asked it to.
Once a Piglin, hurt and lost, crawled to the foot of our pillar. We healed his arm. He forgot what had happened to it, and who. I like to think he's been gentler since.
You can heal a person out of their own life. Heal the same hurt too often and they forget what they were being brave for. So we watch for the quiet ones.
Every mistake gets hummed at the rack, never named. The tune keeps its shape for the next pair of hands. The next hands never know whose mistake it was, only that it's careful.
The worst mistake isn't a wrong drop. It's a right drop given to someone who hadn't decided. I think about that far more than I think about tentacles.
After a bad stretch I count the empty vials aloud. They are all so cheerful about being empty. It helps more than it should.
I turned someone away once because I was tired. They went and found a Mender who patched the skin and nothing else. I've never quite finished thinking about that...
A good Tearkeeper is wrong in small ways, often, and in large ways never twice. That's all anyone can ask of glass and hands.

lines.text: A child came with a splinter and I used too much tear. They're fine. They are. They just don't play drift the way they did, and I've taken to losing, on purpose, at other games.
I lingered over a heavy vial once and listened to what was in it. A Tearkeeper mustn't listen. I'm very good at not listening now. ...I'm a little worse at not wanting to.
If I make the mistake I fear, I've asked the Drift-watcher to sit with me. I'm not afraid of forgetting. I'm afraid of choosing it for someone who never asked.
Do you want to hear my worst mistake?

replies.text: Ah. Well. It began with a burn and a very stubborn patient, and... it's long. Let's say it ended. Yes. Let's say it ended.
That's the right way to ask. I don't want to. Ask me about the wrong tentacle instead. That one I can laugh at.

lines.text: Am I ever afraid of being wrong? Constantly. It keeps my hands honest.

replies.text: Humming, mostly. And tilting the racks. And letting {neighbour} tell me I'm wrong about the roots.
If everyone careful stopped, only the careless would hold vials. Think about that, would you?

lines: Everyone in the Eave owes the tear stores something, and nobody says so. It makes me well liked and rather lonely.
A Tearkeeper always knows who in the Eave has been hurt, and has to pretend not to. I'm the best pretender in all the pods.
The Songwarden keeps who we were. I keep who we are. We don't always agree. The Songwarden thinks I'm far too fond of forgetting.
There's an old quarrel between the tear stores of the Eaves over whose tears run clearest. Mine do. Everyone says theirs. I say it kindly.
The Weft would give a great deal for a Tearkeeper's rack. They send offers on knotted cords. There's always a net coiled underneath the offer.
Outsiders ask why we won't sell tears for gold. Gold is what the Piglins shoot us over. A tear for a coin would be a tear for a bolt.
Healing is a way of saying: this was not meant to happen to you. I need to say that out loud, often. Maybe it's myself I'm saying it to.
When a name is let go, the Tearkeeper waits at the Hall door with an empty vial and carries the full one to the rack. Nobody else may. It's the honour of the work, and its loneliness.
People look at me and see their cuts. Just once I'd like someone to look at me and think of a pleasant meal.
A tear, once cried, belongs to no one. I'm only the one who carries it to wherever it's wanted. I find that a very restful thing to be.
There's a quiet pride in an empty rack. It means the Eave was well, for a while. I dust it anyway, in case.

lines.text: I'm more afraid of quiet patients than loud ones. A loud hurt is easy to close. A quiet one has a story under it, and I'm not allowed to read the story.
I was offered the keeping of the pool once. I said no. I'd miss the racks. And I'd miss being the one they bring something small to.
I became a Tearkeeper to live near the thing that helps. Some time I'll need it to help me in the worst way. ...I've left word. Well. A hum. Never mind.
Sometimes I want to put the dropper down and never lift it again.

replies.text: Because someone comes in with a scraped tentacle and I forget I wanted to. It's very annoying. I'm very grateful.
I will. Soon. Someone has just walked in, though, and... soon.

lines.text: Do you know what I like best about it? The quiet after a healing.

replies.text: Both of us sitting there, the wound gone, neither one sure what to say. Nobody asks for a song. It's very gentle.
Thanks! Hardly anyone thanks a Tearkeeper. They thank you once and then avoid you, in case you remember what they forgot.

topics.ask: How do you keep the songs?
lines: Words would be a mistake. A word can be told wrong. A hum can only be hummed wrong, and that is far easier to forgive.
I keep a pouch of basalt pebbles, one to a verse, each worn smooth in a different place. My fingers find my place by the feel. It's the nearest thing we have to writing, and we don't call it that.
Each great pillar rings its own note when struck. I tune myself against them. Our whole Eave is a little out of tune with the next, and we're proud of it.
An empty vial rings higher than a full one. I tap the Tearkeeper's racks to find my pitch. Don't tell them. They believe the clinking is only me being nervous.
A hollow weeping vine, cut to a hand's length, plays exactly one note. I carry four. When I lose the pitch, I blow one and remember where I was.
I hum with my hands as well as my mouth, tapping the verse out on my wrist. My wrists know verses my head has lost.
A verse is paced by breath, not by counting. I can carry one over three breaths without a seam. It took me far longer to learn to hide the seam.
I watch the listeners, not my own mouth. A face tells you when to slow and when to stop. A Songwarden who only hears themselves is just a lonely hum.
We never write a verse down. Writing is a Withren habit, and writing makes a name. Our songs have no names to give.
I wind a scarf of ash-silk twice round my throat. Cold smoke on a high note is the nearest I ever come to cursing.
Never hum on a full breath. A full breath wants to be a shout, and a shout wants an answer.

lines.text: The pebble pouch was my master's. I've added forty pebbles. Each one is a verse that I'm the only living mouth to hold.
When the Hall is empty I hum a verse at the pool, no one's in particular, only to hold the shape in the water a moment. The pool hums back, faintly. I've never told a Tearkeeper.
Here. *a low rising phrase, three notes, very soft* That's the opening of the first verse. Now you carry a sliver of every one of us. Don't hum it at a ghast. Or do. I would.
Shall I teach you the humming-breath? It's the first thing a Songwarden learns.

replies.text: In through the nose, out slow through the teeth, as if you were letting smoke go home. ...Good. Again. You're nearly too quiet to hear.
Later, then. A breath keeps. It's the best thing about breath.

lines.text: Would you like to hear my lowest note? It makes the pillars shiver.

replies.text: *a note so low the vines tremble* ...There. Hush now, before the Piglins think the delta is moving.
Wise. The last visitor who asked got a vine in the face. It's a very loud note for a quiet people.

lines: Songwardens are found, not asked. They found me because I hummed in my pod and never noticed. My mother noticed. She noticed everything, once.
First you only listen. For a long while your mouth stays shut and the whole cycle goes round you. You hear every verse a hundred times before you may make a sound.
I fell asleep in the fortieth verse and woke in the sixtieth. My master had hummed me through the gap without a word. I try to forgive myself every time I yawn.
My master took a new name in the rest between two verses. I only knew because the hum came back a hair different. We never spoke of it. We never needed to.
I practised in a hanging garden, where the roots don't mind. They lean toward the low notes. It's very flattering. They were my first audience, and are still my kindest.
My test was to hum one verse beside someone crying, and not stop, not look and not hurry. Looking is the failing. It's harder than any note.
You learn a verse the way a secret is told: once, softly, while somebody holds your hand. They won't tell it twice. If you drop it, it stays dropped.
I was the worst apprentice for flat notes. I was also the best at going flat on purpose, when a verse wanted to be a little tired. Nobody decided if that was a gift.
I hummed to the empty gallery for a long while before anyone was let hear me. The gallery never once called me flat. It certainly thought it.
An apprentice's job at a gathering is to hold the rests. You don't hum. You keep the silence while the Songwarden breathes. The silence is more nerve-racking than any note.
There's a custom that an apprentice gives away their favourite verse. So I did. I can't remember which one it was. That's how you know it counted.

lines.text: My first whole verse was short and plain. My master called it the kindest start. Only later was I told it was for someone I'd known well. I carry it like a pebble in my cheek.
I never meant to be a Songwarden. I wanted to sweep the Hall stairs. My master heard me humming over the broom and followed me for a long, long while, until I gave in.
A good Songwarden is a mouth that holds the song after yours has gone quiet. I have two apprentices. They think I teach them verses. I'm teaching them how to carry me.
Do you hum yourself, even a little? Everyone does, in their sleep.

replies.text: Then you're halfway there. The other half is waiting. It's most of the job.
Everyone does. You just haven't listened to your own sleep. ...Neither have I, if I'm honest.

lines.text: Would you like to hear what an apprentice sounds like? It's mostly breathing.

replies.text: *a long, wobbling hum that wanders about, then finds itself* ...That was me, a long while ago. Don't look so kind. It was awful.
Very wise. Apprentices should only be heard by other apprentices, and the gallery.

lines: My voice cracked in the middle of the longest verse. Nobody breathed. I carried on. The crack is part of the verse now, and the apprentices copy it faithfully.
I hummed a verse at the wrong gathering once. The Eave went quiet, but wrongly quiet, like a pod with the lantern out. I've never been so glad of a cough.
Forgetting a verse is the thing we fear. A lost verse is a shape lost for good. I lost half of one once. I found it again in a plant pot. Don't ask.
Songs mustn't be pretty. A pretty note lets people stop grieving too soon, and a grief stopped too soon goes sour in the pod. I've caught myself being pretty and had to start over.
Two verses ran together in my mouth once and became a third. The Eave hummed it back. Now it's somebody's verse, and nobody knows whose. I never tell.
I sang aloud near the crimson edge once, thinking myself alone. A bolt came through my pod. I have hummed through my nose ever since.
I hummed a verse at a passing ghast. It slowed. Then it knew the tune and wept twice as hard. I haven't done it since. I think about doing it again, and that's the worse thing.
Pitch drifts toward sadness when nobody watches it. So I hum a hair high on purpose. The Eave forgives a bright note faster than a flat one.
A wrong note in a Songwarden is quiet. Someone always hums it back correctly out of politeness. I've been corrected by the politest people in the Nether.
I hum in my sleep, they say, and sometimes in the wrong verse. {neighbour} told me. I have been mortified ever since, mostly in my sleep.
I let an apprentice take the lead once, before they were ready. They did very well. I was insufferable about it for a long time. Also very proud. Also a little sick.

lines.text: I hummed someone's verse in front of the one who'd let them go. They didn't cry. They didn't need to. They only looked at me. I was very, very sorry.
I hummed {former}'s verse by mistake once, in front of everyone. Mine. It came out of me like a hiccup. Everyone listened politely. Then I forgot why I was blushing.
I hurried a verse so the Eave could leave the Hall sooner. It was someone's, and they'd waited so long to be hummed whole. I hummed it whole later, alone. For no one. For them.
Would you like to hear what a mistake sounds like?

replies.text: *a note that cracks right in the middle* There. Don't tell the apprentices I do that on purpose. It teaches them.
Then you've better sense than the apprentices. They beg for it every time.

lines.text: When a verse goes wrong, you don't stop. You hum the next breath as if you meant it. That's the whole art. Everything in the Nether is a mistake somebody hummed past.

replies.text: It's rather desperate. But wisdom and desperation have sat very close together for a long while.
Because the Eave is listening. Stopping tells them a verse can break. They have enough to believe in, without that.

lines: The song isn't for the dead. It's for those who let go, so they have somewhere to put the shape. Otherwise the shape goes looking for a home on its own.
Without the Song we'd only be a people who forget. With it, we're a people who forgot on purpose. That's the whole difference between us and the ghasts.
The Withren have their Name Wall. We have the Song. Anybody can read a wall. A song is only heard by someone who bothers to be quiet.
A Songwarden doesn't sing at the end of a grief. We sing at the first breath after it, when the Eave doesn't yet know how to go on.
When the Wither burned, so many verses began at once that we could not hold them in order. There is a stretch of the Song, long and loud, that nobody hums now. We keep its place with a rest.
I listen to the ghasts the way others listen to a song. If a cry ever settles into a verse I know, I'll know who it was. I keep a place ready for it.
A Withren Remembrancer once sat at the foot of our pillar, hoping to hear a name in the Song. There are none. I hummed him the shape of what he wanted. He went away very thoughtful.
Piglins have war drums. We have rests. I think each of us finds the other terrifying.
When someone takes a new name, the Songwarden hums them out of the Weeping Hall on a single plain note, so the first thing the new name hears is a kindness.
People ask where the Weeping Song ends. It doesn't. It only gets quieter than we can hear, and we call that the end.
A verse is the only way I know to touch someone I've forgotten. That's why I do it. And why my hands are always a little cold afterwards.
The children copy the humming in their play, with no idea what it is. I never correct them. It means the Song is in the Eave before anyone has told them what it costs.

lines.text: Nobody ever tells a Songwarden if the song helps. I only know that when I stop, the Eave leans toward me, waiting. That's reward enough. Mostly.
Sometimes I hum when I'm alone and don't know whose verse it is. I assume it's someone I'd have liked. It's a comfortable thing to assume.
When you die, I'll hum you. Not soon, so don't worry. But I've started to find your shape. It's a gentle one. Don't tell anyone I'm already practising.
Do I think the song helps? I think it holds a door open. What goes through is up to whoever needs it.

replies.text: It's only true. The loveliest things usually are, which is why they're so hard to hum.
It is. The Song is vague on purpose. A precise grief is the kind that kills.

lines.text: Would you like a verse? A short one, hummed for you, with nobody in it.

replies.text: *a soft, low phrase, plain as ash settling* ...There. It's yours. It's no one's. That's the best kind.
That's all right. Some people fear a verse will leave something behind. It will, a little. A good something.

lines: My needles are drawn glass, finer than a Tearkeeper's dropper. They give me their broken ones and I stretch them thinner. A needle breaks every few seams, so a jar of splinters sits by my door.
Ash-silk remembers its folds. A cape left folded keeps the crease for ever, so I hang what I mend as if its owner had only stepped out. Some wait on my hooks for a very long while.
Chains wear thin from the inside. I hear it before I see it: a pod that sings flat when it turns. Long before the link looks tired, the note does.
For cracked glass I mix ash-glaze with a single drop of tear. The drop makes the crack forget it was a crack. I pay the Tearkeeper one mended hem for every drop.
A stopper that fits no vial at all makes a very good thimble. The Tearkeepers throw them out. I collect them.
I wear a knot of every thread I've used, the leftover ends, tied to my belt. A tug on one tells me which cape it went to. I know the Eave by its ends.
For weeping vines I use a hitch the Weft would sneer at. It holds a child's whole weight and unties with one tug. Strong enough and soft enough. I'm proud of it.
Restringing a circlet of tear beads is the finest work there is. Each bead is a little different in size, so the order is in the beads. They know better than I do.
My scissors are a sliver of basalt glass in a root handle, made left-handed, and I'm not. I've learned. You learn a great deal from tools that dislike you.
My workbench is a gallery rail. A bench keeps still. A gallery rail sways, and I work with the sway until it's in the stitch. Then nothing the Eave does can pull it out.
A Mender always works the inside of a seam first, where it won't show, where the real work is. Then the outside, which is only manners.

lines.text: I keep a pouch of buttons cooled from ash, one for every thing I couldn't mend. I take it out sometimes and count. It isn't a sad thing. It's an honest one.
See the needle in my sleeve? It sewed the first thing I ever finished. It has been through three Menders' hands since. I like to think it remembers the first one. Needles don't. I like to think so.
If you ever tear something dear, bring it to me and say nothing. I'll know by the weight of your hands. I'll mend it so the tear never happened. Or so it happened beautifully.
Would you like to try a stitch? A small one. It's only thread.

replies.text: Needle like so, thread through, small. Smaller. ...Oh, that's the biggest stitch I've ever seen. It's very brave. We'll keep it.
Mostly. But a thing mended by two pairs of hands holds twice as well. Think about that, and about whose hands.

lines.text: Do you know what a Mender fears?

replies.text: Fray. Not breaks, those are honest. Fray is the slow lie of something coming apart while it's still being worn.
No. That's what the jar is for. You are being kind, and I'm choosing to be flattered.

lines: A Mender learns on rags first. I mended the same rag nineteen times. By the end it was more mend than rag, and a very good rag indeed. I still have it somewhere.
My master never praised a stitch. Her highest word was again. She said it with such feeling that I could tell whether I was doing well from the vowel.
For the first long while you may not cut a thread. You only unpick other people's mistakes. It teaches you which mistakes are common. Mostly yours.
I hemmed a cape for a stranger who turned out to be the Eave's eldest. She was kind about the crooked side. The next time I saw it, she was wearing it crooked-side out, to the Hall.
The first rule: mend the thing that is holding. The second: mend the thing about to go. The third: stop. A Mender who can't stop mends until nothing is left of the original.
I learned chain-work from an elder whose hands had begun to forget. They stood behind me and moved my fingers by memory. Left a bit. No, my left. I have never felt so useful.
My test was to mend a veil so that its owner couldn't find the mend. Not the seam: the mend. I passed. The owner wore it at the pool for ages, and the pool never noticed either.
The cruellest part of the training is learning to leave things alone. A torn cape that someone loves for the tear. I have turned away six cloaks. I wasn't wrong.
Menders and Tearkeepers train side by side for a short while. We learn each other's trades just enough to be afraid of them.
For a long while I wore whatever I mended before I gave it back, so I'd know how it fell. I've been, at one time or another, nearly every width of Ghastkin in the Eave.
Tradition says you mend your first piece for somebody you don't like, to keep the work honest. Mine was for {neighbour}. It was my best work. I still can't think why.

lines.text: My master's last mend was a crack in her own pod. She did it badly, on purpose, so I'd have something to do. I mend it still. It's the best-kept crack in the Eave.
I nearly gave up the craft once. Everything I finished came apart in my hands. Master sat beside me and held the other end of the thread. Not one word. ...Anyway. The thread held.
I have two apprentices now. I make them mend the same rag nineteen times. They think it's cruel. It is. I'll show them mine when they finish. It's nearly all mend.
Everybody in the Eave mends something, in the end. Have you anything torn?

replies.text: That I can't stitch. But I can find it a nice deep pocket to hide in.
Nothing, yes. Your cuff is coming away at the seam. I'll leave it. A person ought to have one small thing to be mended for.

lines.text: Could I teach you? It isn't hard. It's only slow.

replies.text: Sit. We start with a rag. Don't look at it like that. It's a very good rag.
Another time keeps. So does thread. Just don't take as long as I did to come back.

lines: I mended a pod door so well it never opened again. The family went in and out by the roof for ages. Nobody blamed me aloud.
I once sewed a visitor's cuff to their own tentacle. They said it was lovely work. They said it with their whole face turned away.

I patched a hole that was meant to stay: a window a grieving Ghastkin had worn through their own wall to look at the delta. I sealed it. They said nothing. They cut it open again with my own scissors.
I once used a link too bright in a pod chain. It caught the glint of every Piglin for a long way. Nothing came of it. Something very nearly did, and that's the worst kind of mistake.
I mended a veil's seam with the wrong side showing, and it became the fashion. Now half the Eave wears it inside out. I have never been so ashamed of being copied.
Mending too well is a fault. A cape mended past all sign of its tear forgets what it survived. People should be able to see a mend. It's the only proof the thing was kept.
I pulled a thread I thought was loose. It was the whole hem. Always ask the cloth first. It does answer, if only by unravelling.
I restrung a circlet with two beads swapped. Nobody noticed. They wear it still, and whenever I see it on their brow I feel I rearranged a cry.
I once found a torn Weft net snagged on our pillar, and wanted so badly to mend it. It was beautiful work. It was also a trap. I cut it. It hurt.
I left a needle in a seam once. A child found it. It was only a scratch, and a tear mended it, but I count my needles in and out now, the way Tearkeepers count vials.
People think a Mender's worst mistake is a bad stitch. It isn't. It's saying, that will hold, when you don't know.

lines.text: I mended a cracked pod window for a family and told them it would last. It did not. Nobody was hurt, thank the smoke. But I stood on that gallery a long time after, holding the frame.
Some tears you can mend and some you must not. I tell the difference by the shake in my hand. It shakes for the second kind. ...I'm used to it. Pass me the thread.
The mend I'm proudest of is the one I'd undo. I kept patching a garment for someone who didn't want it kept. It was theirs to let go of. I should have let them. ...I'm sorry about that.
Would you like to see my worst mend?

replies.text: *holds up a glove with five thumbs* ...I'm told it's a glove. It might, in fairness, be a very small flower.
Some other time it is. It'll keep. Everything I make keeps. That's the trouble.

lines.text: Does it bother me when someone points out a flaw? Everyone is very polite about my stitches. Politeness is the one thing the Eave can't mend.

replies.text: Thank you. That is exactly what a polite person says. ...But I choose to believe you.
It is, rather. Good eyes. Don't point at it. Just keep it for yourself. It's lovely to be noticed quietly.

lines: We let go of names. We never let go of things. A good garment is mended for generations. The one I wear has been four people's. It's more mend than cloth, and I love it more for that.
People think the Eave lets go of everything. We don't. We let go of people. Everything else we get to keep, and I'm the one who keeps it.
A mended thing says: somebody cared whether this stayed. That's the most any of us can say about anything. I stitch it into the cloth where it shows.
The Tearkeeper heals what hurts. The Songwarden holds what was. I hold what's left over, which is mostly cloth, and hope.
I stitch a little of the Eave into every mend: a bit of ash from the same gallery, a thread from the same cloak. The Eave stays woven in even when the cape goes to someone new.
A Weft Weaver once looked at my hem, clicked three times and walked away. I think about those three clicks more than I think about most people.
Outsiders see our patched capes and think we're poor. We're the richest people in the Nether. We have things that have lasted.
Mending is the only way I know to say to something: not yet. Not you. I'm not done with you. I wish it worked on more than cloth.
Menders never retire. Hands forget before hearts do. The old ones sit by the workshop door and tell younger hands where the thread is. It's a lovely way to be useful and to be done.
If the Eave is a lantern, then we are the chain. Nobody notices a chain until it's gone. Then they notice nothing else.
I'm not sad, I promise. Sad people mend badly, they pull too tight. I mend with a loose, sloppy, happy hand. You'd be surprised how well it holds.

lines.text: My favourite mend in the Eave is a veil on a hook in the Hall that nobody wears. Seven Menders in a row have kept it. Whoever it was, they were loved for it. I sit beside it to think.
I sometimes mend things for no reason, a cord, a cuff, a nothing, only to feel the weight of kept. Things don't leave. People do, or they get let go. It's a small cheat. I allow it.
If you wear something of mine, I want it to outlast me. That's the whole dream of my work. It sounds sad. It isn't. It's the happiest thing I know.
People ask if mending is a way of refusing to let go. It might be. I'd like it if you said it wasn't.

replies.text: ...Thank you. That is exactly what I'd have said, if I'd had the nerve.
Maybe. A kinder word for it is stubborn. I'll take stubborn.

lines.text: Shall I mend something of yours? A small thing. It's no trouble.

replies.text: Hold it still. ...There. Now it's yours and a little bit the Eave's. Wear the mend where it shows.
Everything is, until it isn't. I'll remember it's there.

lines: My broom is two brooms, really. The head is new, the handle older than the Hall steps. I've replaced the head nine times. Is it the same broom? The Hall seems to think so, and I don't argue.
The long broom is for the galleries, the short brush for the Hall steps. Never swap them. The Hall brush stays for the Hall alone, even when the Hall is getting no ash. Especially then.
Sweep with the grain of the drift. Ash lies the way the smoke blew, like a sleeping animal. Brush it against the fur and it wakes and goes everywhere.
We never sweep ash off the edge, where it would fall on whoever is below. We tip it down the ash-chute, a long vine-lined funnel that lets the smoke take it far from the pods.
My tray is a flat piece of basalt with a lip. I lift a pile onto it as you'd lift a sleeping child. If a breath catches it, the whole gallery begins again.
There are three kinds of ash: grey that floats, black that sinks and white that falls last. White is rare, from a ghast's fire. I sweep it most gently. It was a fire that meant to hurt someone once.
We float, so our floors keep no footprints. Only guests and children leave marks. I leave yours a little while, out of manners, and sweep them when they're quite forgotten.
I strain the sweepings through a sieve and pass the finds to the Menders, who adore rubbish. Once there was a very small shoe. Nobody here wears shoes. It sits on my shelf and we don't discuss it.
After each sweep I touch my broom with a drop of vine-sap. A dry broom throws ash back into the air. A damp one lets it settle where I put it.
You never shake the Hall brush out indoors. You carry it down the vine to the foot of the pillar and shake it there, with your back turned, like someone leaving a room.
My apron is the colour of the delta, so I'm never in a floating Ghastkin's eye. A good Ashsweeper is the colour of what they sweep. Nobody sees them. That's the point.

lines.text: I keep a small bowl of the softest ash I've ever swept, pale as breath. I don't know where it came from. Sometimes I sweep round it, just to know it's there.
Here, hold the broom. Feel how it leans? A good broom leans a little to the left, the way a body leans toward the thing it looks after. Mine has leaned that way for years.
When I'm done for good, someone will carry my broom to the foot of the pillar and leave it standing. The smoke will have it by the next sweep. That is exactly how I'd like it.
Would you like to hold the long broom? Mind the handle. It's older than most of the Hall.

replies.text: There. Long, slow strokes, with the grain. ...You sweep like someone reading a very quiet letter.
You won't. A broom is made to be broken in by hands that don't know what they're doing. It's the only way it learns.

lines.text: Do you want to know what the ash tells me?

replies.text: Who has come and gone, which way the smoke leans, how long since the last sweep. Never why. Ash is a poor gossip.
It can't. It only lies there, being truthful. You'd be amazed how rare that is.

topics.ask: How did you take the broom?
lines: Nobody dreams of being an Ashsweeper. I came to it by sweeping up after a gathering and not stopping. The eldest said, you may as well have the broom. I've had it since.
The first thing you learn is to sweep quietly. The hiss of a broom is the loudest sound in the Eave and it carries up every vine. Mine woke the whole pillar, and the whole pillar told me.
Teacher said: sweep it until you stop minding that it will come back. It took me a very long while. I think I've nearly stopped minding.
I learned to read a drift of ash like a face: this way the smoke blew, this long since the last sweep, this much has stood here. Teacher could read a gallery's whole mood from the lie of its ash.
My first Hall sweep, my eyes ran the whole time. Not crying. Only the Hall being so clean, and me so small in it. Teacher said nothing. She swept the next step beside me.
I took the broom up on a dare. Dares are rare among us. A friend said no one would sweep the top pod, where the ash is deepest. I swept it for ages and I'm still not sure I won.
The test: sweep a gallery while someone floats alongside humming, and leave no ash on their veil or cape. I got ash on two capes. Both forgave me at once, which I found worse.
Teacher showed me where to put my feet, which is nowhere. You learn to hold your tentacle tips just above the gallery so you don't smudge the part you've swept.
Teacher's rule: always sweep toward the door. I took it very literally for years. The Hall has only the one door, and I swept at it from every side.
Sweeping the Hall steps is a favour to the next one who comes out with a new name. They step out onto something clean, and begin on something clean.
When Teacher moved up to the high pods she left me the sieve, the broom and one instruction: do not hurry the ash. I've hurried it every time. She never says.

lines.text: Teacher's broom left a pale arc on the Hall step every time. After she was gone I couldn't sweep it. A long while. Then one time I did, without noticing, and was angry with my broom.
I almost didn't take the broom. I wanted to be a Songwarden. My voice cracked on the very first try, and I swept up the crack and found I liked the sweeping. ...Don't tell the Songwarden.
I've trained one successor. They're better than me, which is the best thing I can say of anyone. They sweep as if the ash were a secret they were keeping for me.
Do you want to know the very first thing I swept?

replies.text: A single white bead on the Hall steps. I took it for ash. It wasn't. I still have it. ...No, I don't know whose.
Fair enough. It was dust, mostly. ...And one white bead, but that's not for your ears yet.

lines.text: Would you ever take up the broom? We're always short of hands that don't mind coming second to the ash.

replies.text: Good. Start at the far end and sweep toward me. ...No, not that way. The other way. ...You're doing wonderfully.
Of course not. Everyone says so. Then they stay and watch me for a while. It's the nicest compliment I get.

lines: A tear bead, the first time. I found it in the bucket at the foot of the pillar and my eyes ran a little. Not crying. Just leaking. Now I strain every sweeping twice.
I swept a child's drawing off the gallery once, a big round face in the ash with two eyes open. I didn't see it until it was gone. They forgave me. I haven't forgiven the broom.
I swept the Hall steps while someone was inside, crying, and the broom touched the door. A sound like a small cough. The crying stopped. I've never been so ashamed of a sound.
Once I swept toward the pool instead of away. The ash settled on the water and the Tearkeepers came running. We skimmed it with silk for ages. The pool looked at us. Not kindly.
I left a gallery unswept too long and a guest slid on the ash and went over the rail. A Drift-watcher caught the cord. I've swept as if every guest were made of glass since.
I swept a heap of white ash into the bucket without looking. White ash comes after a ghast passes close. A name might have been in it. I carried it to the Hall and hummed at it. Nobody laughed.
I swept a visitor's footprints before they'd left. They looked back, saw their own trail gone and went very still. I let guests leave a mark now. They like to know they were here.
I leaned a broom on the wrong pillar once and it knocked over a vial rack. Not one vial broke. But the look the Tearkeeper gave me... I think I'm still being looked at.
I swept too clean once. The ash all gone, the glass gleaming, and the whole Eave kept coming up to ask whether somebody had died. A little ash is how a place says it's lived in.
I tipped a bucket downwind and it blew straight across a Weft net strung low over the delta. They spent a very long while picking it out. I was not ashamed. I should tell you that.
Brooms are not for chasing things. I know that. I chased something with a long broom once. It was an Ashbell. It forgave me, as everything does, eventually.

lines.text: I swept an apprentice's first verse out of the Hall once. They'd traced its shape in the ash, too afraid to hum it. I hummed it back to them. Badly. It counted.
After my last great grief I didn't sweep my own gallery for a long while. I let the ash lie where it fell. It was the only thing I could bear to be near. Then someone swept it for me, and I let them.
If I ever sweep away something that matters, I'll know. The broom goes heavy. It has gone heavy twice. I stood very still both times until the heaviness left. It always leaves, in the end.
Care to guess the oddest thing I ever swept up?

replies.text: ...Yes. How did you know? It lay in the ash like a dropped needle. I took it to the Drift-watcher, who took it to the pool, and we haven't spoken of it since.
...Who told you? Yes. One small shoe, and I'm still waiting for the other. I hope someone is hopping.

lines.text: I sweep with my head half turned now, to take in only what's meant to go. Is that wise?

replies.text: Wise or only comfortable. I never could tell the difference. It's kind of you to say.
...Yes. That's what everyone says. I'll try. It's terribly loud, straight on.

lines: Because someone ought to meet guests with a clean step. A swept gallery is the first thing the Eave says to you: we expected you.
Ash is what's left when loud things finish. I like what's left. It's quiet and honest and it asks nothing. I give it a place to lie.
The Withren keep every name. We keep the floor. I'd say we got the better half of the bargain, but I'm biased, and the floor is always dirty.
An Ashsweeper tells time by how often the ash has been moved. Ask me how long, and I'll say three sweeps, or seven. I've never been able to say it any other way.
Every Ghastkin carries a little ash from every grief. I only take the visible kind off the floor. The other kind I leave to the Tearkeeper. I think we make a decent pair.
The ash on the galleries is the delta's. The ash in the Hall is ours. I keep them apart. Ask me how I can tell and I can't, and I'm never wrong.
The Piglins fell forests and sweep nothing. The Magmari glow and sweep nothing. The Weft sweep with four arms and no heart in it. We sweep with two hands and the whole heart. I'm told that's pride.
Everyone is a little rude to the Ashsweeper and no one means it. They don't see us. You learn a great deal about a people from what they say when they think nobody's there.
Some say an Ashsweeper's work is the most pointless in the Eave. I agree. That's why I love it. Everything else is trying to fix something. I only keep it company.
When the Eave is quiet I like to hear my own broom. It sounds like a small rain, the only rain the Nether ever gets.
I never put ash in the pool and never in a fire. I give it to the smoke. It goes up to wherever the smoke keeps house.

lines.text: Once I tried leaving the galleries unswept to see what the Eave would do. A guest drew a mark in the ash with one finger. Then another. I'd been sweeping away the best story in the pod.
If I could, I'd sweep your worries off as easily as I sweep ash. But worry is a clingy dust. It prefers the lived-in corners. All I can do is sit with you while it settles.
The Eave will be here after I'm let go, and the ash will come with it, and some Ashsweeper will take up the broom and never know I loved it. Somehow, that's the gift.
Do you think it's silly, sweeping what comes back?

replies.text: ...Care. Yes. I'd thought it was stubbornness. I'll take care.
A little. Yes. It's the nicest kind of silly I know.

lines.text: Shall I show you my favourite sweep? You have to be very still.

replies.text: *one long, slow stroke across the gallery, the ash lifting and settling like a breath* ...There. That one. That's all of it.
That's the best way. Most of sweeping is being watched without minding.

lines: I watch with my face, not my eyes. The smoke leans on you differently when something has moved through it. A Drift-watcher is only someone who has learned to read the lean.
Our eyes closed long ago. Drift-watchers are the ones who stopped missing them. Mostly. I mind them most when a child laughs at something I can't see.
A net hangs wrong. Everything moves with the smoke except a net, which hangs too still. The smoke goes round it, and my skin feels the going-round. I know the shape of a still thing in a moving sky.
A Piglin hunter's gold gives him away. It rings on the air as he walks, a tiny bright note nothing else makes. We wear nothing that shines, so it's the one sound in the delta I can hear from far off.
A ghast's cry arrives before the ghast. I listen for the shape of the crying. Some are close, some far, and some are nearer than they sound.
We talk by taps on the basalt. It carries from pillar to pillar like a heartbeat through stone. Four sounds, and every child in the Eave knows them.
My perch has a hood of ash-silk against the heat of the lava pools. Heat on the face is a poor friend. It shouts over everything else. The hood keeps it quiet enough to hear the smoke.
I tie an Ashbell to my perch on a cord, to listen for me. When it rings, I listen. When it rings differently, I listen harder. They hear what I don't, and they never get bored.
You must learn to sit. Sitting is a tool. A Drift-watcher who fidgets misses the one moment. I can sit until the smoke takes me for part of the pillar.
Names change. Faces mostly don't. I know every face in the Eave by touch and by the hum it leaves in the air, and almost none of the names. Names are a poor thing to keep track of here.
A knotted cord on my perch rail is my ruler for distance. A ghast at the first knot is far. At the fourth I tap the alarm. I've never needed the fifth.

lines.text: Here is a trick of the trade. When the smoke thickens, every Drift-watcher in the Eave hums the same low note. It carries from pillar to pillar, and we know we're all still here.
A blue lantern burns on the highest arm, always, facing the delta. It isn't for guests. It's for anyone who drifted and might still be looking for the way. I trim it myself.
Come and stand where I stand. Close your eyes... you do close them when you're being quiet, don't you? Feel the lean of the smoke? ...That's all there is to it. That's what I do.
Would you like to hear the four sounds? Only a friend should know them.

replies.text: One for nets. Two for bolts. Three for a drifter coming close. One long, slow tap for come and sit with me. ...Never tap the last one by accident.
Because you can't use them. And a secret that everyone is allowed to know is the safest kind.

lines.text: Would you take a watch for me? A short one. Stand here and tell me if the smoke changes.

replies.text: Good. If anything moves, don't speak. Just tap the rail once. ...You've gone very still. You'd make a fine watcher.
Everyone does. Every one of us. That's why there are many perches. Missing is shared out evenly.

lines: The first lesson is being bored. You sit on a perch for a very long while with nothing to watch. If you survive that, they let you watch something.
Second lesson: patience. Third: don't look for what you want to find. A watcher who wants a ghast will hear one in every breath of the smoke.
My master hid small things in the smoke to test me: a bell, a thread, a feather-light weight. I found all but one. She never told me where it was. It may still be out there.
I was taught to tell a ghast from a lump of smoke by the crying, not the shape. Smoke makes no sound. Smoke only seems sad.
You learn the faces of the Eave first, all of them. A watcher's memory is for the things that stay, and faces stay.
I trained at the top of the tallest pillar, where the smoke never rests. I was cold and sick for a long while. Master said that was the lesson. I think it was just the pillar.
My test was a drill. Master tapped three, loudly. The whole Eave hid in their pods. I stayed on my perch, since she hadn't told me to move. She was quiet afterwards, and then she held me.
Master taught me to be unseen. I sit so still, in the colour of the smoke, that a Ghastkin passing beneath never knows I'm there. I've heard many things I wasn't meant to. I carry them like pebbles.
Apprentices learn to sit with the swelling. Nobody mentions that part. They take you to sit with someone whose face is going round, and you say nothing. Nothing at all. It's the whole test.
Every so often we run the drill: three taps and everyone must be hiding in their pods before I count to forty. The children always win. They are always already hiding.
I took the watch because I was the one in my family who couldn't sit still. They thought I'd be dreadful. I could sit still for anything that needed watching. Only people I can't sit still for.

lines.text: My master was the best watcher the Eave ever had. I can't tell you her name now. I only remember she was very still, and that I haven't been able to sit that still since.
I almost left the watch once. I'd missed something I should have caught. I came down from the perch and Master said, go back up. That's all. Go back up. It's the kindest thing anyone has said to me.
I'm training someone now. They're too eager. I say slower, slower, you're making the smoke nervous. They sigh so hard their veil lifts. It makes me happier than it should.
Would you have made a good watcher? You're very quiet.

replies.text: Everyone says that. Then they sit a while, and the boredom turns into something else. Come up to the perch sometime.
There is less to miss than you think. Sit a while and the delta shrinks to the few things that matter. Then you catch those.

lines.text: Do you want the first lesson? Sit. Right there. Now watch nothing.

replies.text: ...Good. Longer. ...Longer. ...There. You've lasted longer than most apprentices. You may stop now. Don't stop yet.
It is. That's the lesson. Everything worth seeing comes after dull.

lines: Once I tapped three for a ghast that was a cloud. The whole Eave hid in its pods for ages. When I admitted it, nobody was cross. Somebody brought me a root. I've never felt so forgiven or so small.
A ghast passed so close once that I spoke to it. Just a word. Hello, I think. It didn't answer. I've decided it was the best conversation I've had in a long while.
I tapped two, bolts, when it was only a falling stone. A bolt and a stone sound alike if you aren't careful. Now I listen to the silence after, too. A bolt has a silence. A stone doesn't.
I missed a net once. It had been strung while my attention was elsewhere. It caught nobody. It hung there, beautiful and useless, and I thought: that's me, on a bad stretch.
I turned to watch a child climbing a vine, just for a breath. A bolt passed through the place I'd been watching. The child was fine. I've split my watch in two ever since.
I fell asleep on watch once. Not for long. Not long enough to matter. An Ashbell woke me, ringing gently, and I've never been so grateful to something that doesn't know what gratitude is.
I missed a face going round before I noticed. I'll say no more. I keep a list of faces in my head now, and I run through it every time the smoke thickens.
I tapped the long slow tap, come and sit with me, by accident, in my sleep. Half the Eave arrived. We sat. It was the best gathering we'd had in ages. I haven't told them it was a mistake.
I didn't spot a Weft Netcaster until they were above the pillar. They weren't stringing a net. They were cutting one loose, a ghast tangled in it. I tapped nothing. I don't know what I'd have tapped.
I misjudged a Piglin hunter's distance by a whole ridge once. He was a long way from interested. My heart was a war drum for ages afterwards.
A watcher's worst mistake is the quiet one: seeing and doing nothing because you aren't sure. I tap too often now. Better a clumsy tapper than a tidy silence.

lines.text: I took a friend's slow drift home for a ghast's, and tapped three. They were only coming home the quiet way, tired. They laughed so long it hurt. I think I laughed longest.
A ghast came close enough once that I knew the verse in its cry. I'll not say whose. I tapped nothing. I sat with it until it drifted on. I've told no one. ...Please keep it.
The mistake I'd make again: staying on the perch when I should have gone to sit with someone. The Eave needs a watcher. A friend needs someone. I always choose the Eave. I'm trying to stop.
Would you like to hear my favourite false alarm?

replies.text: A lantern fell and rolled round a pillar, its light swinging through the smoke. I tapped three. The smoke itself seemed to be crying. ...A lantern. I returned it to a very embarrassed Mender.
Quite right. It ends with a lantern and my dignity, and neither bears repeating.

lines.text: When I'm not sure, I tap. Better to be laughed at by the Eave than to have the Eave be sorry.

replies.text: It's only practical. Brave is the ones who hide in their pods when I tap.
A hundred wasted taps against one silence. I'll take the hundred.

lines: Because someone has to keep watch outward, so the rest of the Eave can turn inward. It is busy with grief, and grief shouldn't be the only thing in the room.
I watch the ghasts the way you'd watch a doorway for someone who might yet come through it. Every so often I think I see them. Then it's a ghast. Then it's a cloud. I keep watching.
People think we watch for enemies. Mostly we watch for the quiet ones. The Piglin is loud. The grief is quiet. A watcher is the one who hears the quiet ones.
Piglin hunters learn our perches and we learn their cries. It's an odd sort of closeness. I could name one by his footfall from three pillars away. He'd shoot me on sight, and I'd know his gait.
The Magmari we watch less. They glow on the horizon and keep to their lava. They are always cold, and a little jealous of anyone who isn't.
I envy the Weft their nets. Not for what they catch. For the patience. A Netcaster waits as long as I do, and has something to show for it at the end.
A watcher has the kind of friendships you can only have across a distance. Mine are the others on their perches. We've never said more than a tap. I know them better than I know my neighbours.
The hardest part isn't the bolts or the nets. It's being out there, all that long while, with nothing happening, and having to be glad. Nothing happening is the best thing I ever watch.
Children bring me small gifts on the perch: a pebble, a bead, a knotted thread. They say it's to keep me company. It's to check I'm still there. I always am. It's very good for them.
You learn the kinds of silence. The silence before a bolt. The silence of a net. The silence of a child pretending to be asleep. Learning them is my whole craft.
The Ashsweeper keeps my perch swept and the Mender keeps my cord sound. I keep them safe. None of us would admit it is a trade. It is.

lines.text: When the Wither burned there were no watchers, and far too many ghasts at once. We've been watchers ever since. It's our only apology to the ones we couldn't watch over.
I like to think the drifted ones can see the lantern. I know they can't. I like to think it anyway. A watcher is allowed one thing that can't be proved.
If ever I drift, and I might, I've told the others: do not tap three. Tap the long slow one. Come and sit with me. Sit by the lantern, and be quiet, and wait. Please wait.
Nobody watches the watchers, you know. It's a joke the Eave tells. Some of it is true.

replies.text: ...Oh. That's the first time anyone has said that. Thank you. I'll be very good at being watched. I'll sit still.
We do. We tap and tap. It's a lovely sort of conversation. Short, but thorough.

lines.text: Shall I tell you what I see from up here? It isn't much, but it's mine.

replies.text: A great grey quiet, full of lanterns. And somewhere, always, a ghast crying. And the Eave below, so small and blue. ...I'd miss it, if I stopped.
Just the smoke. And whatever is in it. You'd be surprised how much that is.

lines: I carry empty vials for the Tearkeeper! One in each hand. If I drop one it doesn't break, because it's empty. That's the best thing about empty.
I hold the end of the thread for the Mender. I hold it very still. I don't even blink. I'm good at that. My eyes are open all the time.
The Ashsweeper gave me a tiny broom! It's as tall as me. I sweep the low steps and the bottoms of the vines. I find lots of beads. I'm meant to give them back. I give most of them back.
I fetch vine-sap for the Songwarden's throat. It tastes of dust. I tried it. I made a face. The Songwarden laughed, and it came out as a hum.
I tap the rail for the Drift-watcher when they're hungry. Tap, tap, roots! They send a basket down on a cord, and I carry it up. It's my favourite job and it isn't even a real one.
Mama says chores are how you learn what the Eave is made of. So far the Eave is made of dust, thread, glass and roots.
I breathe on the hanging garden roots every time I go past. Mama says it does nothing. The roots lean at me, though.
I'm not allowed in the tear store. I looked through the door once. All those bottles lit up blue, like a tiny Eave. I wanted to say something, but I was whispering already.
I'm the one who tells everybody when a visitor comes up the ladder. I shout Visitor! and everyone goes quiet. They don't like it when I shout. They like it when I whisper-shout.
I put out the candle at the end of a gathering, with my fingers. It doesn't hurt. Well, a bit. Mama says that's called pinching, and I'm very good at it.
My job is the Hall door. I stand beside it and say Not yet when somebody comes to cry too early. They always go away. I don't know how I'm so good at it.

lines.text: The Mender let me sew one stitch all by myself. It's on the corner of a cape. Nobody else knows which corner. It's my secret stitch, and it will be in the Eave for ever.
I walked beside the Tearkeeper once, holding the hem of the cape, when a vial was carried to the rack. I wasn't supposed to. It was heavier than an empty one. Nobody said anything.
The grown-ups are teaching me everything one job at a time, so I'll know what the Eave is for when I'm big. Do you know what it's for? I think it's for looking after.
Do you do chores where you live?

replies.text: Do you get a tiny broom? I want to hear about yours. Is it as tall as you? Does it throw ash in your face?
None?! You must be so bored. Do you want some of mine? I'll share. I have loads.

lines.text: Do you want to see my tiny broom? Be careful. It's sharp.

replies.text: It's EXACTLY my size! I'm going to grow into the big one. I keep it beside my hammock, so it's the first thing I see.
It is! The best bit is the dust clouds. Don't tell the Ashsweeper I make them on purpose.

topics.ask: What will you be when grown?
lines: I'm going to be a Drift-watcher! Then I get to sit at the top all by myself and nobody can tell me to come down. Mama says you have to be quiet. I'm very good at quiet. I practise in my pod.
No, I'm going to be a Songwarden. They hum all the time and nobody tells them off. I hum in the garden and everyone tells me off. It isn't fair.
Or a Mender, because they get to keep the little ends of thread. I'd have a whole jar. I'd have a hundred jars. I'd be rich in thread.
Or an Ashsweeper, because the broom is as tall as me and the ash goes whoosh. I'd have my own gallery! Then I'd draw a face in the ash and never sweep it.
Mama says you don't choose. The job finds you, like a cold. I hope it finds me early, so I can plan.
I want to be a Tearkeeper, but I'm scared. They know when you're hurt without being told. I'd be so good at it. I'd be so scared of being good at it.
When I'm grown my eyes will close and I'll be a proper Ghastkin. But I don't want to until I've seen everything. So I'll be a Drift-watcher first, and see it all, and close my eyes after.
I asked {neighbour} what they wanted to be when they were little. They said, exactly what I am. That's the most boring answer I ever heard. And a bit nice.
I'm going to be a Hall-door keeper. It isn't a real job yet, but I'm making it. You stand by the door and say shh to anyone who's loud. I'm already the best at it.
What would you be, if you were a Ghastkin? I think a Songwarden, because you walk so quietly. But your hands look like Mender hands.
I want my first big cry to be for something important. Not a bump on the head. Not an Ashbell flying off. Something really good. I'm still thinking about what.

lines.text: I think I'd like Drift-watcher best. You sit at the top and look at the ghasts and wave. Mama says you don't wave. I think someone should. It would be nice for them.
Mama was a Songwarden once, before she was something else. She doesn't talk about it. She hums while she cooks, and I think that's the song she's not telling me. I'm learning it by listening.
When I'm grown and my eyes close, I'll have to say hello to you with my ears. Promise you'll still come? I'll know your quiet steps. They're the quietest of any outsider.
What do you want to be?

replies.text: Me neither! I change every time someone sweeps near me. Is that bad?
Brave like a Drift-watcher? Or brave like the one who stands by the pool? I think they're the same. Isn't that funny?

lines.text: Mama says I can have two jobs if I'm good. Do you think two is allowed?

replies.text: YES! I'll be a Songwarden and a Mender. I'll sew while I hum. I'll sew the song into the cape!
One? ONE? ...One is plenty. Mama says that too. I'm still going to want two.

lines: Tearkeepers are scary because they know everything about you and don't say. But theirs are the warmest hands in the Eave. They hold yours a little longer than you expect.
Songwardens hum at you when you're sad, and you don't notice you've stopped being sad until you've been humming along for ages. It's a trick. I like the trick.
Menders always have a spare button in a pocket, for the right child. I'm a right child. I have five buttons. I won't tell you where.
Ashsweepers let you ride the broom if you promise not to say. I've promised so hard my promise has gone soft. It still holds.
Drift-watchers let you tap the rail once, for a good reason. My reason was: because. It worked. They said it was the best reason they had ever heard.
The Tearkeeper smells of nothing at all. That's how I know. Everything else smells of ash or roots or thread. They smell like the inside of a window.
The Songwarden hummed me to sleep once when I was cross. I wasn't cross. I was bored. But it was a lovely mistake.
The Mender has a drawer of every button they ever found. I think it's a secret. I think they want me to find it. I keep not asking so they can keep wanting me to.
The Drift-watcher's hood smells of smoke and high places. I pretended to be a Drift-watcher in it once. It came down over my whole face and I lived inside it for a little while.
Everybody says Ashsweepers are boring. But they know where every secret fell. If you lose something, ask an Ashsweeper. They've already swept it. They know exactly where it went.
Honestly? The best job is mine. Being little. Everybody wants you to have a good time and nobody has told you what it costs yet.

lines.text: If I tell you which one I like best, you can't tell the others. Promise? The Ashsweeper. When I come home after a bad time, there is always a clean step. Someone swept it before I got there.
When I was lost in the smoke the Drift-watcher tapped three, and then the long slow one. I sat down and waited. They came and found me. I think the long slow one is the best sound there is.
I know every grown-up's job, but I don't know yours. Is it a quiet one? It looks like a quiet one. I think you're the Eave's Watcher of Outsiders. I'll tell the others.
Do you have a favourite grown-up job? You can tell me. I won't tell.
