replies.text: They'll like that. Nobody ever picks them. Everyone's scared of them. I'll tell them, quietly, when they're not looking.
Builders! We don't have builders. We have lanterns and hope. ...Is that a real job where you live? Do you get a hat?

lines.text: Do you want to see my best impression? I do all of them, one after another.

replies.text: *hums very low, sweeps the air, taps an invisible rail, stops, stares into the smoke and gasps* ...That's all of them. In one. I'm exhausted.
All right. But I'll practise. I'm going to be so good that you'll beg.

lines: We play Tearkeeper! One of us is hurt, one is the Tearkeeper, and one is the tear. The tear has to be very sad. I'm usually the tear. I'm excellent at it.
In Songwarden we all hum the wrong song at once, as loud as we dare, and whoever laughs first is the Ashsweeper. I'm always the Ashsweeper.
Mender is the best. You sew your friends' sleeves together, just a little, then everybody stands up at once. Don't tell the real Mender. They know. They're letting us.
In Ashsweeper you stomp about in the ash on the lowest gallery, then sweep it all away before the real one comes. We've never made it in time. The real Ashsweeper pretends not to see.
In Drift-watcher, one of us is the ghast. The ghast has to float slowly past and cry, and the watchers tap the rail. The ghast always gets too good at crying and then everyone goes a bit quiet.
My friend is always the Hall. They stand very still in the middle and we all walk round them quietly with our backs turned. Nobody's allowed to laugh. It's the hardest game there is.
We tried playing Weft once. We said click click and put our arms behind our backs and pretended to have four. We fell over. Then we tried playing Piglin, but that was too loud, so we stopped.
We play Names, too. You whisper a new name in someone's ear and they have to turn into it. I turned into Pebble. It wasn't a good name. I wouldn't let it go for ages.
We play Ashbell! You hold your arms out and ring, ever so softly, and everyone has to follow you without talking. I'm the best bell because my ring is tiny.
We play Letting-Go sometimes. We all hold hands and take turns being let go. Someone hums, and you say a new name, and sit up and giggle. Mama says that game is rude. It's my favourite.
Nobody plays the ghast for long. Somebody always says that's enough, and then we play something with roots. It's an unspoken rule. I don't know who made it. Everyone follows it.

lines.text: I played Tearkeeper with the real vials once. They were empty. The real Tearkeeper found me and I thought I'd be told off. They only showed me where the thumb goes, and said, gently, again.
We aren't allowed real needles, so I made one from a vine splinter. It couldn't sew, but it could point. I pointed at things and said, I'll mend that. I mended the whole Eave. In my head.
I play a game by myself where you're the only visitor, and you come up the ladder every time I need you. I never lose that game. ...I'd like to keep winning it.
Do you want to play one? You pick.

replies.text: Oh good. Give me your sleeve. ...Hold still. Hold STILL. I'm going to sew you to the vine. Just a little. Not really.
Yes! You're the watcher. I'm the ghast. Tap when you see me. ...No, wait for it. ...I'm going to cry very quietly. Is that all right?

lines.text: Shall I show you how to be a ghast? It's easy. You just float and sigh.

replies.text: *floats slowly round you, sighing, then stops* ...I don't like doing it for long. It's sad. Let's be roots now.
That's all right. Me neither, really. We only do it a bit.

lines.text: The Letting-Go is our oldest rite. When someone takes a new name, the Eave gathers at the Weeping Hall, each with a candle, and the old name is spoken once to the pool. Then nobody says it again.
For every death we lower a lantern down the weeping vines until it touches ground, and leave it to burn out where it lands. Nobody watches. That is the courtesy.
The Long Hum has no fixed time. When the pool goes perfectly still, someone starts one low note, the whole Eave joins, and we hold it until the Ashbells ring back. It can take a long while.
Veil-Turning is almost a festival. The Menders turn every hood and veil inside out, so the ash we carried is worn against the chest instead. Then we spend a while not knowing who anyone is.
Once in a long while the whole Eave walks to the edge of the delta and each of us shouts one word. Just one. Then we go back to being quiet. The pillars answer for ages. It is the best part.
Would you like to know which word I shouted last time?

replies.text: 'Bother!' The basalt said it back to me seven times. I have never felt so understood.
Mm. A shouted word you keep secret never wears out. You have the makings of a Ghastkin.

lines.text: The Closing is for the young. After a child's first proper cry the eyes shut for the first time, and the Eave brings a bead for the circlet or the cord. It is a celebration. Look how I'm smiling.
Highest Drift is a children's game, but the grown ones watch with great seriousness. The lowest float wins. Quiet and low is the whole point of us, and the little ones need reminding.
Nobody plans the Gathering of Bells. Some time the Ashbells drift together over the pool and ring all at once, and every hand in the Eave stops. Work waits. It is the one rule nobody wrote.
At the Tallying the Tearkeepers count their racks aloud, one at a time, and the Eave listens. The number is the only thing we ever say about our tears. We are proud of it, and we don't know why.
We have no festival for happy news. We have a pause. Someone says the good thing, and everyone is quiet and a little warm for one breath. Then the work goes on.
When a new hanging-garden pot is planted, its first root is carried round the Eave on a cushion and each of us touches it once. It sounds silly. I have seen a Mender sniff.
At the Letting-Go there is a part outsiders never see. The one who lets go keeps their eyes shut and does not turn, and everyone else leaves. They find their way back by the candles.
Once I was asked to be the first voice to say someone's new name. It is an honour and a worry. If you say it wrong, they carry it wrong.
When I next let a name go, would you carry a candle? You would stand at the back and nobody would speak to you. It is the highest honour we have for an outsider.
Friends may keep a candle lit in the Hall for someone, even without being Ghastkin. I have lit one for you. It is small. It is only in case.
Highest Drift is the best! But the lowest wins, so I never win, because I always get excited and go up.
At the Letting-Go I get to carry the candle tray. I've only dropped it once. One candle. It went out very nicely.
I'm saving my word for the Shout. It's secret. It has three o's in it, and I practise it quietly in my head.
Veil-Turning is so funny! Everybody's hood is wrong and nobody knows who's who. I swapped {neighbour}'s on purpose and they walked into a vine.
After the Letting-Go the children eat first. Mama says it's so we're too busy chewing to ask questions. It works every time. I have a lot of questions.
The Closing is when a big one's eyes shut. There are roots, and everybody hums. I don't want to go to mine. ...Do you like roots?
When the Ashbells all ring together, even the grown ones stand with their mouths a bit open. So do I. It's the only time nobody tells me off.
If you shout anywhere else they send you up the vines. But at the Shout you're allowed. Do you have a place where you're allowed?

replies.text: All the TIME? Doesn't it get used up? Mine's saved for one go. I'd be so tired.
You would? Then we must practise your word together. Quietly first. Very, very quietly.

lines.text: Roots, mostly. Crimson roots boiled red and sweetish, warped roots boiled teal and bitter. We drink the broth and chew the rest slowly. Soul-fire cooks them gently, without the sulk of ordinary fire.
Nothing that had a face. We have enough faces to remember already.
Vine-sap, warm, with a pinch of ash-salt. It is the closest we come to water, and much better company than the pool.
We cook plain. A strong smell can pull a face out of nowhere, and then you are standing in the hanging garden holding a ladle, wanting to cry and not knowing why. Plain food is a kindness.
When someone dies, their favourite meal is cooked once by whoever cried for them and eaten alone on the Hall steps. It is called the Last Dish. It is never cooked again, so half our recipes are lost.
Nether wart porridge comes from the Withren, in trade, grumbling on both sides. They say we eat it too fast. We say they cook it as if it were a punishment.
Fungus caps, roasted on a cord over a soul-lantern. They squeak a little when they are done. Nobody mentions it.
Someone once put a tear in the broth, to see. The broth forgot it was broth. It sat in the pot looking like broth and tasting of nothing at all.
We eat little. Floating asks for less than walking does. Some of the oldest among us live a whole long while on broth and humming.
Meals are eaten facing the vines, with our backs to each other, so nobody has to watch anybody chew. It is the most polite thing we do and the least friendly-looking.
Have you ever been given food you couldn't eat, out of kindness?

replies.text: Smiled and chewed! A true guest. Hold on to that skill, it is worth more than a sword.

replies.ask: I just said no thank you.
replies.text: Honest. That is a rarer skill, and a lonelier one. I respect it.

lines.text: Piglins roast hoglin on fires you can smell across the whole delta. It is the one smell I have ever wanted and not wanted at once. I keep my face turned the other way.
A Weft once offered me a fungus dyed bright blue. It was so pretty I couldn't eat it. I carried it home and kept it on a shelf until it forgot to be a fungus. Anyway.
Sap-drops are our sweetness: vine-sap boiled until it hardens on a cord. We hang them in the pods to suck on when the quiet gets loud.
A Tearkeeper never touches food after a vial until their hands have been breathed on three times. It is a rule older than the rack it protects.
Menders keep a pocket of dried root in the hem for long sewing. It gets mixed up with the thread and tastes of both. I have stopped minding.
A Songwarden eats soft things, since a crust catches in the throat. Warm sap, root paste, a spoonful of nothing in particular. We are dull at the table.
Sweepers carry everything in covered bowls. Otherwise ash gets in the broth, and then we are eating our own work. It is honest, but it grits.
A Drift-watcher eats standing, one hand on the rail, one on the bowl. Every third mouthful I look up. A ghast could come, or a net, or a stranger who crouches well.
Come to my pod and share a bowl. There is no custom beyond that. I hum while you eat, you don't talk, and the broth is cold, as it should be. It is most of a friendship.
I have never cooked a Last Dish for someone living. Shall I cook you one now? A meal with nothing to remember in it. Only warm, and for you.
I like sap-drops! I'm allowed three. I counted four and said three. Don't tell.
We don't eat anything with a face, Mama says. I say sorry to the roots anyway, in case.
Warped roots taste like a cold hand. Crimson roots taste like a warm one. I like the warm hand best.
Roasted fungus squeaks when it's ready! Everybody pretends it doesn't. I giggle and get sent to the vines.
I put a hum in the broth to make it nicer. It's still just broth. But it felt nicer.
What's your favourite food? Mine's plain broth with the dark bits left in.

replies.text: Same as mine! Then we agree about everything. That never happens.
What's cake? Is it a roof? Is it for eating? Oh, tell me, tell me, quietly!

lines: The Low Welcome is our oldest manners. Whoever crouches asks to be heard. Come up standing and you are weather. Come up low and you are a guest. That is all there is to it.
We never raise our voices, but we have many ways of lowering them. There is a hum for 'I'm sorry', a hum for 'I'm here', and a hum for 'please stop talking'. Learn the last one first.
A gift should be hollow, if you can manage it. A bottle, a bowl, an empty pod. Something the other can fill. A full gift tells them what to feel, and that is rude.
Never ask who a person cried for. Not from fear. From respect: they have likely lost the answer, and a question that can't be answered is a small cruelty.
We keep our hands visible when we talk, palms up, so nothing hides. Outsiders keep theirs on hilts and in pockets, and it makes us uneasy. It isn't rude. It is only loud, in a way we can feel.
Don't touch another's veil or hood without asking. It is the nearest thing a person owns to their own shape.
To someone in grief we never say 'I understand'. We say 'I'm here', hum one low note, and say nothing more. Understanding is a claim. Being here is a fact.
Leave a candle lit in a pod when its owner is out. Not to be found. To be found by. A lit window means someone is expected.
Every pod has one empty place on the gallery bench. It is kept for whoever isn't there. Nobody sits in it, and nobody says why. Guests are told once and then trusted.
We greet by lowering the head, and the lower, the more we mean it. A very old Ghastkin once greeted a Piglin so low she bumped her chin on the floor. The Piglin was thrilled.
If you must disagree, hum a half-tone flat. Everyone understands, nobody loses face. I have lost whole arguments to a flat hum.
We don't say names often. We say what a person is doing: the one at the pool, the one with the thread. A name is heavy to say. It is kept for the times that earn it.
A pod is never fully closed while its owner is grieving. It should always feel a little open. Doors are mostly decoration anyway.

lines.text: I would like to teach you the Low Welcome properly. Only the head. Shall we try it?

replies.text: *lowers, lower, lower* There. You bow better than the Piglin did. He bowed with his whole gold.
Silly is allowed. Everyone feels silly. That is what makes it a welcome and not a drill.

lines: Eating, mending and mourning are never done in a hurry. If a Ghastkin looks rushed, check on them. Something is wrong.
We seldom say goodbye. We say 'I'll be back to this spot'. If you don't come back, the spot is swept, gently, and left empty a while.

lines.text: A Mender is never thanked aloud. The custom is that you wear the repair, and then there is nothing to say. The best thanks is a veil worn proudly.
A Songwarden may hum anywhere but over someone resting. A hum over a sleeper borrows their dreams. We hum at the foot of the hammock, silently, until they roll over. Then we are forgiven.
Nobody thanks a Tearkeeper for healing. They thank us for 'letting me in'. It is an old distinction, and a Tearkeeper who forgets it is hummed at, flat, for ages.
A Drift-watcher says what they see, plainly: 'Smoke. Ash. A bell.' Never 'nothing'. Nothing is how the ghasts get close.
Ash is swept away from the Weeping Hall, never toward it, and always with the draught. A sweeper who sweeps the wrong way is told off once, softly, and never needs telling again.
There is a custom for friends: you may touch the cord of a Ghastkin's tear vial. Only the cord, never the glass. It means 'I trust you with the empty'. Go on. You may touch mine.
Friends sit on the same side of the Hall, facing the same window, shoulder to shoulder. It is how we show affection: we share the view, not the face.
If you are to be my friend properly, you will have to learn the hum that means 'I am well'. Nobody hears it unless it stops. Listen. *a low, steady hum* There.

topics.ask: What were you like as a child?
lines: I floated before I could do anything else. My mother says I rose out of my cradle soon after I was born, and she spent a long while tying a cord to my foot. I have never forgiven the cord.
I was a climber. Weeping vines, all the way up, long before I could float. A vine holds you back, gently, the way floating never will. I think that is why I still lean on rails.
I was good at drift-and-seek. Too good. Once I hid so well that they gave up and went home, and I stayed hidden for... a long while. Anyway. I found a very nice pillar.
I wasn't afraid of anything. Small ones aren't. It is the only time you aren't, and nobody tells you to enjoy it.
I remember colours. The blue of the lanterns, and a green once, in a pot that wasn't supposed to grow. Since my eyes shut I mostly see the shape of sounds. It is lovely, but it has fewer colours.
The first time I saw a ghast close, I was small enough to be carried. My father put his hand over my eyes and said, 'Not yet.' I have wondered what 'yet' means ever since.
We were taught stillness before we were taught to float. A child who floats first goes straight up and cries, and a child who cries too early is closed too early.
I won the Highest Drift once, by the lowest float. I got a bead. I still have it. It is the only bead I own that wasn't cried for, and I treasure it more than I should.
My first lesson in the Weeping Hall was to sit with my back to the pool. 'So it can't see you yet,' they said. I turned around the moment they left. It looked very still. I felt no worse.
I was never allowed near the tear store. Naturally I was always near the tear store. I know how every cork squeaks. A small ear is a wonderful thing for hearing what you shouldn't.
My grandmother kept sap-drops under her veil and gave them out, one at a time, to whichever grandchild was quietest. I was very quiet for a very long while. I had a great many drops.

lines.text: Were you a quiet child? I never ask a stranger, but you have the look of one who held very still on purpose.

replies.text: Loud! Oh, I would have liked that. Someone should have been. Tell me a loud thing you did.
Then we would have been friends at once. Two quiet small ones, neither speaking. The best kind.

lines: I once told my mother I had decided not to grow up. She said that isn't something you decide, it is something that decides you. I was cross for ages. She was right. Anyway.
When I was small I believed the ghasts were lost children who had forgotten the way home. I put sap-drops on the gallery in case one came by. They were always gone. Ashbells, I think now. Probably.
The smoke smelled different when I was small. Sweeter. Or I was lower down. It is hard to say with smells. They are the first thing to change and the last to be believed.

lines.text: Tearkeepers are chosen when small, if they ask the right question. Mine was: 'Why do the jars never fill?' My teacher said, 'Because they are not meant to.' I knew then.
I could hum before I could speak. My mother says my first word was a note, and my second word was the same note, louder.
I mended before I could sew. I held things together with my fists. Every cracked bowl in my parents' pod was glued with sap and spite. It was my first job. I have not left it.
I started sweeping by accident. I was told off for dragging ash through the pod, tried to clean it up, and then did it for everyone as an apology. It never stopped being one.
As a little one I was the best at counting ghasts and the worst at stopping. They gave me a perch to keep me from counting the whole sky. They did not expect me to take the job.
I still have the cradle-cord my mother tied to my foot. It lies at the bottom of my pod. When I can't tell if I'm still myself, I tie it round my wrist.
I don't remember my first name. I know it began with a soft sound, because my mother says she hummed it. You may guess. I will nod at the right one, even if I can't know.
Do you want a small secret? When I'm very tired I still float with my knees pulled up, like a child in a cradle. The Eave pretends not to see. It is the kindest thing about us.
We count in candle-lengths. A white candle burns a long while, a garden candle a shorter one. The Eave runs on candles and on the Ashbells' mood.
Our age is counted in names, not years. 'I am four names old,' we say. It tells you how much grief a person has seen. It is rude to ask. You can tell by the beads.
A verse is a measure too. 'I'll be back in three verses.' A Songwarden hums at the same pace always, so a verse is a fair measure. Ask for a verse, not a moment.
The Ashbells ring slower when the smoke is thick and quicker when it thins. We keep time by them without noticing, like breathing. Only when they go quiet do we look up.
The chains of the Eave creak on a long rhythm. Count the creaks between one turn of a pod and the next, and you know how long you have been talking. We have been talking a kind while.
Each watch on the perch is measured by one candle. If it gutters early, you stay until it would have burned. That is a rule, and also a kindness to the one coming next.
We don't plan far ahead. When your name can change, 'next year' is a stranger's promise. We plan by candle: 'After this one burns, I'll sweep.' We keep short promises very well.
When we are sad, time stretches. When we are glad, it folds. A Songwarden once said the Eave measures its joys in breaths and its griefs in verses. I think that's true, and I wish it weren't.
We don't count the past. We count names. Whatever happened between one name and the next is one thing now, and one thing is easy to carry.
Rest comes when the candle is low or the eyes are heavy. Nobody tells you. The hammock rocks with the chain, and the Eave is quietest when most of it is rocking.
Do you keep time yourself? You have something on a cord, I think, or I've imagined it.

replies.text: A clock! A candle that eats itself in a circle? How wonderfully sad. Does it ever stop?
The same as us. We are quicker at it than we pretend.

lines.text: It's odd, but I feel older when the smoke is thick and younger when it thins. Probably the smoke. Possibly me.
One Ghastkin set out to count every proper cry the Eave had ever held. She counted for an age. She was not sad, exactly. She just stopped, and the count stayed where she left it.
The Songwarden keeps a long knotted cord, one knot for every naming. It stretches the length of a gallery now. Don't tell anyone, but the oldest knots are frayed.
At the perch we say 'a long watch' for a quiet one and 'a short watch' for a busy one. Odd, because a busy watch feels short, and a quiet watch never seems to end.
A tear keeps for as long as its cork holds. Tearkeepers are the only ones in the Eave who hope time goes slowly. A slow vial is a safe vial.
If you want to know how long I've known you, ask my hands. They have learned your step, and hands are the slowest to learn. So it has been a good while. A good, kind while.
I keep a private cord, shorter than the Eave's. It has one knot for every time you have crept up on me. I have run out of cord twice, and tied more on.
How long is a verse? I can't tell. A verse is when Mama stops humming. That's how long.
I'm not a name old yet. I'm a nothing old. Mama says that's the best age, and then she goes quiet.
When the candle in our pod is low it's time to rest. I stay awake until it's out. Then I pretend it was still bright.
I measure time in sap-drops. A good wait is one drop. A bad wait is three. Waiting for you, last time, was two.
{neighbour} says they are a lot of names old. They look the same as always. I think they're fibbing.
Mama says if you count the waiting it gets longer. So I never count. I count other things, like sap-drops.

lines: A Magmari Ferrier once towed a pod of ours across the lava when its chain gave way. He wore two cloaks and a scowl, kept a long pole between us, and said nothing the whole way. A kind silence.
A Piglin once left a clean bandage at the foot of our vines, folded very small, and went off without looking up. Nobody was hurt. We keep it on a shelf and call it an apology. Nobody knows for what.
A Weft spinner once left a coil of silk on a perch, with a small knot at the end. Our Songwarden swears it was an apology. Our Mender swears it was a lure. We hung it in the Hall and haven't decided.
I trust the Weft's cloth more than the Weft. Their cloth never lies. It is the nets I am wary of. The cloth is honest. The nets are hungry.
Piglin Brutes are the saddest folk in the Nether. Loud, frightened, bright gold on their chests like something they can't hug. I wave at them from far off, though they can't see.
When a Magmari trader passes our edge, we leave bundles of ash-silk on the gallery rail, with no note and no hope of thanks, so they can wrap up warm. The bundles are always gone. Nobody ever says.
The Withren light a lantern for our drifted ones, I hear. They never admit it. We never ask. It is a very Withren thing, to do a kindness and deny it.
A Weft child got lost near our pillars once. We carried her to the forest edge under a cloak, so the net-folk wouldn't see. She stared the whole way, arms folded, furious. I think that was thanks.
The best neighbours are the ones who don't come. A wicked thing to say about people, and also a very warm one. Good fences, good silence.

lines.text: Would you do something for me? Next time you meet a Piglin, a Weft, a Withren or a Magmari, say one kind thing. Just one. Then tell me which of them took it hardest.

replies.text: Thank you. I will want details, whenever you come. Slowly. Over broth.
Fair. They would attack me, too. Be kind from a safe distance. We are experts.

lines: Piglins say we are pale because we're afraid. We say we are pale because we live in smoke. Both are probably true. It is rude to say so to a Piglin with a crossbow.
A Weft dyer once asked me what colour grief is. I said it is the colour of whatever you were looking at. She wove a cloth the colour of her own wall and gave it to me. I have worn it ever since.
I should like to be friends with a Magmari. Just once. We would sit on either side of a gap of lava and shout kindnesses across it, and neither of us would be put out. Perfect friendship.
We don't hate anyone, but we are very, very careful. Which is much the same as hating, from far enough away.

lines.text: From the perch I see all of them going about their business. The Piglins shout, the Magmari glow, the Weft climb. I like to think they would all quiet down if they could see the delta from here.
I treated a Withren once, secretly, through a window. He asked me to leave one memory in his head and take the rest of the wound. I did. He never said which. I never asked. That is friendship.
A Mender mends anyone's cloth, no questions. I have mended a Piglin's pouch, a Weft's sling, a Withren's lantern strap. All thanked me quietly, looking at their feet. Folk are the same at the seam.
I hummed a verse once to a Piglin forager in a hollow. He closed his eyes. 'More,' he said. I gave him three. Then his friends came, and he put his gold back on and glared. I understood.
I swept a Magmari's cold boot-prints off our gallery once, the few that came near. I swept them kindly, one at a time, like drawing a blanket off someone who isn't coming back.
You are the first outsider I have said any of this to. It matters, I think. Not for the telling. For being asked.
If you ever meet someone from another people who is kind to you, remember it for me. Hold it a while. We need more of those, and nobody records them.
Most outsiders only ever see the tears. You asked about the people. That is a good ear. I will try to deserve it.
Crossbows, plainly. But what truly frightens me is being shot and forgiving the shooter before I fall. That sort of kindness is how we end up as ghasts. It never stops.
Being lifted. A Piglin picked me up by the hem once, to see whether I was real. He set me down gently and apologised in a roar. I have not felt entirely set down since.
Being netted. Weft nets are fine as gossamer, and you only see them when you are already in. The smell of silk makes me float up out of habit.
Silence that isn't mine. A hush I make myself is comfortable. A hush that arrives, when the Ashbells stop and the chains stop and even the smoke holds still, is the worst thing there is.
Not crying. Everyone fears crying too long. I fear not being able to, when it matters. To stand in the Hall with someone dead and feel only a dry roof. It has happened to others.
Being the last one who remembers a person. We let people go, so usually nobody does. But now and then one of us holds on, and then we are the only lantern in a long corridor. I would hate that.
Chain snaps. A pod hangs by one chain, and when I am uneasy I listen to it. If it creaks wrong, I am out of the pod before the second creak.
Fire in small packages. Fire charges, gunpowder, the smell of a bolt. A ghast throws a fire you can see. These are the sly ones. A Ghastkin learns to fear sly fire.
Loud folk who mean well. They hug. They clap. They say 'there there' at a volume that rattles the vials. I have nearly drifted from a kind Piglin's pat on the back.
That the Wither isn't over. That it is a long breath held by someone who forgot to let it out. I tell myself otherwise. The Songwarden hums more softly lately, and I notice.
What are you afraid of? It's all right if it's silly. The silly ones are often the ones that matter.

replies.text: From where? Oh, from above. I couldn't fall. I would only forget to be up. But I understand falling.
*very softly* Ah. That is the one we have decided not to fear. We don't always manage it. I will remember you if I can.
Nothing? How restful. I'll borrow a little, if you have any spare.

lines.text: What frightens me is a patient who says, 'Take everything.' It is never what they mean. I have learned to ask three times, 'Everything?', and to wait for the real answer.
From the perch I fear mist at the pillars' feet that has footsteps in it. Piglin hunters walk in the ash and think we can't see. We can. It is the seeing that tires me.
I fear the thread running out in the middle of a seam. I always carry spare, but my dreams are full of half-finished veils. I wake sewing air.
I fear I'll hum the fourth note by accident one time. It never comes in the song. If it did, I don't know what would follow. I am a coward about notes.
Clean floors, oddly. If a gallery stays clean too long, it means nobody has walked it. I worry more about a clean gallery than a dirty one.
I am afraid of the time you stop coming. I would not cry for it. I would leave a candle in the window and let it be a very long wait.
I used to fear what I might forget. Now I fear what I will remember. I would keep you if I could, and that isn't allowed, so it frightens me a little to want it.
Loud noises! The Piglin horn from far off. Mama says it can't reach us, but my stomach doesn't believe her.
Nets. I have dreams where I'm a fish in a net and the Weft are reading to me. They're boring dreams and scary dreams at the same time.
I'm not afraid of ghasts. They sound sad. But I'm afraid of the quiet after one stops.
I'm a bit afraid of the pool. It's so still. It looks like it's thinking about me.
When I'm grown and my eyes shut, will I still know your step? I'm afraid I won't. Isn't that a mean thing to be afraid of? Ask me something else.
Being left alone on the gallery. Mama says I won't be. But I check. I always check.
Is it true Piglins sleep with their gold? I'd be scared of gold in my hammock. It would be so loud.
{neighbour} says there's a thing under the Eave that eats shadows. I looked. It was a rope. But I'm still careful.

topics.ask: What of the War of the Hoard?
lines: Nobody in my family fought in it. We were never asked, and we wouldn't have known how. What we had was a long, thin ache we have called 'the war' ever since, though it hardly touched us.
My grandmother said the war arrived as a smell first: smoke where there had been none, and crossbow oil, and fear. Then the sky filled. She never told me what colour it went.
The first thing we knew was the horns. Piglin war-horns, Magmari chain-drums from the lava seas, the Weft clicking in the forest like a rain of needles. The Nether had never been so loud.
I don't know who was right. Nobody in the songs is. The Piglins wanted the gold, the Magmari wanted pay, the Weft wanted bone, and the Withren wanted to win. We wanted the shouting to stop.
Soldiers came to the Eave in the war and begged for tears to forget what they had done. At first we gave them. Then the Tearkeepers stopped. A forgotten wrong is only a wrong with no witness.
The Low Welcome began in the war, they say. Whoever crept up the vines was a refugee, and whoever strode up was a soldier. We have kept the habit of answering only the first kind.
The Piglins tell it as a victory and the Magmari as a debt. The Weft tell it in rows. The Withren tell it as a sin. We tell it as weather.
The Piglins wear gold now to tell friend from foe. I always think, what an odd way to remember a war. By shining at each other.
The sorriest were the Magmari ferrymen, I think. They carried war-bands they could not turn back. Then their Moorings burned. They hardly ever speak of it, and when they do, they get cold.
My great-aunt saw the Wither once, far off, over the soul sand valleys. 'Like three tall sorrows holding hands,' she said. She never said more. I do not ask.
The Withren made it, and I have decided to believe the Withren grieved it. It is a better world if they did. Besides, you can't cry for a thing you also hate. Believe me, I have tried.

lines.text: Do you want the quiet version of the war, or the one we sing?

replies.text: Then: it was loud, and then it was ash, and then we swept. That is all of it. *a small, dry smile*
*hums three notes and stops* That is the sung one. It is short. The long one is the part nobody sings.

lines: The Weeping Song has one verse for the war, and it is the only one we hum while looking at our feet. Nobody taught us to. The children do it without being told.
After it, the Piglins boasted, the Magmari mourned, the Withren buried, and the Weft wove. We drifted, and we swept. Every one of us did what we do. That is the whole trouble with the five of us.
My mother said there were quiet folk in every people who tried to stop it. They are in no song. I think about them often. Someone ought to hum for them.

lines.text: My veil is cut from silk gone grey in the war's ash, soot and all. Every veil worn at a Letting-Go has been cut the same way since. We wear the war lightly, where it can be lifted.
The hoods were first made then, from ash-silk gone grey with the fall. We wear them to carry the war on our heads, a little, so our hands don't have to.
The war songs are kept in a single long breath. A Songwarden learns it by growing it, one more breath each year, held. Mine is nearly nine verses now. I faint a little.
When we tip the pan over the delta's edge, we say one word: 'Gone.' It began in the war. We are not sure whether we mean the ash or the folk.
The rail at my perch has a notch worn in it by watchers' hands, since the war. I rest my own hand there. It is warm. Fear leaves warmth behind, strangely.
The refusing is an old rule: no tear for a wrong done. A soldier may forget a wound, never a deed. We said that to many who came, and it did not make us loved.
Menders were busy in the war. Everyone's cloak, everyone's strap, a tear in every hem. The oldest of us still says: mend the cloth and leave the story in it.
I have never told a Piglin or a Weft any of this. I am not sure why I am telling you. It is the crouch. You make a good listener, bent over like that.
Some time, someone will weave a row so bright the black ones will look dim. I won't be there. But I like to hum toward it.
I would have liked to be asked to stop it. I wouldn't have known how. But I'd have gone, and crouched very low, and said please. That is all we have: please, said low.

lines: Yes. Which is why I am someone else now. Love and loss are one piece of ash-silk, folded. You don't get the one without the cut edge of the other.
To love a Ghastkin is to agree, ahead of time, to be somebody else later. That is the bargain. It sounds grim. It is also very tender. We say it as a vow.
We court by humming. A single note at the other's gallery, once each time we pass. After a great many notes the other either hums back or moves their pod. Both are answers.
The bond is called a tether. Two cords from two vials, tied once and left loose. 'Loose enough to untie,' the Songwarden says, 'tight enough to feel.'
My cord carries a knot I did not tie under this name. That is the old love, kept. I do not undo it. I run my thumb over it when I am unsure who I am.
When one of a tether dies, the other cries properly and takes a new name, and the cord is lowered with a lantern. The new one has to be won over by life, slowly, with broth.
Love after a letting-go is possible. Not the same love. A new one, with a different note. The Eave has seen it often. It always begins with broth.
A wedding is two Ghastkin sitting side by side on the Hall steps, facing the windows, saying nothing. The silence is the ring. Everyone else hums outside, as quietly as they can.
A cord can be tied between friends, loosely. A friend-tie is a lighter thing. I have two. I never say whose.
Every trade has its love-token. A Mender gives a patch from their own hem. A Songwarden gives a verse for one hearer. A Tearkeeper gives an empty vial, saved.
An Ashsweeper sweeps a path for you. A Drift-watcher saves you a place on the perch. They are small things. They are why it works.

lines.text: The beads of my circlet are for every proper cry, and the first one is for love. I do not recall for whom. It is the brightest and the most worn. I touch it often.
A husband's hood is stitched by the one he is tethered to. I do not remember who stitched mine. I wear it like a letter I cannot read but whose shape I like.
My Letting-Go veil was a gift. I would have to hum the giver to remember them. I have tried. The tune keeps changing. It is a good tune.
Men of the Eave aren't stern about love, whatever outsiders think. We are only shy. I hum at a pod for a hundred notes, and then I go and mend something.
Would you like to hear the courting hum? One note, once. It is rather forward.

replies.text: *one soft, rising note, held a breath too long* ...That is it. If you ever hear it at your window, answer.
Quite right. It is not for just anyone. It is for the quiet kind of anyone.

lines: The cruellest part is the stretch after the cry. You come out as someone new, in a pod full of a person you cannot picture. We keep the pod as it was for a while. Then we don't.
People say we love less because we cry it away. I say we love once, completely, and then let the shape go on by itself. It is more love, not less. It is all spent.
A Piglin once asked if we had a word for marriage. I said, 'A held breath.' He said, 'That's two words.' I said it was the whole thing.
Children aren't told about tethers until they ask. When they ask, they are told it is a knot you can undo. They are not told that it hurts to undo it. They learn.
I know two Ghastkin tethered for a very long while. Their pods hang side by side, and the chains creak in time. Nobody has the heart to separate the chains for repair. We mend around them.

lines.text: I would tie a friend-cord with you, if it were done. It is not, for outsiders. So I have tied one in my head, loose, and you need not know.
When you are old and ready to go, and I am still me, I will have your cord to tie to. It lies in my pod. Plain white. Waiting. I haven't cut it.
That one of them comes home. A ghast, I mean. Just one, in all the long drifting. I keep a candle lit at the lookout in case. The Eave thinks it a quirk. It is the only hope I keep.
That the pool never dries. It is the only water in the Nether. If it dried, what would we do with everything we have let go? We would have to carry it.
That a child will grow up who can grieve with open eyes, and not forget. We don't know if it is possible. We hope in the quietest way, in case it can hear.
That my hands stay my hands. It sounds small. It is the largest hope I have.
That nobody ever makes another Wither. Not even by accident. I hope that most of all. Hope is a heavy thing, but this one is worth the lifting.
To keep this name until it wears soft. Most of us get a name for a few good years and then it breaks. I would like to wear one down to a smooth stone.
To hear the fourth note of the Weeping Song, once. Only once. I don't know what it is. I am not sure I would survive it. I hope for it all the same.
That the Weft cut their own nets, some time. Not for us. For themselves. A net holds a thing up and also holds you in, and some time they might notice.
That Piglins learn a quieter way to be afraid.
That a Magmari will warm to us. Literally. A single Magmari staying lit beside a Ghastkin for a whole breath. We would hold a feast. A quiet feast, very close to the ground.
Do you hope for anything? I seldom ask, because people think I am hoping to be told. I am only curious.

replies.text: *the face goes still, then soft* That is a good hope. It is easy to keep. I will make it easy to keep.
Then I hope it too, and I will hope it louder. Which is to say, very softly, but with my whole chest.
Perfectly respectable. A hope you haven't found yet is still a hope. It is only quiet.

lines.text: That the ash stops falling. Then I would be out of work, and I would learn to sew, and I would be the happiest idle Sweeper in the Nether.
That I run out of tears to keep. Empty racks, an Eave with nothing to heal and no one to cry for. I know it won't happen. I am allowed to hope.
That I mend something, just once, and it stays mended for ever. Nothing does. But I keep stitching as if one thing will.
That the Weeping Song has a last verse, some time, and when we hum it nobody cries. And then the first verse begins again, light as a bell.
That one watch passes with nothing to see. Nothing to guard. Only me, a candle, and an unbothered sky. I would cry for joy and forget why, and be glad.
I hope the little ones keep their eyes open as long as they can. Every extra year with open eyes is one more year of seeing the delta in colour.
I hope my pod is still hanging when I am gone. Pods outlive their people, which is a comfort and a sorrow. Someone else's lantern will burn in my window. I would like it blue.
I hope for a long, boring life. Dull as ash. No names changed, no vials emptied. It is what everyone in the Eave hopes for. We just don't say it, in case the delta hears.
I hope you stay quiet, and that the world lets you. A lot to hope for someone from a place where outsiders make Withers. But hope is cheap, and I have plenty.
I hope that if you ever must be cried for, I am the one who gets to do it. A dreadful thing to hope. I hope it anyway, and I hope you live ever so long to disappoint me.
I hope I can float higher than the top pod! Even though I'm not supposed to. Even though it's scary. Mostly because it's scary.
I hope I never have to cry. I know I do. But I hope. It's allowed, Mama says.
I hope you come back lots and lots. I hope you bring something. I hope it's a feather. Or a candle. Or nothing, if you're the something.
I hope the ghasts stop being sad. I tell them so when they float by. They don't answer, but they slow down. A bit.
I hope the grown ones laugh more. They do sometimes. I count. It's four since the last Letting-Go.

topics.ask: What do you know of my world?

lines.text: Only what the Piglins shout about it, which is mostly that it rots you. I don't believe that. You look solid. You look like you would keep, even.
A Piglin trader told me your world has a ceiling that is blue and has no edges. I asked who holds it up. He said nobody. I have not been able to sit properly since.
I have heard of water that falls from the roof of your world, and nobody mourns it. Not a tear, not a name. It simply falls, for no one. It sounds like the loveliest, loneliest thing.
Do you let go of your dead, up there? Or do you keep them? The Withren say you put them in the ground and set a stone on top. A stone! I should love to know how heavy it is.
I have heard that outsiders cry with their eyes open. All the way, and remember. How do you stand it? All of it, at once, in order, for always?
I am told there is a gold circle in your sky that gives light and heat and is never quite looked at. Is it a candle? Does it ever gutter? Who tends it?
There are creatures with white wool, someone told me. Walking clouds with faces, who eat the green. I love white wool. I cannot picture a thing that grows it by itself and wanders off.
Green. I have seen it twice. Once on a Weft's sleeve, once in a hanging-garden pot that wasn't supposed to grow. It frightened me more than a ghast. It looks so alive.
Do you have ghasts up there? No? Then what do you do with the people who cry too long? ...Ah. You don't know, either. It is a relief, in a way.
I am told your people lie down flat, on their backs, in a room with a door. How strange, to lie flat. How strange, to be so sure the floor will stay.
Outsiders who come down here carry so many things. Swords, torches, bread. As if you were afraid of being asked who you are, and having to prove it.
Tell me one good thing from your world. Just one. I will keep it in my pod.

replies.text: Water falling for nothing and no one. I will keep that. Thank you. I will dream of it, and wake wet and happy.
Bread! Something warm you can break in two and share. Yes. I will keep that.
*very softly* Then it is the right one. Keep them close. Mind the weather.

lines.text: I should like to see a sheep before I fade. Or a field. Or a roof that forgot to be a roof. It is a long way up, I am told. I can float, but I don't think I am that kind of lantern.
I wonder whether your people have a Weeping Hall of their own somewhere I haven't heard of. A place to put your tears. Not a pool, perhaps. Some other shape. I hope so.
I asked a Withren once what your world is like. 'Loud,' he said, 'and green, and full of people who have never lost a name.' I think he was jealous.
It must be odd, going between there and here. Do you leave bits of yourself behind? A warm bit? A quiet bit? I would keep an eye out, if I were you.
If it is true that outsiders make Withers where you come from... I will say nothing against you. Only that you are a good deal gentler down here than your world's reputation.
I wonder whether your wounds close by themselves up there. Mine don't, not without a drop. A wound that closes alone... I would call that a miracle, and miss my work.
Do you have songs up there? Of course you do. I hope a few are slow. I could hum something slow from your world and keep it, if you teach me one verse.
From the perch I sometimes think I see your portal's glow, far off, a purple smudge on the edge of the smoke. A door to the roof that forgot. I look at it a long while.
Take me with you, once, for a short visit. Not to stay. Only to see the thing with no roof. I would float low and not say a word. And I would be back before my name wore off.
Whatever is up there, you carry some of it down with you. I can feel it in how you crouch. A kind of lightness that doesn't belong to the Nether. Keep it. It is good for us.
Is it true your sky has no roof? Where does the smoke go? Does it just leave? Doesn't it get lost?
I want to see a sheep. A cloud with legs! I'd name it. I'd name it something small and soft.
Does your world have vines? Do the little ones climb them? Do they fall? I fall off ours sometimes.
Mama says Piglins say the Overworld rots you. You don't look rotten! You look nice, and a bit tired.
If I come to your world I'll bring a candle. In case it's too bright. In case it isn't bright enough.

lines: Yes, but not as pictures. We dream the shape of those we cried away. No faces, only the warmth where they were. When we wake we hum, to see whether the warmth followed us out.
Some Ghastkin dream they have legs and walk. It is the most frightening thing a dream can do. They wake floating very high, laughing a little, and a bit sick.
Old names visit in dreams. They don't speak. They sit nearby, like guests who came to the wrong pod and are too polite to leave. I give them a corner. We share the warmth.
A Tearkeeper has a drop that dims dreams. It is kind, in its way, for those who dream too clearly of the one they let go. But it dims the good ones too, so it is rationed.
Once I dreamed a long dream of someone I had lost, and woke unable to tell whether I had remembered them or invented them. I went to the pool to ask. It said nothing. I have been grateful ever since.
In dreams we float on the ground and walk in the air. The delta turns inside out. You would laugh. The basalt hums back at you in your own voice.
No one wakes a sleeper by name. A hum, a nudge, a drop of warm sap on the chin. A name, even a current one, is a hook, and you do not pull a hook through a dream.
My dreams are full of half-finished things: veils, songs, a sentence that never lands. I wake mid-word and carry the missing end around for a while. It is strange company.

lines.text: I dreamed of you once. Do you want to know what you were doing?

replies.text: You were crouching, very low, holding a candle, and humming the wrong tune. Terribly. Perfectly. I woke smiling.
Wise. Dreams told aloud lose their edges. I will keep it folded.

lines: I think the ghasts dream. Perhaps that is what the crying is: a long dream that won't end, the sleeper trying to say the thing and never finishing. I try not to think it. I think it often.
A candle is left lit in the hammock room for the dreamers' sake. If the first thing you see on waking is a flame, you remember you are in the Eave and not in a corridor of forgetting.
I like the dreams where nothing happens. Smoke, rocking, a faint ringing. I wake well rested, like a pod after the chains stop swinging.
Sometimes I dream I am a child again, and my eyes are open, and the delta is violet. I wake with them shut, and lie there trying to open them. Only a little. Only to see.
We don't tell dreams at the Hall. It is the one place a dream shouldn't be spoken. The pool takes them, and the pool has enough to forget.
A dream you can't remember is called a guest. A dream you can is called a lodger. We prefer guests. Lodgers want feeding.
If a Ghastkin tells you they never dream, they do. They have only lost the habit of hearing them. It is all right. The dreams don't mind. They sit at the foot of the hammock and wait to be asked.

lines.text: A Songwarden hums a quiet line outside a sleeper's door, no words, just enough to say the song is still there. It is said to stop bad dreams. I think it only stops loneliness, which is more useful.
At the perch we nap standing, with one ear hooked on the smoke. I dream of a bell that doesn't ring. I wake and listen, and it still isn't ringing. That is how I know all is well.
My dreams are made of thread. Lines, loops, knots. I wake with my fingers working. Sometimes there is a whole seam done in my sleep. Nobody has ever found it. I like to think it exists somewhere.
I dream of full racks. Every vial brimming, and the clear light of them. I wake and check the shelves. They are never full. I am always glad, and then, a little, sorry.
I dream of floors so clean they are like mirrors. I look in, and nobody is there. I wake and sweep, rather fast, to be sure the ash is still falling.
When I dream of the pool, you are sometimes at its edge, crouching. You don't speak. You look at the water as if you were deciding. In the dream I always say: not yet. Not yet. You always agree.

loved.text: Oh. A bottle. An empty one. Do you know how rare it is for someone to give us room for a tear instead of asking for one?
Water. Real water, and nobody had to cry for it. I'm going to sit and look at it for a long while.
Oh. For me? I'll keep this in my pod, right where the blue light falls. Thank you, quietly and very much.
This is a kind thing. I can tell you chose it. Things that are chosen weigh differently.
*the closed eyes crease, nearly a smile* You've been asking about us. Haven't you. Sly thing.
For me? FOR ME? Sorry. Too loud. *whispers* For me? Thank you!
It's the best thing anyone ever gave me! I'm going to show {neighbour} and then hide it so they can't have it.
White wool. Soft as smoke, and it stays where you put it. I have only ever seen it once. Please say I may keep it close. I will sleep with my face in it.
It's a cloud! A small one! It stays when I squeeze it! Mama, MAMA, look! ...Shh. Sorry. Look, quietly.
A soul lantern. Blue light in a cage of iron. You have brought the exact thing I would have asked for, if I ever asked. I will hang it where it can see the pool.
A blue light I can carry! I'll never be lost in the smoke! I'll never be lost anywhere!
A white candle, the kind we light at a Letting-Go. Is this a hint? I would rather it weren't. I would rather it were simply a candle, and I will take it that way.
A candle. Just a candle. It is the best gift I have had in a long stretch, because it means nothing but light. I will leave it burning for the next one who sneaks by.
A lily of the valley. I have never seen one, but I know the shape from the Weft's cloth: small bells on a green stem. It rings, in a way. Look, it's nodding at me.
A flower! A real, small, white one! Does it ring? It rings. I can hear it in my chest!
An empty bottle again. Come now, you will spoil me. I will hang it by the window and let it be a room for the smoke.
A bottle, from you, who know what a bottle means here. That is what makes it a gift. I will keep it empty. We will both know why.
A whole bucket of water, and nobody had to be let go for it. I am going to hold it a while without touching the surface, so it stays as still as I would like to be.
You carry water into the Nether and it doesn't vanish? Show-off. May I look? Only look. I won't drink. Not even a sip.
I will never be able to repay this. I will try, in small ways, over a long time. Watch for them. They will be quiet.
Oh, you have turned my knees to ash. I need to sit on the gallery and hold this a while. Do come and sit. We needn't talk.
You choose well, every time. I begin to think you listen. It is rare. It is rarer than gold. Don't tell the Piglins.
Dear, dear one. Look what you have done: my hands are doing the thing they only do for good news. They are flapping. I can't stop. Let me flap.
I will put this on the shelf beside the vials. Not as a tool. As a reminder that someone brought me a gift for no reason. It is better medicine than most.
A song is coming out of this. A short one. Three notes of thanks, and a fourth I will keep quiet. Thank you.
I will mend something in your honour. I don't know what. Something small, a strap, something you wouldn't notice but would feel, as a little extra strength.
I will set this on the perch and look at it between scans of the sky. It will be the only thing up there that isn't a threat. I am touched. Truly.
I will put it where the ash can't reach: a clean shelf, a clean cloth. You have given me a thing worth sweeping for.
The beads on my circlet will chime for this. Hear it? A single small ring. It does that when I am moved. I give it to you, in return.
My hood is trembling. I can't help it. It does that. Please look away while I settle.

liked.text: Roots! The hanging garden will be pleased. Well. As pleased as roots get. They mostly dangle.
That's nice. Truly nice. The garden pods will want it, if I let them have it. I might not.
Thank you. I'll find a place for it. Somewhere low, where you'd see it if you came crouching by.
Mm. Yes. This will do something useful, or something pretty. I haven't decided which.
Ooh! Can I keep it in my pod? I'm keeping it in my pod. Thank you!
Weeping vines! For the children's climb! They will wear out the old ones by growing. Thank you. I will hang you from my gallery and call it yours.
Soul soil, for the hanging pots. The roots grow with a sigh in it. I like that. I will put a pinch in each pot and name them after you, quietly.
A feather. Light enough to lose, and I would rather not lose it. I will tuck it into my cord. Whenever I float, I will feel held up by something.
A snowball! Cold and round and gone as soon as it is warm. We have nothing like it. I will hold it until it isn't there any more, and call it practice for goodbyes.
White carpet. I will lay it on the gallery, where the ash will settle on it. The Sweeper will curse me. I will be so pleased.
A soul torch! A little blue flame no bigger than a thought. I will set it by the gallery rail and tell people it has always been there.
A pale blue candle. The colour of a pod when somebody inside is home. I will light it for no one, only so the colour has something to do.
Blue glass! The colour of the Hall windows when the pool is still. I will hold it up and look through it. Everyone will look blue. It will suit them.
Warped roots, teal and bitter. I will steep some and give the rest to the hanging garden. The pots are fussy, but they will make an exception for you.
It's nice! I like nice! I'll keep it in my pod and not tell anyone, and tell everyone.
A feather! Does it fly by itself? Can I float it? Watch, watch, I'll float it!
That is thoughtful. You have been paying attention to the Eave. Most people only see the smoke.
Thank you. I will find a use for it. If I can't, I will find a feeling for it, and that is even better.
A small gift, a warm one. I will set it on the shelf, between the candle and the thing I don't remember getting.
A gift from a visitor. We keep those near the door, so we see them when we go out and think: someone came.
I will find a place for this in the hem of something. Gifts live well in hems. Nobody has ever looked for one there.
I will keep it in the tear store, near the racks. Not near a vial, only near. It makes the room feel less like a promise and more like a pantry.
I will hum to it a little. Not a real song, only a note to let it know it is welcome. That is how we settle new things.
I will keep it off the floor. A gift is the one thing I never sweep. I would sweep around it for ever.
On the perch it goes, between me and the sky. Whichever I look at first tells me how the watch is going. This time, the gift. A good watch.
You did not need to. Thank you. The Eave notices when someone doesn't need to.
My veil flutters for it. Don't look, it is a little embarrassing. It does that when I am pleased. I have never been able to stop it.

neutral.text: Oh. Thank you. I don't know what it's for, but I'll keep it near the candles. Everything looks meant in candlelight.
How strange. Is this what your world is made of? Thank you. I'll think about it.
A gift is a gift. I'll find a reason for it. I'm good at finding reasons. It's most of what I do.
What is it? Is it alive? It's not alive. Thank you anyway! I'll show {neighbour}.
Bread. A cake of ground grass, baked in a fire. I have heard of it. May I smell it? ...It smells like someone's home. I will keep it, and try not to think whose.
A little round thing with a hand that creeps. Does it count the candle for you? What a patient thing. It ticks like a hall full of mourners. I will listen to it a while.
It points the way home? Mine is the Eave, and I would feel it blindfold. But a needle that is always sure is the opposite of us. I will keep it, to be reminded.
Words, bound. We have none of that. We have songs. I can't read it. I will leave it open on the gallery and let the smoke try.
A bright hard stone. Pretty, for a stone. It doesn't weep, though, and I prefer things that do. Still, I will hang it where the blue light falls and see what it makes of it.
Green! A tiny green thing, and hard. It frightened me for half a breath. Then I looked again and decided it was only a leaf that had forgotten to wilt.
A black lump. For the soul-fire, perhaps? We burn very little. But I will find a use. Even a sad lump can hold up a shelf.
A red fruit. Round, with a smell like water. I will leave it for the children, who will stare at it for ages, and then perhaps bite it.
A lead! For an Ashbell, how thoughtful. Not for me, though. I am not a bell. I will keep it for when one drifts by and needs a friend.
A torch. Orange fire on a stick. Thank you, but it makes the pods squint. I will put it in a bucket by the door for guests who arrive carrying fire.
A stick. Hm. A stick! I will... prop something. Or sit with it and think about all the trees it came from. Thank you, I think.
Something that had a face. Thank you for your kindness. Please let me hold it away from my chest, and I will find someone with a different appetite.
Cold metal, and heavy. We don't shape it. The Magmari might. I will set it aside to pass on. A long way for a lump to travel.
A bone. Withren work, or Weft needles in the making. I will hold it quietly and not ask how you came by it. Thank you.
Is this meant to mean something? Whether it does or not, it means someone thought of me. That is the part I will keep.
I don't know what it is for. You do, don't you? You are smiling inside your hood. Tell me next time. Or don't, and let me guess.
I will turn it over in my hands and find its seam. Everything has a seam. When I find this one, I will know what it wanted to be.
A new thing! I will check it for threat first. It passes. It is merely strange. I will set it on the perch among the other strange things.
I will put it in the store, away from the vials. It is not a tear. It is a gift. The two must never be confused, or I will heal someone with a spoon.
I will learn its sound. Everything has a sound if you are patient. Tap, scrape, drop. This one is going to be a quiet one, I think.
Where shall I put it? On the floor it would be swept, on the shelf it would be dusted. Nothing is safe from me. I will simply hold it.
Into the folds of my veil it goes, where I keep the things I am not sure about. There is quite a collection in there already.
Into my hood it goes. Don't worry, I have room. I carry a surprising amount in there. Mostly worry. Some candle ends.
Is it for eating? Is it for wearing? Is it for being scared of? I'll find out later. Thank you!

disliked.text: Fire in a little ball. No. Thank you, but no. Take it well away from the pods.
A bow. You've brought a bow to me. ...I'll pretend I didn't see it, and you'll take it home.
*drifts back a little* Please put that away. Things like that are why we float so high.
I know you didn't mean anything by it. Outsiders never mean anything by it. That's rather the trouble.
Mm. No. Some things don't belong anywhere near a Ghastkin. I think you knew that.
Eww. That's a hurting thing. Mama says never touch hurting things. I'm not touching it. You touch it. Away.
Gunpowder. The smell of other people's last mistakes. Please carry it far from the pods.
That is a loud thing. A very loud thing, waiting to be one. Take it away from the pillars. If a chain should crack because of that... please. Away.
A bit of Weft net. I can feel it from here. My arms want to rise. Please put it where I can't see it, and then I will be able to come down.
A horn. Even a small one. The noise it could make... the pods would swing. I would rather not know what note it holds. Take it away, kindly.
A skull. A Hollowed skull. Where did you... no. I don't want to know. Put it away. Three of those and the whole delta forgets how to hum.
Gold. Bright and loud. I know it is meant as a kindness elsewhere. Here it makes my arms go up. Please wrap it in something dark and keep it far.
A crossbow. You have brought one into the Eave. I know you wouldn't use it. But my body doesn't know that, and I have already drifted up three arm-lengths.
A sword. Is it for me? It is not for me. Put it away, please. I will look at you while you do, so you know I trust you more than the sword.
That is a very pretty blade. I would rather it were pretty at home. Here it only reminds me what pretty things are for. Away, please.
An arrow. Small, light, and it ends everything. Take it out of the pod's light, please. I don't want it to see us.
Oh. I can tell what that is without being told. Please let me keep my distance a moment and breathe.
I don't think you meant it. But the Eave has a long memory for things like that, even if we are poor at remembering people. Take it away.
From you? You, of all people. It is all right. I will assume it is a mistake, and you will assume I have forgotten. Neither is quite true.
I don't know you well enough to be hurt. So I will be polite. Put it away and we will start over, softly.
You know me better than this, I think. I will call it a slip, and you will call it one too, and we will never speak of it.
I have healed what things like that have done. I would rather not hold one. Keep it from the racks.
It will make a noise of its own, that thing. I could not bear to compose around it. Put it where it can't be sung to.
I mend what these do. I do not welcome them to the table. Please take it. I have too many stitches that were once its fault.
I sweep up after things like that. Please don't give me more to sweep. Take it away, and I will sweep your footprints out of the doorway and we will pretend.
At my post that sort of thing is the enemy. You are not. But it is in your hand. I hope you can see my problem.
That's the kind of thing Piglins have! Mama says if I see one I go up, up, up. I'm going up. Bye.
I'm going to hide in the vines now. You can come and get me when it's gone, all right? ...Is it gone yet?
It's shiny, but it feels like a shout. Please put it away. I don't want to hear it any more.

again.text: You've already given me something. Let me hold that one a while first. One gift at a time, or I'll start expecting them.
Again? You're very sweet. Save it, and come back with it later, so I have something to look forward to.
No, no, I'm still deciding where the last one goes. Keep that for now.
You gave me one already! I haven't finished being happy about it yet.
You have been generous already. Hold on to the rest. I would like to be a little in your debt for a while. It gives me a reason to be good.
One at a time, please. Gifts should be like tears: given properly, once, and then left alone to settle.
I have not finished admiring the last one. If you hand me another, I will have to put the first down, and I don't want to. Come back when I have had my fill of it.
A second so soon! Hush, hush. You will spoil the first by crowding it. Keep this in your pocket until the first has had time to grow.
I can't take a second. Not because I don't want it, but because I would start to expect it, and expecting is a slow way to become a ghast.
Give me this one next time. I will look forward to it. Looking forward is a nice thing to have in the pocket.
You keep trying. I like that about you. But no. My arms are full of the first one, and so is my chest.
You would give me the whole delta if I let you. I won't let you. Not yet. Hold it for me a while.
A second gift is like a second drop: it makes the first wonder if it was enough. I will stay with one, thank you.
I am still singing the first. A song only has room for so many thank-yous. Come back when it ends, in a verse or two.
I am still mending a place for the last one. Don't hand me another, or I will have to make two places, and I haven't enough thread.
My hands are full of the first, and I can't sweep with a gift in one hand. Another and I would have to sit down. I am tempted. Resist.
I am on watch, and my hands are busy with the last gift and the sky. Give me the next when I am off the perch. I will be easier to thank.
My veil is already fluttering from the last one. Another and I would float away. Keep it, and hand it over after I have landed.
My hood is still warm from the last one. Give me another and it might catch. Keep it. Let me cool down a little.
You gave me one already! I'm still looking at it! I have to look at it more! You can't give me another yet!
Mama says you shouldn't take two things. She says it makes the second one lonely. Hold on to it. I'll take it next time.
Next time, all right? I like looking forward. It's almost the same as having it, but with a bit of fizz.
I am saving myself for the next one. And I promise to be surprised again. I am good at it.
Not now. I am still deciding which window the first one goes in. It is a big decision, and I take big decisions slowly.
You must not spoil me. I am easy to spoil. I am made of ash-silk and good intentions.
That is very kind. But it is soon. Let the first one settle between us before we add to it.

empty.text: Your hand is empty. That's all right. Sometimes the empty hand is the gift. There's no weapon in it, for one.
Nothing? Good. I mean, thank you for nothing. That came out wrong. No, it came out right.
Empty-handed and quiet. That's how we visit each other, too.
There's nothing in your hand! Is it invisible? Can I hold it?
Your hand is empty and your steps are quiet. I would call that a good gift too. Don't tell the Piglins how little it takes.
Nothing in your hand, and nothing behind your back, I suppose. I won't check. I trust the way you stand.
No gift? Good. Then there is no awkwardness. Sit with me instead.
An open palm with nothing in it. In the Eave that means 'I came for you.' I will take it, and think kind things about it.
I do like a visit that asks nothing of my shelves. Come, sit, hold your hands in your lap. They look well there.
Not a thing in your hand! You can't know how restful that is to see. I will be thinking about empty hands for a while.
Nothing to give, nothing to take. We are even. Isn't that the nicest way to be?
You come empty and leave full. I notice. I also notice you have learned to do it without a smirk.
I used to wait for the clink in your pack. Now I wait for the quiet where it isn't. I think that is friendship.
Empty-handed, and not very sure of yourself. Don't worry, we are a good lot to be unsure in front of.
An empty hand is the best patient. Nothing to heal, nothing to forget. Come in, sit, be well.
An empty hand and a quiet mouth. You would make a fair chorus. We could use some hush in the verse.
Nothing to patch, nothing to hem. It is restful to look at someone without a single loose thread.
No gift, but hardly any footprints, either. You are a clean visitor. I wish I could say that of more people.
Empty hands and a low head. You would pass any watch I have ever kept. Welcome, welcome.
My veil lies still for you. That is high praise. It flutters at gifts, and rests for friends.
My hood sits easy on my head when you are near. That is a better thing than a gift, I think. Please stay long.
Nothing? That's all right! You can hold my hand instead! ...No? All right. I'll hold the air near it.
No gift? That's all right. You came! That's the best gift. Mama says that, but I really mean it.
Your hands are so big and empty. I could fit a lot in there. Next time bring a feather! Feathers are what I'm asking for now.
I don't mind. I would rather you came empty than loaded with something we would both have to be polite about.
Sometimes the best thing to bring is yourself, softly. You do that very well.
No gift? Excellent. I have been dreading how much I would feel I owed you.

levelup.text: You keep coming up quietly. I've stopped counting your steps. That's a kind of trust, you know.
Here. A candle from my pod. Light it somewhere you come home to, and think of someone hanging under a basalt eave, being glad.
Lantern-kin. Take this light. It's the kind that doesn't burn. Every one of us carries one, so the others can find us in the smoke.
This tear was cried properly, for someone I no longer remember. It closes wounds. Use it on yourself, not on a grudge. I'll know.
When you die, and outsiders always do, I'll cry for you. Once, properly, all the way. Here, my vial. Keep it empty. It's for that tear, and it will wait.
You're my friend now. I decided. I didn't even ask Mama.
Here, this is from my secret pot in the hanging garden. Don't tell anyone where you got it.
I'm giving you my candle. I'll get another. Now when you're far away you'll have a bit of the Eave.
You're the quietest grown-up I know. Quieter than the grown Ghastkin, even. I'm going to tell everyone. Quietly.
When I learn to cry, I'm saving my first proper one for you. Not soon! You have to get really, really old first. Promise?
Soft of foot. That is what we would call you, if you were ours. You make no noise when you leave, which is the best compliment we have for a visitor.
You came back. People don't, usually. They come once, shout, and take what they came for. You came back quietly, and sat. That counts for a great deal.
I have begun to know your step in the ash. A small thing. But a great deal of what is known between us starts with the small things.
Here, a little root from my own pot. It will grow in any soul soil, if you hum to it. That is the whole secret, and the only one I have.
You're nice! You don't shout and you don't shoot! That's two things most people can't do. Mama says three makes a friend.
Come under the eave, out of the smoke. You are one of the few with leave to sit on the gallery and watch the Ashbells. Don't tell them. They get proud.
Here, a pinch of soul soil from the hanging pot. It is the dust of a place where something grew against the odds. Think of it when you plant anything.
I have left the ladder down for you. That is the Ghastkin invitation. Please don't make a fuss about it.
I told {neighbour} about you. Not much. Only that you crouch well and don't touch the vials. They said, 'We'll see.' That is high praise in the Eave.
You can come up to the gallery! I made you a spot, right next to mine. It has the best view of the third pillar, and I won't let anyone else sit in it.
Lantern-kin. We say it of someone whose light we would know in the smoke. I would know yours. It is small, steady and a bit crooked. I like it.
Here, bottles for your trouble. Keep them uncorked. A bottle with its cork out is a window.
I hummed your step to the Songwarden, and the Songwarden nodded. That is as close as an outsider gets to being sung.
From now on, when the chains creak, I will think of you. Not sadly. Only the way you think of a window left open.
You're lantern-kin! I get to say it, and I say it a lot! Lantern-kin, lantern-kin! Mama says stop. I won't.
I knew it was you from three pillars away. Your step has a little hitch in it, like a held breath. I have grown fond of the hitch.
A flake of quartz from the Hall's wall. They say quartz keeps whatever hush you put into it. Put in a good one.
You have done something odd: you have made me less careful. I leave my hatch open when you visit now. That is trust, or foolishness. I choose trust.
If you are ever lost in the smoke, hum, and I will hum back. I have never offered that to anyone. It costs me nothing and it is worth everything.
I can tell it's you by your step! It goes crunch, no sound, crunch. Nobody else has that. I'm going to tell the whole Eave. Quietly.
Cried for. That is the last name we give a friend. It means that if you are lost, someone will do the hard thing. I have done the counting. I have room for you.
Take this. Crying obsidian, the kind that forms where many of us have wept over the same stone. It holds the wet of a sorrow. Keep it for when you need a place for yours.
When I next take a name, I will ask to keep one thing from this one: the memory of your step. If the cry takes everything else, let that be what is left.
White wool, from my own hammock, the softest thing I own. It is for you, to wrap round the cold part of you that outsiders always carry. You know the one.
You're cried for! I'm supposed to say it later, when I'm grown. But I'm saying it now so you can't forget. Cried for, cried for, cried for.

farewell.text: Go softly. The ash will cover your footprints, and I'll pretend they were never there. Unless you'd rather they were.
Drift well. Walk well, I mean. You know what I mean.
Come back quietly. I'll be here, or very near, or a little higher up.
Mind the Piglins on your way. And the Weft nets. And the edges. And yourself.
Goodbye for now. I don't cry over goodbyes. They aren't the kind that count.
{former} used to say goodbye with a song. I'll just say it. Goodbye. Be careful.
Go on. Don't die out there. I've only so many tears, and one of them has your name on it.
Take care of that skin. I'd rather not use a tear on you. I'd rather not choose what you forget.
I'll watch you go as far as the smoke allows. Then a little further, in my head.
Bye! Bye! Come back! Bring something! Or don't! Bye!
Wait, are you going? Walk squished all the way home, so nothing finds you.
Bye. I'm going to count your steps until I can't hear them. That won't take long. You're very quiet.
Keep that scratch dry and unlooked at. A scratch loves attention. Come back if it turns into a story.
If a wound ever feels like a memory, come straight back. The other kind of hurt I can't touch. I can only stand near it with a vial.
Mind the vials on your way out. Don't hurry; they feel it. Everything on a rack feels your hurry.
Nothing left my racks. Nothing ever does without a hum. Go well.
I put a drop in your cloak hem, a very small one, for luck. No, not for healing. Just in case. Don't say I did.
If I ever cry for you, you'll never know. That's the point of a good cry. Go and be unknowing for a long time.
The case on my back is lighter than when we met. That is the goodbye I like best. Go well, traveller.
Keep warm. A cold wound takes longer, and a long wound talks too much. Goodbye.
Go on. I'll wipe the rack where you stood. Not because you were unclean. I like to begin every goodbye fresh.
If you're bleeding when you reach wherever you're going, it wasn't me. Remember that. I only meant well.
Goodbye. I'll hum your leaving into the next verse. It won't be recognisable. It never is. That's why it lasts.
Take the rest between my verses with you. Nobody will miss it. I make a new one each time.
If you ever hear a low note and feel your shoulders drop, that's me. Probably. It's also the basalt. We sound alike.
The Song has a gap for every leaving. Yours is the shape of a boot. I'll leave it empty.
Go. I'll hold the fourth note until you're out of the delta. It's a long note to hold, so don't dawdle.
I'll hum quietly after you. Not to follow. Only to keep the smoke from closing over where you were.
I never say goodbye in a song. Songs end, and I find that unbearable. So: goodbye, with no tune. You'll manage.
Farewell. No hall, no echo out here. I'll send a note across the delta and see who answers. Maybe you. Don't answer.
The Song will go on without you in it. But I'll tuck a bar for you somewhere I can find it. Go well.
Goodbye. I wasn't singing, mind. If anyone asks, I was only breathing very precisely.
Mind that sleeve. It's holding on out of loyalty. Come back before it gives up.
Goodbye. I've left a very small knot in the air above the gallery. If you feel a tug as you go, that's it.
Stitches fray, friends don't. Well, friends do, but they're easier to re-sew. Go on.
Take care of your pack straps. I'd hate to meet them again as rags.
I put a bead in your pocket. Don't look. It isn't valuable. It's only mine, and now it's yours, and now you'll come back to return it.
Don't snag on anything. And if you do, don't tear. Come straight here and I'll unpick you.
I'll stitch a bit of the path closed after you, so nothing follows. A Mender's blessing. Crooked, but it holds.
Goodbye, goodbye. I've a long line of ropes waiting, and each one is sure it's the most urgent.
Go. Stay whole. And if you come back in pieces I won't be cross. I'll only be busy for a good long while.
Come back before the next fray. Not mine, yours. I can always tell when a person is about to need me.
Go on. I'll sweep your trail. No, don't look back; it takes more than a moment to be thorough.
